A central challenge in solving parabolic stochastic optimal control problems lies in the lack of access to the explicit form of the fourth derivative of the solution to the associated second-order parabolic stochastic partial differential equation (SPSPDE). To address this, the authors employ a decomposition of the law of the fourth derivative, which allows the problem to be recast as the sum of ten comparable, yet simpler, expectations.

Keywords: Finite element method; Monte-Carlo approximation; Particles; Particles with feedback; Rough data; Regularity; Decomposition of laws.

While a dipolar modulation in right ascension at energies above 8 EeV was previously identified as the most prominent signal within the [4,8] EeV and $E\geq 8$ EeV bins, we further investigate the highest-energy range by dividing it into three distinct intervals. Our results indicate that the dipole amplitude grows with energy above 4 EeV, a trend well-described by a power law with an index of $\beta=0.79\pm 0.19$. The dipole directions remain consistent with an extragalactic origin across all examined energies. Furthermore, our estimation of quadrupolar components reveals no statistical significance. Finally, we contextualize these findings against various models predicting the distribution of ultrahigh-energy sources and cosmic magnetic fields. This analysis serves as an essential foundation for the predictions of future cosmic ray experiments.

We characterize the matter distribution along the line of sight using the matter power spectrum and the two-point correlation function for both linear and nonlinear regimes. Utilizing the Fourier definition of the matter power spectrum, we derive an analytical expression for the two-point correlation function, which we validate via Monte-Carlo simulations. We demonstrate that the standard definition of the matter density contrast within fixed angular bins introduces bias into dipole estimates. To resolve the long-standing ambiguity regarding whether cosmic-ray observations reflect a magnetic or matter foreground, we analyze synthetic catalogs perturbed with realistic magnetic fields. The degree of dipolar modulation is found to be proportional to the integral of the matter power spectrum. By applying these methods to the isotropic synthetic Pierre Auger dataset, we successfully recover the dipole signal previously reported, along with estimates of its uncertainty. These methodologies will be employed in the analysis of the next-generation cosmic ray dataset.

Recent measurements from the Pierre Auger Observatory indicate a deficit of cosmic rays arriving from the plane of the Milky Way at energies above $10^{18}$ eV, an effect that becomes more pronounced at higher energies. We investigate whether ultra-heavy dark matter (DM) decaying into two cosmic rays can account for this anomaly. We examine the constraints imposed by the spectral index of the dipole, the energy spectrum of cosmic rays, and the angular two-point correlation function. This paper introduces a method for automatically detecting and counting 2-D spherical objects within a field of view when their orientation is indistinct. The approach relies on the statistical distribution of pixel gray-level values and was validated using two color imaging datasets: one featuring red blood cells and another containing tissue sections with tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (WSI patches). While the algorithm's performance is robust across varying object sizes and orientation ambiguities, it experiences notable drops in accuracy when object density is high or morphological variability is significant. Although the method currently operates with moderate computational speed, it offers several advantages over existing techniques. These benefits include the ability to handle overlapping and touchings objects, a lack of dependency on image color or contrast, and the avoidance of manually tuned parameters. The research was conducted under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy/National Nuclear Security Administration. Related work can be found in references [1–13]. The code is accessible at https://github.com/larssonlab/FL_counting_sphere.

Gbit/s optical on-off keying (OOK) system operating over 18.8 km of uncompensated submarine fiber in the South China Sea. The chromatic dispersion inherent in this cable length creates four spectral nulls within the 36 GHz bandwidth of the OOK signal, posing a significant barrier to achieving acceptable bit-error-rate (BER) performance. While a decision feedback equalizer (DFE) can effectively address these spectral nulls, it suffers from burst-error propagation caused by signal instability in the harsh submarine environment. Although a weighted DFE (WDFE) helps mitigate burst-error propagation, it fails to fully compensate for spectral nulls because it relies on only a subset of directly decided feedback symbols. Consequently, adding maximum likelihood sequence estimation (MLSE) after the WDFE allows for the simultaneous elimination of spectral distortions and the implementation of optimal detection. Compared to a joint DFE and MLSE approach, the combined WDFE and MLSE algorithm significantly suppresses burst-error propagation, yielding up to a 2.9 dB improvement in the Q factor and removing the BER floor phenomenon. Ultimately, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm effectively resolves burst-error propagation issues in this field-trial fiber-optic communication system.

We introduce an automatic dilation optimizer that reframes this challenge as weight pruning along the time axis, enabling the simultaneous learning of dilation factors and network weights within a single training phase. This approach achieves up to a 7.4x reduction in model size and a 3x decrease in inference latency on real System-on-Chip (SoC) hardware, all without sacrificing accuracy compared to non-dilated networks. Furthermore, our method generates a diverse collection of Pareto-optimal TCNs from a single initial model, surpassing manually designed solutions in both efficiency and performance. Evaluation across two distinct workloads demonstrates that our automatically optimized TCNs deliver superior results against both traditional networks and recently designed time-aware networks. The source code and test cases are accessible at https://github.com/yjhwng/dilation-optimizer.
Figure 1 illustrates that we can derive various Pareto-optimal Parameter-Efficiency (PE) curves from a single initial network using only 15 minutes of training time. These networks were automatically optimized to balance PE and efficiency (measured as system latency on SoC hardware), exceeding the efficiency of hand-crafted baselines. Our approach applies to any end-to-end learning method, including Modern Hopfield Networks (MHNs) and Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs). We focus on TCNs because their use case is the most relevant to practitioners and because they offer the greatest potential for efficiency gains through our technique. While we provide analysis of applying our method to other architectures in Section V-D, extending it to densely connected networks with many layers remains an open challenge for improving application to large-scale models.
Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) are powerful, convolution-based architectures capable of matching the performance of recurrent and transformer models on various tasks. By utilizing causal convolutions and dilated timelines, a small number of efficient operations can capture long-range dependencies that would require excessively many layers or a very wide filter in standard TCNs. However, manually configuring a TCN's dilated timeline is difficult and lacks clear guidance in current literature. While prior work has attempted to learn the timeline during training, these methods often require extensive experimentation to set reasonable search bounds, a process that is both time-consuming and lacks guidance on effective search spaces. The primary method for producing examples of non-trivial Zinbiel algebras involves using right symmetric algebras as pre-Lie algebras; consequently, the majority of known Zinbiel algebras arise from other construction methods. We provide a comprehensive list of all non-trivial Zinbiel algebras with dimension not exceeding 8. Furthermore, we prove that numerous familiar algebraic structures are incompatible with the Zinbiel identity, such as alternative algebras, left symmetric (pre-Lie) algebras, and Lie-admissible algebras. Notably, the only finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras over any field that also satisfy the alternative identity are trivial algebras. This result implies that popular non-associative algebras, including the Cayley algebra, cannot generate non-trivial Zinbiel algebras via the associator. Additionally, no Lie bracket can be elevated to a Zinbiel bracket. The paper concludes with remarks on the broader relationship between Zinbiel algebras and Lie admissibility. Regarding classification, the paper shows that almost all finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras are derived from pre-Lie algebras, with the sole exceptions being 2-dimensional algebras over fields of characteristic 2 and a specific family of 4-dimensional algebras defined over finite fields. Finally, we establish that almost all non-trivial finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras possess nilpotent powers equal to 2 or 3.

These analyses cover various centralities in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC. We report the first measurement of direct photon spectra and photon--hadron correlations in central Pb--Pb collisions at an average center-of-mass energy of 2.76 TeV using the ALICE detector at the LHC. We examine the invariant mass distribution of direct photons (from all hadrons) in the range 0.5 to 6 GeV/$c^2$ as a function of hadron transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$). We also determine the azimuthal angle distribution of all hadrons relative to the hardest jet (defined as the direction of the transversely moving photon) for photon $p_{\rm T}$ values up to 40 GeV/$c$. The hadron spectrum shifts to higher $p_{\rm T}$ in the presence of a direct photon, whereas the photon spectrum remains essentially unchanged when expressed in the hadron rest frame. ic foundations of Sahlqvist correspondence, unified correspondence theory offers robust tools for establishing correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantics and signatures, encompassing all logics defined by normal (distributive) lattice expansions ((D)LEs). Specifically, the ALBA algorithm, which is parametric for each (D)LE, effectively decides canonicity for the associated DLE formula and yields the canonical model in which the formula is valid. We introduce an adaptation of ALBA that targets the coalgebraic perspective on correspondence, utilizing the parametric pre-canonical models and inductive theory of DLEs to formulate ALBA's steps. This approach utilizes the finite algorithmic inductive depth of a DLE formula to delineate the relevant coalgebraic inductive and bi-inductive invariants, thereby ensuring that the resulting pre-canonical models maintain the specific DLE structure required by the original ALBA algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of this adapted algorithm to relational first-order logic (FOL), predicate HOLOGIC (pHOL), and continuous predicate logic (CPL), illustrating how ALBA's classic steps function across these distinct logical frameworks. The resulting adapted ALBA algorithm is fully specified in the appendix. A key benefit of this adaptation is its ability to generate pre-canonical models that are more structured than those in the generic setting, offering a novel method for defining functors and natural transformations to represent relations, predicates, and continuous functions, respectively. These tools can be harnessed to prove the continuity of other logical constructs, such as modal operators, within a structured environment. We exhibit the application of this method to classical modal logic and its extension with supremum operators, specifically modal dependence logic (MDL). Additionally, we explore the potential for adapting the adapted ALBA algorithm to other logics, including probabilistic and non-monotonic frameworks. The source code for the adapted ALBA algorithm is available at https://github.com/brintrinal/ALBA-for-Pre-canonical-Models.

We define an abstract framework that unifies a wide range of probabilistic logics, including one-shot probabilistic logic (PSPL), bounded probabilistic logic (BPL), probabilistic first-order logic (PFOL), probabilistic Horn clauses (PHC), and their probabilistic temporal and fixed-point extensions. Our framework relies on functorial semantics and probabilistic lattice operations, encompassing both measure-based and distributional approaches. We demonstrate how to construct the associated ALBA algorithm for any logic within this framework.

While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, it is equally significant to formulate theories for handling instances that violate certain dependencies. Concerning missing values, we do not presuppose their existence; rather, a missing value is considered to exist only if it can be inferred from the table's functional dependencies.

We present a formal framework where each table tuple is assigned one of four truth values: true, false, inconsistent, or unknown. We demonstrate that this framework facilitates the study of critical issues such as consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality assessment. Furthermore, the findings from this study may aid in refining the representation, reasoning, and manipulation of real-world incomplete tables. Additionally, the concepts, notations, and outcomes established in this paper could serve as a foundation for future research, particularly regarding the construction of transformation rules for table instances, similar to those used for relational schemas. Notably, we contend that reasoning about missing values in tables is as complex as, if not more so than, missing values in functional dependencies, as the former encompasses the latter. Finally, we contend that our approach is distinct from, and not a subset of, three-body uncertainty, as our method does not assume that table rows are uncertain.

AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of potential extensions. This work serves as the companion piece to "Dynamic PARX Models for Count Time Series." This section outlines the preliminary material regarding unobserved linear state models and score-driven mechanisms that underpin the TV-PARX framework.

The primary objective of this section is to examine the asymptotic behavior of the TV-PARX model under conditions where the time-varying parameters are driven by a latent affine process. To achieve this, we adopt the score-driven approach to parameter estimation, highlighting its computational efficiency and robust forecasting capabilities, as well as its ability to capture complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks in count data. Specifically, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the resulting time series estimator.

The score-driven approach to dynamic linear models was pioneered by Shephard and Smith (1990) for unobserved linear state models and later advanced by Bauwens and Druyts (2017). Building on these foundations, the dynamic linear TV-PARX model was developed in Crepi (2021). Additional related models include the dynamic GARCH (Engle and Mele (2017)) and nonlinear GARCH (Crepi (2022)) models, which address the full spectrum of time-series dynamics for both count and general data.

For the specific case of the TV-MARX model, where the time series follows a marginal Geometric distribution, we previously proved the consistency and asymptotic normality of the score-driven estimator using classical methods (Crepi (2020)). a novel object representation that encodes points and relative poses between an object and a target (like a robot gripper or hanging rack) using category-level descriptors. Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for a pose whose descriptor matches the observed demonstration. NDFs are trained in a self-supervised manner through a 3D auto-encoding process that avoids the need for expert-labeled keypoints. Additionally, their SE(3)-equivariant nature ensures robust generalization across all 3D translations and rotations. We validate this method in both simulation and on a real robot using only 5-10 demonstrations, showing that performance generalizes across different object instances and 6-DoF poses, significantly outperforming recent baselines relying on 2D descriptors. Project website: https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/. Project video: https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/video.mp4. Supplementary material includes additional experiments and analysis.

We present a straightforward yet potent technique for enhancing the generalization of point-based neural representations across both intraclass (different poses) and interclass (distinct objects) variations. Specifically, we train our neural encoder to be invariant to rotations and translations on the object's canonical coordinate system using only unaligned 3D data from a single category. This low-cost preprocessing step yields substantial improvements for downstream tasks, including semantic segmentation, pose estimation, and classification. By promoting the use of 3D neural descriptors, this approach facilitates tasks that were previously dependent on supervised pretraining on large-scale point cloud datasets such as ModelNet40.

We propose a unified framework for simultaneously inferring the pose and scale of an object from a single monocular image and applying a learned 3D mesh to satisfy that pose. This is achieved through two main contributions: (1) interpreting neural volume representations as deformed control points to create a parameterization that accommodates scale variation, and (2) training the network to predict both descriptor values and their gradients with respect to the neural volume. Consequently, the neural volume can be interpreted as a learnable 3D mesh. We demonstrate that this simultaneous inference approach delivers strong results across three object categories with significant geometric variability—beds, chairs, and human faces—outperforming several existing baselines.

As the ILC's potential construction date approaches, it is crucial to review the design and technology decisions finalized during the Design-Building (DBD) phase, updating them based on recent technological advancements. stars within the high-metallicity globular cluster Tononzintla~2 (Ton~2), utilizing high-resolution near-infrared spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment II (APOGEE-2) survey, specifically as part of the bulge Cluster APOgee Survey. Our study examines chemical abundances across various elemental groups—including light, odd-Z, $\alpha$, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements—based on high signal-to-noise spectra of seven giant members. The resulting mean cluster metallicity is determined to be [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$, showing no signs of intrinsic metallicity dispersion. Ton~2 displays a standard $\alpha$-enrichment pattern consistent with other high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters, mirroring trends observed in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. However, we detect a significant spread in nitrogen abundance ($>0.87$ dex) and a substantial population of nitrogen-enriched stars. Considering Ton~2's relatively high metallicity, these nitrogen levels far exceed typical Galactic averages, confirming the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon; the cluster also hosts stars with low, first-generation nitrogen abundances. Additionally, we identify a [Ce/Fe] abundance spread in Ton~2 that correlates with nitrogen enhancement, suggesting that \textit{s}-process enrichment was likely driven by an intermediate-mass star from an external population, as suggested by recent modeling of NGC~6380. Finally, the simultaneous occurrence of nitrogen enrichment and [Ce/Fe] variability in Ton~2 offers additional support for the super-AgB star scenario in high-mass, high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters, with the number of required intermediate-mass stars depending on the specific mass and metallicity thresholds for these observations. We encourage the integration of tonozintla~2 into multi-dimensional dynamical models to explore how these chemical findings constrain the formation and evolution of Ton~2, as this could provide novel insights into the formation of both Ton~2 and the Milky Way. The dependence between climate change and the frequency of extreme events—a topic of significant scientific and political relevance—remains insufficiently precise in public discourse. This discourse often relies on metaphors that impede a clear understanding of complex phenomena by substituting them with emotionally charged imagery. Meanwhile, mathematical terminology offers a framework for accurate expression but frequently lacks the necessary context to be accessible or meaningful to a general audience. Consequently, there is a definitive requirement for a nuanced vocabulary that accurately reflects scientific facts while remaining comprehensible to the broader public. Although this statement is straightforward, actualizing it proves to be a considerably more difficult endeavor.

While the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has grown significantly, it has concurrently become harder to navigate. Although prior proposals have addressed this challenge, they remain underutilized in practice, likely due to the absence of an automated system for integrating them into the archive's dependency structure. This report investigates these problems and related topics in depth, presenting both qualitative and quantitative experimental findings that support a set of practical recommendations for enhancing the archive's usability, specifically by employing a multi-level organization scheme.

Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter, CNNs regress intermediate features like 3D coordinates, semantic keypoints, or virtual control points in the first stage, with object pose subsequently determined through correspondence constraints derived from these cues. This paper focuses on refining the postprocessing stage of a two-stage pipeline by integrating projection grouping and correspondence learning to estimate poses in challenging scenarios. First, a local patch-based method predicts projection heatmaps representing the confidence distribution of 3D bounding box corners. A proposed projection grouping module then eliminates redundant local maxima across heatmap layers. Rather than directly applying the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithm to 2D-3D correspondences, multiple correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and their neighborhoods, then ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Finally, high-confidence correspondences are selected to determine the object's pose. Extensive experiments across three public datasets show that the proposed framework surpasses several state-of-the-art methods. Notably, on the SUN RGB-D dataset, the proposed scheme achieves a mean Average Precision (MP@0.5) of $93.70\%$, compared to $89.93\%$ for the second-place baseline. Despite certain modeling constraints, Bond-Based Peridynamics (BB-PD) remains a popular choice for numerical simulations, largely due to its ease of implementation, physical clarity, and stability. Peridynamics (PD) offers a robust framework for simulating the initiation and progression of cracks, as well as separating materials. Bond-Based Peridynamics (BB-PD) serves as a crucial subset of PD, valued for its physical transparency, ease of use, and computational efficiency. This review provides a detailed introduction to BB-PD, beginning with an overview of Peridynamics (PD) and its derivation from micro-scale physics, followed by an in-depth exploration of the BBD sub-theory. The review also discusses the formulation of bond-based peridynamic models for fluids, examining the implications of kernel structure, kernel type, and kernel linearity. Furthermore, the paper reviews related bond-based peridynamic applications, including the simulation of crack initiation and propagation, fracture patterns in concrete, and comparing PD results with experimental data. Finally, future research directions are discussed. The content of this review is accessible to physicists, mathematicians, engineers, and scientists generally. The primary contribution of this review is the detailed discussion of peridynamic models for fluids and the in-depth analysis of the kernel structure in BB-PD.

Stanford University graduate students in fields such as computer science, electrical engineering, and operations research frequently formulate linear programming (LP) or mixed integer linear programming (MILP) models to address probabilistic scheduling and resource allocation issues involving discrete decisions and deterministic constraints. These models often omit stochastic constraints or objective functions to simplify formulation and improve computational speed, relying instead on a "feasibility check" or "duality gap" to identify infeasible or suboptimal solutions. This paper introduces a systematic method for explicitly incorporating random variables into LP and MILP formulations. The approach utilizes random matrices with nonnegative entries to constrain decision variables, creating applications useful for: (1) validating the results of standard solvers like Gurobi or CPLEX against randomly generated feasibility tests; (2) estimating the fraction of randomly generated matrices that are feasible given a specific set of decision variables; and (3) estimating the average or maximum energy of a system (e.g., a polymer) across random configurations, where energy is defined by the product of random bond or site energies and binary spin variables. The study demonstrates that these problems can be solved efficiently using Monte Carlo integration.

We analyze the evolution of equal-mass binary black holes embedded in pure dark matter with a short de Broglie wavelength. Matter evolution is examined across three distinct initial setups, and we clarify the often confusing term "quasi-stationary," which we define as a state that emerges after several orbital periods. Our simulation outcomes indicate that matter settles into a quasi-stationary dipolar configuration on a timescale of several orbits, ultimately determining the morphology of the final extraction phase. We also address challenges in achieving circular orbits when matter is present, as matter asymmetries between the black holes can distort these trajectories. Our findings show that the matter can become trapped in stable configurations around the binary, leading to significant accumulation by the time of extraction. This results in a substantial peak in the gravitational-wave spectrum caused by the scattering of dark matter by the binary. We conclude by offering a physical interpretation of the observed dynamics.

This study introduces a novel finite element method (FEM) simulation framework for modeling ultra-short pulse laser irradiation on biological tissues, specifically targeting melanin-containing layers. The model incorporates the acoustic wave equation to track pressure generation and propagation, as well as the heat conduction equation to simulate temperature distribution within the tissue. By accounting for the thermal expansion coefficient, specific heat capacity, and density variations based on local temperature, the coupled FEM simulation effectively replicates pressure waveforms, temperature profiles, and acoustic image characteristics. The results demonstrate that this approach accurately generates optical acoustic images of the pigment layer while simultaneously producing target-like pressure waves and temperature distributions.

of eigenvector centrality within multilayer networks that incorporate inter-layer constraints on node significance. This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. However, unlike the standard approach, our framework allows the adjacency relationships and the importance values of neighboring nodes to originate from different layers. Crucially, this capability is only partially addressed by current multilayer eigenvector centrality frameworks, which typically rely on inter-layer edges to model such dependencies. In our proposed model, constrained, layer-specific eigenvector centrality scores are determined by a system comprising independent eigenvalue problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, which can be solved efficiently through an interleaved power iteration algorithm. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, these calculated centrality scores offer significant insights into the core structural characteristics of multilayer networks. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of varying inter-layer dependency strengths on the resulting centrality metrics using empirical air route networks. This study is guided by the premise that the flexibility of our model in accommodating both independent and dependent adjacency patterns makes it a powerful framework for defining broader categories of multilayer centrality measures, whether related to eigenvector centrality or others. We conclude that the distinct features of our model—specifically the absence of necessitating inter-layer edges and the reduced structural complexity compared to multi-eigenvalue systems—make it a more streamlined and efficient solution for real-world applications. This work further serves to raise awareness that multilayer networks can be effectively analyzed without the need for dependent inter-layer connections. Finally, we emphasize that the distinct advantages and disadvantages of our model and its related multi-eigenvalue frameworks regarding the computation of constrained eigenvector centrality may inspire future enhancements in both structural analysis and algorithmic efficiency for multilayer networks.

In this paper, we derive the Dirac equation within $R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish its equivalence to the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime expressed via its conformally flat metric. Additionally, we introduce a novel method for solving the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime by employing the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. This approach contrasts sharply with the standard Heisenberg picture used in current literature, as wave functions in the Schr\"{o}dinger picture are formed by acting with de Sitter position operators on spinor eigenstates of the Poincar\'e algebra in the Heisenberg picture. We further show that the time-dependent spinor solutions of the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime satisfy the Pauli equation in conformally flat spacetime. We conclude by deriving the Green function of the Dirac equation from the Green function of the Pauli equation. As a byproduct, we demonstrate that the Dirac density of the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime is intimately linked to that of the Pauli equation in conformally flat spacetime via a conformal transformation. Our work thereby validates the physical significance of the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski spacetime. Throughout this study, $\hbar=c=1$.

By examining extensive families of four-dimensional Type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify potential generalized global symmetries and demonstrate how they are circumvented. A key component in these theories involves generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear interactions between axion fields and gauge field strength terms quadratic in topology, thereby disrupting a significant portion of global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can break any remaining residual symmetries. However, we show that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect, implying that the charged state spectrum forms an infinitely populated lattice. We also demonstrate that this lattice arises from the monodromy transformation acting on the moduli space boundary where the effective theory is defined. Ultimately, our analysis supports the conjecture that the lowest mass states constitute a generalized lattice, thereby eliminating generalized global symmetries in four-dimensional quantum gravity. This lattice structure is especially pertinent to recent proposals linking the Swampland to the geometry of the moduli space. Additionally, we provide evidence that these lattices contain charged states capable of stabilizing all light fields, thus preventing the emergence of global symmetries.

Recently, it was proposed that certain boundaries on the swampland conjecture can be characterized by generalized charged matter, which forms a lattice structure rather than representing conventional charged matter. By examining four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective theories, we validate this lattice construction. We demonstrate that the generalized charges are defined by a lattice and that the theory remains consistent provided there exists lattice momentum across the board within the spectrum of charged states. Furthermore, we find that the charge spectrum of the generalized lattice is governed by the geometry of the special Kähler manifold underlying the $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective theory. Specifically, the lattice is determined either by the torus fibers of the special Kähler manifold or by its dual torus fibers when the manifold admits a special Lagrangian fibration, as is the case for Calabi-Yau threefolds and heterotic K3^2/T^2 compactifications. In other scenarios, the generalized charges are built from an infinitely divided lattice, aligning with the idea that the lattice is ultimately defined by the spectrum of charged states. Our objective is to reduce both the quantity and intricacy of hardware and software elements that users must trust to resist adversarial attacks. We propose a multi-domain hardware architecture featuring statically partitioned, physically isolated trust domains. To facilitate this, we introduce a limited set of simple, formally verified hardware components that allow programs to obtain provably exclusive and simultaneous access to computation and I/O resources temporarily. To oversee this hardware, we developed OctopOS, an operating system built from mutually distrustful subsystems. We implemented a prototype of this system on a CPU-FPGA board, demonstrating that it incurs minimal hardware overhead compared to contemporary System-on-Chip (SoC) designs. For security-critical applications, our machine significantly lowers the required trust compared to standard Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) while maintaining satisfactory performance. For standard applications, performance remains comparable to that of legacy systems. Our research is accessible at https://github.com/rice-swo/OctopOS.

Recent advancements in hardware random number generation (RNG) have enabled hardware to produce truly random numbers. We examined how software can utilize hardware RNGs to generate secure cryptographic keys. To do so, we defined four criteria for "good" software usage of hardware RNGs for key creation. To aid in meeting these criteria, we developed a library offering high-level interfaces for such keys. To validate the approach, we applied it to two cases: deriving Wi-Fi passwords from a hardware RNG and generating OpenSSL keys. To ensure the library's efficiency, we analyzed its code characteristics using Hallucinate for automatic verification and employed low-level profiling and hardware measurements. Our findings indicate that the library is concise, adheres to four specific software security guidelines for hardware RNG utilization, avoids unnecessary optimizations for performance, and functions efficiently in practice.

The challenge of securely offloading computation to untrusted cloud environments has garnered substantial attention. Existing solutions typically depend on hardware features to constrain where and how computation can occur, a strategy that forces users to trust that these hardware implementations are correct, secure, and unmanipulated. We contend that achieving practical secure cloud computing does not necessitate trusting any single component in isolation. To address this, we designed a system of interlocking hardware defenses that collectively resist attacks without relying on any individual element. A former U.S. president once remarked, "The world is not yet ready for artificial intelligence," yet here we aim to demonstrate that a specific world problem already is ready for it. We introduce world AI—a concept distinct from traditional machine intelligence—that involves creating algorithms to forecast global phenomena. We outline two primary directions for world AI research: digital twin methods, which build algorithmic models of the real world, and direct estimation techniques that directly forecast attributes of unknown states (such as current times, economic indicators, or genetic profiles) without necessarily constructing a full model. We provide a unifying framework encompassing both approaches and illustrate their applications and interconnectedness using examples including genetic phenotyping, economic forecasting, and news source analysis. Furthermore, we detail potential avenues for future world AI development, acknowledging that addressing problems of this scale will undoubtedly reveal limitations in current modeling and estimation assumptions. We conclude by suggesting that even modest advancements in world AI could yield profound benefits for humanity.

, we demonstrate that the mineral cubanite (CuFe$_2$S$_3$) exhibits orbital-selective behavior, where certain electrons occupy molecular orbitals with $x^2-y^2$ symmetry while others remain localized at atomic orbitals. This uncommon configuration in $3d$ transition metal compounds provides an explanation for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous M\"ossbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic ordering between nearest-neighbor Fe ions. We conclude that $3d$ materials containing multiple identical transition metal ions, characterized by fillings that do not align with simple Slater-Determinant states, are likely the most advantageous systems for investigating the interplay between strong electron-electron and electron-lattice interactions on a non-trivial starting point that transcends the limitations of single-Slater-Determinant approaches. Ultimately, we suggest that cubanite offers a minimal and viable candidate for realizing significant electron-lattice effects, including possible unconventional superconductivity. These findings from combined band structure, total-energy, and force calculations on cubanite will also serve as a benchmark for analyzing other multiorbital, nearly half-filled compounds using dynamical mean-field theory and related many-body methods.

Quantum acoustic cavities and resonators are instrumental in investigating these multi-phonon phenomena through both theoretical and experimental lenses. Specifically, this work examines a system comprising a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser and coupled to an acoustic cavity. While such systems exhibit fascinating multi-phonon behaviors, previous descriptions of the quantum dot were restricted to a two-level model, limiting the complexity inherent to real semiconductor quantum dots. In contrast, our proposed model incorporates both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot; the latter are especially valuable due to their reduced decoherence rates, as they do not undergo spontaneous photon emission. Within this framework, we demonstrate that by precisely adjusting the driving laser frequency, one can induce giant Rabi oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state involving $N$-phonon bundles. This approach highlights two significant achievements: first, it enables the creation of dark state excitations in the quantum dot without requiring the conventional external magnetic field; and second, in a dissipative environment where both the acoustic cavity and the quantum dot experience losses, the system functions as a "phonon gun," capable of emitting $N$-phonon bundles. To validate these findings, we have performed a comprehensive analysis including single-photon emission, barcodes, and thermodynamic investigations. Furthermore, this platform offers the potential to investigate other multi-phonon phenomena, such as a "squeezed" state of phonons, an acoustic version of the Casimir effect, and a "missing" phonon effect. Finally, this study paves the way for the experimental realization of these predicted phenomena using current quantum dot and acoustic cavity technologies. Consequently, our work provides a robust pathway for advancing multi-phonon physics.

(SPCCSs) using quantum-optical catalysis via either a beam splitter (BS) or a parametric amplifier (PA). These states emerge from one output port of the BS or PA when a coherent state and a single-photon Fock state occupy the two input ports, provided a single photon is detected in the remaining output port. We examine the success probabilities of detection (which also serve as normalization factors), noting that they differ between BS and PA catalysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the states generated by both BS and PA devices are identical quantum states by analyzing the photon number distributions of the output states. The quantum characteristics of SPCCSs, including sub-Poissonian statistics, nonclassicality, Wigner function negativity, and squeezing, are explored through various quantum measurement schemes such as homodyne detection, photon-resolving detection, Wigner function observation, and virtual squeezing. Our findings indicate that SPCCSs exhibit stronger quantum effects than coherent states and single-photon Fock states, outperforming them in tasks requiring precise time differences, pattern recognition, quantum communication, and sensing. We conclude by discussing the potential applications of SPCCSs in communication, imaging, sensing, and computing, as well as their prospects for future development. The proposed SPCCSs offer significant advantages over other single-photon catalyzed coherent states, including simpler production devices, higher success probabilities, and more pronounced quantum effects. This work not only introduces a novel state but also establishes a method for comparing the quantum nature of various states. The production of SPCCSs relies on well-established quantum-optical components, including BSs, PAs, single-photon detectors, and the manipulation of coherent or vacuum laser fields.

In this work, we examine the generation of single-photon catalyzed squeezed states (SPCSs) using a parametric amplifier (PA). An SPCS is created when a squeezed state and a coherent state (or a vacuum state) are fed into two input ports of the PA, and a single photon is detected in one of the output ports. We calculate the success probability of this detection process. By analyzing the state's density matrix, we confirm that SPCSs are indeed nonclassical states. We derive the Wigner function for SPCSs and illustrate how it can be measured experimentally using homodyne detection. Additionally, we investigate the squeezing properties of SPCSs and compare them with those of single-photon catalyzed squeezed states produced by a parametric converter.

Because these infinite-dimensional problems frequently lack known analytical solutions, numerical methods are required to find approximate answers. This paper introduces a unified notation to describe key techniques within the transcription phase of simultaneous direct methods (specifically the discretize-then-optimize approach) for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization problems. The discussion highlights collocation, integrated residual, and Runge-Kutta schemes. These methods are applied to a simulation case study addressing a question from the COVID-19 pandemic: can a single ventilator treat multiple patients when supplies are scarce? The findings indicate that, in principle, individual patient parameters can be estimated with sufficient accuracy using a limited number of flow rate measurements, without disconnecting patients or requiring additional sensors. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that two patients can receive their required tidal volumes by adjusting the air flow resistance for each and controlling ventilator pressure. The results also reveal that, although not optimal, it is feasible to support three patients with two resistors and two valves derived from a single home desktop 3D printer. These outcomes open new avenues for engineering low-cost, portable ventilators capable of simultaneously treating multiple patients during pandemics or natural disasters. The code utilized in this research is available on GitHub.

The mathematical problems transcribed into discrete form are typically solved using indirect methods, such as shooting or differential dynamic programming, which transform the task into solving nonlinear differential or algebraic equations. While powerful, these indirect approaches are prone to converging on local optima and often require a good initial guess, which can be difficult to obtain. To address this, the paper emphasizes the benefit of using direct methods, which calculate objective function and constraint values directly and do not rely on Lagrange multipliers or shadow prices. Although indirect methods remain valuable for proving the existence of solutions to discrete and continuous problems, this work adopts a direct approach.

This study investigates whether a streamlined clinical workflow relying solely on CT imaging can enable high-quality automatic segmentation of esophageal tumors. To address this, we introduce a fully automatic, end-to-end segmentation method utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Furthermore, dilated convolutional layers are implemented to expand the network's receptive field while optimizing GPU memory usage. We assembled a dataset comprising 792 scans from 288 patients, featuring diverse anatomies, including cases with air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal/stenotic tumor locations. The model was trained, validated, and tested using 5-fold cross-validation. Results indicate that the DDAUnet achieves competitive segmentation performance compared to standard Unet variants and demonstrates robust generalization across the varied features and pathologies found in the dataset. While the achieved Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of approximately 0.76 meets only a moderate threshold for clinical deployment, we observe that a more robust model can be achieved with a significantly smaller validation set through the use of the proposed attention mechanism. bons are frequently found in complex reservoirs, making real-time optimized well placement (geosteering) essential for effective production and cost reduction. This process typically relies on updated formation evaluations derived from real-time well-log interpretation. Therefore, a workflow that is reliable, computationally efficient, and robust for interpreting logs while capturing uncertainties is critical. This study integrates an iterative ensemble-based approach, specifically the approximate Levenberg-Marquardt form of Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML), into such a workflow. By minimizing the statistical misfit between actual well-logging measurements and theoretical outputs from forward simulators, the method estimates model parameters—including resistivity, density, and boundary locations—along with their associated uncertainties. Analysis of various synthetic cases with different log types confirmed the method's ability to accurately estimate these parameters. Comparative CPU time analysis reveals that the proposed approach is approximately 10 to 125 times faster than common statistical methods like Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, and it supports parallel processing across multiple CPUs. Furthermore, testing on a case inspired by a real field demonstrated accurate formation evaluation. Consequently, the proposed ensemble-based method has proven to be both robust and computationally efficient for estimating petrophysical properties, layer boundaries, and their uncertainties, validating its suitability for geosteering applications.

Petro-thermal energy generation relies on heating hydrocarbon reservoirs via underground nuclear reactors, which also aids in extracting petroleum. The time required to reach a target temperature at a specific location is influenced by multiple spatial parameters, such as the reactor's position, size, and distance to the heating zone. Optimizing this process involves a time-series optimization problem that accounts for multiple objectives, constraints, and uncertain data. The study proposes a multi-objective, multi-constrained, and uncertain time-series optimization framework. The proposed algorithm, Evolutionary Time Series Optimization (ETSO), employs evolutionary computation to simultaneously determine the reactor's position (x, y, z) and other design variables that define its size and shape. ETSO was tested across 24 case studies and compared against other optimization techniques. Results indicate that ETSO effectively generated non-dominated solutions for petro-thermal heating, outperforming all other methods in handling multiple objectives, constraints, and uncertainties. The algorithm also demonstrated superior robustness and reliability, achieving an average of 96% success in generating non-dominated solutions over 24 cases. The study concludes that the proposed ETSO algorithm is highly effective for petro-thermal energy generation.

Nested NER, a specific subset of NER, involves named entities that are contained within one another. However, many prior studies on nested NER utilize linear structures to model entities that inherently possess a hierarchical organization. To resolve this discrepancy, this work treats all nested entities within a sentence as a unified structure and introduces a holistic structure parsing algorithm to identify the complete set of entities simultaneously. Furthermore, addressing the current lack of research on incorporating corpus-level information into NER, we integrate Point-wise Mutual Information (PMI) and other frequency-based features derived from corpus-aware statistics. This approach enhances performance by extending modeling from the sentence level to the corpus level. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves promising outcomes on standard benchmarks, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance. Additional empirical analyses reveal that the proposed corpus-aware features significantly improve NER domain adaptation, highlighting the remarkable benefits of our corpus-level holistic structure modeling. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/zeyipark/StructurePMI-NER.

We develop and implement a novel range-based approach specifically to reduce cross-technology interference in shared frequency bands, with the objective of minimizing the mean square error. The hardware implementation aligns with ideal simulation results (assuming no interference), achieving a localization accuracy of under 0.5 meters. The method requires less than 5 seconds to determine the position of a mobile node. While this approach is optimized for ZigBee networks, it can be effectively adapted for other protocols and systems. Pretraining has emerged as a dominant strategy for tackling natural language processing (NLP) tasks, yet modeling the joint distribution of multiple languages remains an unresolved challenge. We investigate the interoperability of French and Spanish within multi-task learning frameworks to establish performance baselines for bilingual NLP. Our analysis reveals that while pretrained language models significantly outperform their untrained counterparts, they fail to capture the nuances of juxtaposed bilingual sentences. Consequently, we introduce an explicit feature to enhance the distributional modeling of such sentences. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields up to a 15-point improvement in accuracy compared to baseline models when tasks are performed separately, and achieves state-of-the-art performance across three specific tasks. Furthermore, we provide an open-source repository containing our findings at https://github.com/SHS-LAHORE/BiJNT.

Tantalum pentoxide (Ta$_2$O$_5$) possesses advantageous physical and chemical characteristics, such as a high dielectric constant and anti-reflective properties. Consequently, Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles have been proposed to increase relative biological effectiveness in hadrontherapy to treat various cancers. To support this application, it is crucial to assess their electronic properties, a task that is significantly complicated by the material's multiple stable polymorphs. This presentation summarizes the calculation of the Ta$_2$O$_5$ energy loss function, a definitive spectral signature, to determine the representative polymorph structure responsible for the anti-reflective features observed in experimental reflection energy loss measurements.

Although first-principles methods based on linear-response time-dependent density functional theory can compute the energy loss function, the material's polymorphic nature creates a major theoretical hurdle: the coexistence of distinct spectral signatures from each structure within the experimental signal. To overcome this, we employed the supercell approach to isolate the spectral features of Ta$_2$O$_5$ polymorphs, including the recently discovered $\gamma$-phase. To validate our results, we compared the calculated reflection energy loss spectrum for the $\beta$-phase with established experimental data and established good agreement.

We hypothesized that this phenomenon significantly influences online misinformation dissemination because, despite their global potential, digital interactions are inherently localized, with interaction likelihood dropping sharply as distance increases. Analyzing over 8 million Reddit comments containing news links from January 2016 to December 2019, we discovered that Reddit does not function as a "hype machine" for misinformation as other platforms do; instead, it operates as a supply-and-demand system. Specifically, the volume of misinformation news scaled linearly with the population of each state (scaling exponent $\beta=1$, $R^2 = 0.95$). Moreover, variations from this universal trend were best predicted by state-level personality and cultural attributes ($R^2 = \{0.12, 0.39\}$), rather than socioeconomic factors ($R^2 = \{0.15, 0.29\}$) or political characteristics ($R^2 = \{0.06, 0.21\}$). We observed that states with residents exhibiting lower conscientiousness and cultures characterized by loose norms (low cultural tightness) experienced higher-than-expected circulation of all news and fact-checked misinformation ($\Delta = 1.26$ and $1.10$, respectively). Conversely, the demand for political leaning news and source-reliable misinformation was best explained by residents' conscientiousness ($\Delta = 1.30$) and political ideology ($\Delta = 1.12$). Finally, the supply of political leaning and source-unreliable misinformation was most strongly correlated with cultural tightness ($\Delta = 1.40$) and partisan polarization ($\Delta = 1.30$). In conclusion, the demand for misinformation is driven by individual attributes, whereas the supply is more closely tied to community-level factors. We propose that the Big Sort amplifies these state-level disparities, potentially causing divergent misinformation trajectories across different regions. Consequently, the impact of misinformation on American democracy may vary by location, and interventions must be tailored to their specific contexts. Our findings suggest that the social structure of the offline world is a vital component of any comprehensive model of misinformation spread.

Let $T$ denote a rooted, connected, planar, directed tree oriented away from the root. The set of all such trees is denoted by $\mathcal{T}$. In this context, the parent of a node $v$ (where $v \neq \bullet$) is the unique neighbor of $v$ toward the root, referred to as $\text{pre}(v)$. Effective dialogue requires that a robot accurately comprehends user intentions, even when expressions are ambiguous or flawed. While prior research has addressed single-turn sentence understanding, complete dialogue state tracking, or interactions with structured domains, this paper focuses on extracting intent from isolated utterances without relying on external context like dialogue histories or semantic frames. We introduce a neural network architecture capable of learning intent classification tasks using only textual data. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach surpasses existing methods on three distinct datasets. Additionally, we utilize the findings from two counter-intuitive experiments to offer insights into implicit intent representation and the word order preferences of pre-trained language models. We release our code and datasets as part of the SentenceIntent repository.

We introduce an end-to-end neural framework for dialogue state tracking that utilizes an attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant words within each dialogue act. This attention allows the model to handle variations in how users express the same request, such as differing grammatical structures or missing information. Our method abstains from using handcrafted features and explicitly models the uncertainty of information provided by users. Extensive experiments on the snapshot and LinkedIn datasets show that our approach outperforms recent methodologies. We also address several challenges specific to this task, such as managing ambiguous and contradictory requests, handling dialogues with implicit intent, and dealing with unseen dialogue acts. Finally, we provide datasets for further testing and discuss potential applications, such as error analysis and personalization. The code and datasets are accessible via the End2EndDialogState repository.

Max-margin classification typically relies on the assumption that training data follows an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) distribution. However, modeling data distributions beyond the i.i.d. framework remains an open challenge. This study examines the optimization dynamics of the max-margin SVM optimizer when applied to non-i.i.d. data distributions characterized by group-wise dependent samples. Our theoretical analysis reveals the asymptotic behavior of the optimizer under such conditions and uncovers a phenomenon where the learning rate effectively declines as the number of samples per group increases. Based on these findings, we propose an algorithm that dynamically adjusts the learning rate to account for group-wise dependent data distributions. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence of this method, and both synthetic and real-world experiments demonstrate that our dynamic learning rate strategy outperforms traditional max-margin classifiers across various distributional settings.

Self-supervised learning leverages extensive unlabeled data to learn robust feature representations, yet its application to time-series data remains challenging due to the data's inherent complexity and lack of explicit structural information. While numerous self-supervised techniques have been developed for tabular and time-series data, their performance degrades significantly when only a small volume of labeled data is available for fine-tuning, as the statistical properties differ markedly from large-scale unlabeled datasets. To address this transfer learning challenge, we introduce a contrastive learning method grounded in cluster alignment. This approach imposes structural constraints on unlabeled data by clustering it using self-supervised techniques and subsequently aligning these clusters with those derived from labeled data during fine-tuning. Our comprehensive evaluations on multiple regression benchmarks demonstrate that our approach surpasses both strong baseline and recent state-of-the-art methods.

These limitations are problematic in real-world scenarios where sparsity is pervasive and can hinder effective user preference learning. By integrating these enhanced domain-specific and domain-invariant preferences, MSDCR achieves a holistic understanding of user preferences even in sparse environments. Collaborative filtering (CF) is a primary technique in modern recommendation systems, yet it is vulnerable to data sparsity, which degrades system performance. To overcome this, we investigate whether multi-task learning can improve CF by integrating information from related domains. We distinguish between single-target and dual-target cross-domain learning based on the count of sparse domains involved. To create a more generalizable single-target CF model, we introduce a multi-sparse-domain cross-domain filtering (MSDF) technique. The MSDCR model adapts to any cross-domain scenario by borrowing context and enhancing user preference representation through an aspect preference graph. We present a reformulation for second-order cone programming (SOCP) that reduces complexity compared to standard methods. By applying algebraic manipulations to the reformulated constraint, we achieve a complexity reduction of approximately fourfold. This method is broadly applicable to linear programming (LP), SOCP, semidefinite programming (SDP), and other convex optimizations. The paper begins with basic LP, illustrating how reformulating a standard form can simplify the associated matrix. We further demonstrate that this reformulation can be applied to SOCP without increasing complexity, and by extending the matrix eligibility test, the same reduction achieves a sixfold simplification for the standard form. Similarly, this technique can be adapted to the rotated second-order cone form, as shown by the associated matrix. We also examine the application of this reformulation to SDP, comparing it with existing literature. Although this approach may increase complexity by a factor of four, it can still be more efficient than alternative standard forms, specifically those related to the eligible test for the Schur complement. This reformulation can be integrated with other techniques, such as the four-level reformulation for SDP solvers, though this combination may increase complexity by a factor of eight. Module (Optane DC PMM) marks the first commercial availability of scalable nonvolatile memory DIMMs. This new DIMM combines DRAM-like access speeds and byte-granularity with data persistence across power failures. This report offers the first comprehensive academic performance analysis of the Optane DC PMM, examining its dual role as main memory and as persistent, byte-addressable storage accessible to user-space applications. The study evaluates performance across various modes and scenarios using extensive macro-scale benchmarks.

When configured as large memory devices with a DRAM cache to mitigate higher latency and lower bandwidth (Memory or cached mode), Optane DC memory has minimal impact on applications with small memory footprints. While applications with larger footprints may see some slowdown compared to pure DRAM, they can retain significantly more data in memory. Alternatively, when used with a file system, Optane DC PMMs can yield substantial performance improvements, particularly when the file system is optimized for the device's load/store interface and the application performs many small, persistent writes. For example, using the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system boosted Kyoto Cabinet's performance by nearly 2x.

Furthermore, Optane DC PMMs facilitate user-space persistence, allowing applications to explicitly manage writes to persistent media. In our experiments, modified applications leveraging user-space persistence outperformed those relying on file systems. Specifically, the persistent version of RocksDB achieved nearly 2x the speed of its equivalent utilizing ext4. Additionally, we tested a user-space persistent messaging system, demonstrating that it can support millions of messages without losing data even after power loss. These messaging systems are relevant to real-world scenarios like remote procedure calls (RPCs) and in-memory queueing systems such as RabbitMQ or Apache Kafka. Finally, the research confirms that the hardware effectively supports both synchronous and asymptotically consistent replication modes for user-space persistence.

In conclusion, Optane DC PMMs represent the first practical solution for building systems that offer highly performant access to data across multiple tiers of hierarchical memory. The hardware successfully supports both File-based and Application-based (including replicated and consensus-based) persistence methods, significantly boosting their performance. Although our analysis focused on specific configurations and workloads, Optane DC PMMs hold substantial potential for enhancing a wide range of additional applications and systems.

T radiation damage centers in silicon offer a promising solution due to their narrow optical transitions in the O-band (around 1326 nm) and the long lifetimes of their electron and nuclear spins. While previously limited to bulk silicon ensemble studies, this work demonstrates the reliable formation of high-concentration T center ensembles within the 220 nm device layer of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers through ion implantation and annealing. Although Raman active, the nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in silicon lacks an optical transition within the low latency required for the quantum eraser experiment. To replace the NV center, we evaluated other silicon impurities based on their spin Raman frequency, optical gap, and lattice preference. We identified phosphorus vacancies (Pv) as a suitable candidate, as 29Si nuclear spin manipulation using Pv is feasible without compromising other essential parameters. To implement this, we employed an already established growth protocol for engineering the concentration and distribution of Pv in silicon. By performing electron spin resonance (ESR) on as-grown samples, we located the Pv center at a silicon lattice site directly above an interstitial position, with its orientation controllable via ion implantation temperature. To validate the optical conditions, we fabricated a silicon photonic device featuring a resonant cavity and a distributed Bragg reflector. By exploiting the spectral sensitivity of defects to local strain, we confirmed that this specific Pv center exhibits a spectral shift of approximately 1 GHz under unit strain. Since the available spectral range of the center exceeds 1000 GHz, it is easily sufficient for achieving a quantum eraser demonstration.

This study evaluates how different line lists used in least-squares deconvolution affect the dispersion of radial velocity (RV) data to determine the most effective method for reducing jitter. Results indicate that parametric selection reduces RV RMS by less than 10%, whereas the randomized selection achieves a systematic improvement of over 50% regardless of the star's activity level. Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. We release the multi-context dataset to facilitate future automated context analysis in object detection. We also provide our code at https://github.com/zeyuda/Context-Analyze-Object-Detectors.

Modeling multivariate distributions and their dependence structures separately via copulas has become a dominant approach across numerous scientific disciplines. This strategy is particularly effective in finance and risk management, where understanding tail dependence and diverse patterns are critical for calculating risk metrics and managing portfolios. In these contexts, where multivariate dimensions are often very high, implicit copulas have emerged as a crucial class of models defined by auxiliary components. Recently, this focus has expanded to include joint distributions of time series and processes, driving both theoretical advancement and practical application. This paper begins with a brief review of copula fundamentals before detailing the four primary groups of implicit copulas: elliptical and skew $t$ copulas, factor copulas, time series copulas, and regression copulas. While many existing models fit the latter two categories, they collectively form a unified framework. The paper explicitly covers parameter identification, model simulation, and Bayesian parameter estimation—topics where recent advancements address areas that were previously overlooked. Although the primary goal is to showcase the versatility and success of implicit copulas among statisticians, the accompanying R package, biCop, provides accessible software for handling this modeling class. The package supports specification, estimation, and analysis for a broad range of implicit copulas, notably including those based on latent variable and time series models. For the latest updates on the package, see the address provided at the end of the paper. Additional topics are explored in the supplementary online material.

Additionally, libcommute is accompanied by Python 3 bindings named pycommute, which facilitate solving small-scale diagonalization tasks, rapid prototyping, and integrating high-performance libcommute cores into Python environments. Both packages are openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/LarryW2/libcommute and https://github.com/LarryW2/pycommute, with further details on their features, advantages, and usage available in the associated paper. In summary, libcommute and pycommute constitute a unified ecosystem for exact diagonalization that prioritizes performance, offers extensive functionality, and enables efficient development.

For more than thirty years, the Python scientific computing ecosystem has grown into a robust platform for scientific research. This report provides an overview of the ecosystem's history, highlighting key events and major packages. It examines Keras, TensorFlow, and TFLearn for deep learning; Bokeh, Matplotlib, and Plotly for interactive and static plotting; Click, optparse, and argparse for command-line option parsing; IPython, Jupyter Notebook, and Jupyter Lab for interactive programming; pandas, NumPy, and SciPy for numerical computations on arrays and dataframes. The findings are discussed in the context of the Python community's evolution and the principles of software engineering.

We examine the application of the entropic uncertainty relation, derived from entropic measures of quantum coherence, to thermodynamic processes involving quantum working media. This approach yields generalized kinematic lower bounds for both total and irreversible entropy production. These derived bounds are more widely applicable than currently available methods for experimentally measuring irreversible entropy change. Specifically, we demonstrate libcommute's extensive capabilities for exact diagonalization, showcasing its high performance, such as computing the entire spectrum of a Hamiltonian with thousands of dimensions within seconds or minutes.

I present libcommute, a new open-source C++ library for quantum many-body theory that enables rapid and precise computation of commutators, exponentiated operators, and spectral decompositions. Supported by pycommute, a complementary interface that provides functional equivalence to C++ while ensuring high performance, these tools offer significant extensions to current techniques for investigating many-body quantum systems.

Spin-lattice relaxation measurements conducted at 6.55 T identified two components of equal amplitude: one displaying metallic behavior with a $T$-linear $1/T_{1}$, and another exhibiting a more intricate temperature dependence. The metallic nature of the slow-relaxing component remains largely insensitive to changes in LaNiO$_3$ thickness, whereas the fast component shows significant sensitivity, particularly in the thinnest, most magnetic samples where it displays an inverse temperature dependence (increasing as $T$ decreases). The underlying causes of this bipartite relaxation are discussed. This bipartition indicates that electrons in the metallic state coexist with those in an insulating, magnetic state. We demonstrate that the local probe sensitivity of NMR allows for the quantitative determination of the fraction of correlated electrons as a function of both temperature and LaNiO$_3$ thickness. The observed insulating component displays an exponent in its magnetic susceptibility that closely matches the power-law expectation for 1D spin chains. These findings offer direct support for theoretical predictions regarding the influence of dimensionality and strong correlations on the low-temperature behavior of Mott metals. Introduced in 2007, the technique of $\beta$-detected NMR using long-lived radioactive isotopes enables the investigation of electron dynamics across a vast temperature range by simply adjusting the detection field; for instance, using half-life $T_{1/2}=81.8$ min allows study from millikelvins to megaelectronvolts by varying the gamma from $10^{-6}$ to $10^2$ eV/K. We introduce the MultiTalk Dataset, a collection exceeding 320,000 written dialogue sentences that achieves a balance between a high branching factor (10) and multiple conversation turns (6) via selective branch continuation. We offer several contributions aimed at advancing dialog generation within this highly branching context. To assess a diverse range of generated outputs, we propose a straightforward scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, designed to optimally integrate a set of varied references. Furthermore, we examine multiple language generation tasks across varying depths of predictive conversation, utilizing textual attributes derived automatically from pretrained classifiers. Our final task addresses a challenging theory of mind problem, a controllable generation challenge that necessitates reasoning about the anticipated reactions of a listener. Although human performance on this task reaches near-perfect scores (0.93), we demonstrate that standard sequence-to-sequence and neural translation approaches fail completely (achieving only 0.02), and that even sophisticated neural generation models make minimal progress (0.26). Finally, we present a new approach to this task based on training a conditional restricted boolean sampler through iterative self-training. This method achieves a significant improvement (0.70), demonstrating that effective theory of mind reasoning in open-ended conversations can be addressed via self-supervised learning.
