Finally, we explore possible origins for this anomalous rotation profile, such as the accretion of a giant planet or anomalous angular momentum transport via tidal inertial waves driven by a close substellar companion, and advocate for additional observational and theoretical investigations. These findings contribute to the growing body of evidence indicating that low-mass star angular momentum evolution cannot be explained by conventional processes. While phosphorus dopants in silicon can be positioned with atomic precision to explore these competing regimes, they typically rely on crystal band symmetry-based wavefunctions that are intrinsically sensitive to tunneling effects. This study directly visualizes lattice-aperiodic valley interference between coupled silicon atoms using scanning tunneling microscopy. Our atomistic analysis reveals how envelope anisotropy, valley interference, and dopant positioning influence the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction. We demonstrate that the exchange interaction can be made resilient to valley interference by strategically aligning dopants along specific in-plane crystallographic directions. This approach restores a vacuum-like behavior, maximizing exchange based on donor orbital overlap and restricting pair-to-pair variations to under a factor of ten, given the precision of dopant placement. This robustness persists across a broad distance spectrum, spanning the strongly Coulomb-interacting regime essential for high-fidelity quantum computation to the tightly coupled donor arrays valuable for quantum simulation in silicon. Our findings offer substantial tolerance to both dopant alignment and positioning errors, significantly surpassing the vulnerabilities inherent in relying on a single valley. These results facilitate the rapid identification of optimal multi-dopular configurations and establish a robust framework for engineering long-lived quantum coherence in solid-state systems.
Distributed quantum networks are anticipated as a prerequisite for a revolutionary quantum internet capable of executing tasks unattainable by classical systems. The protocol layer of these networks must navigate the inherent heterogeneity of available quantum nodes, a challenge that becomes increasingly complex with the expansion of the network scope. This paper introduces GraphQL, a novel approach to semantic web services tailored for quantum nodes within distributed quantum networks. Similar to the World Wide Web, GraphQL addresses the inherent heterogeneity of quantum hardware by defining standard interfaces that enable protocol layers to establish connectivity and execute distributed protocols across nodes of varying hardware architectures. We have prototyped a GraphQL server to demonstrate its ability to abstract diverse silicon-based quantum platforms, including single qubits, qubit registers, and photonics nodes. Our prototype reveals that a protocol layer can leverage this server to calculate exchange interactions between connected phosphorus-in-silicon qubits. Furthermore, we illustrate how this setup can be upgraded to allow users to configure and measure additional protocols, such as single-qubit rotations and two-qubit gates, without requiring modifications to the underlying protocol layer.

Although graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a valuable relational inductive bias for modeling these systems, research into their ability to generalize to new instances within the same system type remains limited. In this study, we trained GNNs to learn time series data from a specific nonlinear dynamical system known as the belief propagation algorithm. Our analysis revealed that the learned representations and model components have straightforward interpretations that align with the fundamental properties of probabilistic inference. We successfully developed a "graph translator" that maps statistical interactions in belief propagation to the parameters of the trained network. This translator facilitates two forms of novel generalization: reconstructing the underlying structure of a new system instance using only time series observations, or directly building a new network from that structure. These findings illustrate a pathway to comprehending both the dynamics and structure of complex systems and demonstrate how such insights can drive generalization. We release our code, synthetic data, and networks open source to support this conclusion.

*Limitations of this study include a focus exclusively on belief propagation and nonlinear dynamical systems, as well as the absence of empirical validation on real-world systems.*

Introducing structural information into machine learning models helps capture dependencies within data and enhances performance. While GNNs are renowned for leveraging structure to improve tasks like node classification, they are less frequently applied to learn from structural signals. Recent theoretical work suggests that when models possess appropriate symmetries or inductive biases, the parameters they learn often reflect insights about the underlying data distribution. For example, training a transformer on subject-verb-object sentences can reveal that "eat" involves an agent and a patient. However, most of this literature concentrates on node classification problems where node identities are fixed. In contrast, we examine the generalization capabilities of models learning from both structural and temporal data, addressing challenges more relevant to time series analysis. Our work features two main contributions: a theoretical examination of how a GNN learns to solve a protocol for estimating marginal probabilities, and a demonstration of the resulting generalization on synthetic data.

Language models pretrained on vast collections of text have recently matched or exceeded human capabilities in numerous NLP benchmarks. This success suggests that these models implicitly grasp linguistic knowledge such as syntax, world facts, and semantic relationships. However, it is not known if and how they acquire specific structural formats, such as those found in knowledge graphs (KGs). This research investigates the efficacy of training BERT and T5 architectures on factual triples from KGs compared to complete sentences. Our findings indicate that BERT fails to learn even basic information from isolated triples, whereas T5 acquires at least some data, though with reduced efficiency when trained on triples rather than complete sentences. To assess performance, we assembled two datasets: WikiMovies and a larger collection drawn from Wikipedia. T5 models trained on the WikiMovies dataset significantly outperformed those trained on the larger dataset in answering questions about movie industry terminology, a category of KGs often rich in such information. Additionally, our work provides the first performance evaluation of BERT and T5 on the MetaQA benchmark.

We evaluate four practical camera setups, accounting for unknown fixed or varying focal lengths with or without radial distortion. Our solvers were tested on synthetic data and over 500,000 real image pairs from the Sun360 dataset and our own smartphone captures using IMU-equipped devices. Results demonstrate that our methods surpass state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. Finally, we integrated our solvers into a real-time 360° photography pipeline, confirming that they generate geometrically consistent meshes suitable for virtual camera traversal while maintaining low latency. Our code, datasets, and meshes are publicly available. We believe these solvers can enhance multi-view geometry pipelines handling uncertain intrinsic parameters and can be adapted for other applications involving 1-DOF rotational uncertainty. Title: Generalizing the cancellation of poles in degenerate Eisenstein series.

Hanzer and Mui\'{c} explored the phenomenon of pole cancellation in degenerate Eisenstein series. We generalize their findings by examining the combinatorics of associated Weyl group cosets that give rise to these cancellations. This approach allows us to identify all possible cancellation instances. The work also clarifies how these cancellations relate to $L$-functions, specifically regarding non-poles and zero-poles. Finally, we apply these insights to locate central points on the critical strip for certain $L$-functions arising from degenerate Eisenstein series.

PD is a neurodegenerative condition characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which disrupts the normal dynamics of the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex circuit. While multiple mechanisms contribute to the disease, a comprehensive understanding of its molecular pathogenesis remains elusive, and no cure currently exists. To bridge this knowledge gap, researchers have suggested computational models that mimic neurobiological features observed in animal models. Our approach employs a data-driven method where biologically constrained parameters are optimized via differential evolution. The resulting models accurately replicate single-neuron mean firing rates and local field potential spectral signatures from both healthy and parkinsonian marmoset brains. To our knowledge, this represents the first computational model of PD constructed from simultaneous electrophysiological recordings across seven brain regions in marmosets. Our findings indicate that this model can aid in investigating PD mechanisms and support the creation of techniques for identifying new therapies. Furthermore, the approach is applicable to other computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can be used to fit multi-scale brain circuit models.

Parkinson's Disease affects over 10 million people globally and claims 50 million lives annually. Currently no cure exists, and existing treatments offer only temporary relief while carrying significant risks. Early diagnosis remains difficult because symptoms are subtle at the onset. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the primary tool for detection, yet there is a pressing need for more effective diagnostic methods. Machine learning offers a potential solution. By employing a data-driven framework, we can derive functional connectivity patterns from Multi-echo Gradient Echo (ME-GE) fMRI data using a sparse autoencoder. These patterns serve as input to a neural mass model of the basal ganglia, which is reverse-engineered through an iterative procedure to generate an image-based diagnosis of parkinsonism. This demonstration shows that the proposed data-driven framework can facilitate functional connectivity analysis and reverse engineering of neurophysiological models in clinical fMRI studies, thereby aiding in the early detection of Parkinson's Disease.

These targets, selected from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS), represent a broad spectrum of merger evolutionary stages. Our data successfully resolve key emission lines—including H$\beta$, [OIII]$\lambda$5007, H$\alpha$, [NII]$\lambda\lambda$6549,6583, and [SII]$\lambda\lambda$6717,6731—at a spectral resolution of $R$ = 1500–2000. This precision enables the construction of spatially resolved moment maps for ionized gas (spanning $\sim$20–100 pc) and facilitates AGN diagnostics within central regions of 1–5 kpc. Our results indicate that AGN-driven [OIII] outflows intensify both spatially and dynamically as mergers progress from early to late stages; specifically, outflow velocities rise from $< 100$ km s$^{-1}$ in early mergers to $> 400$ km s$^{-1}$ in late mergers. Furthermore, we observe that while AGN-driven outflows are more prevalent in late-stage mergers, they are significantly more massive relative to the available gas in early mergers. Additionally, we determine that the fraction of star-forming gas placed into outflows increases with merger severity. Comparison with simulation data from the MANIFEST project suggests that our findings align with models assuming uniform mixing between stellar and gas components. Finally, we note that ultra-powerful outflows previously identified in one of our sample galaxies using multi-wavelength methods are confirmed to occur within the context of an intermediate-stage merger. These discoveries offer novel insights into the co-evolution of galaxies and highlight the value of targeted studies on the ionized gas phases of U/LIRGs across various merger phases and cosmic epochs.

Current approaches typically rely on sensor arrays or in-vehicle cameras to forecast weather, yet these methods incur incremental costs and offer limited scope. To guarantee the uninterrupted operation of all transportation services regardless of conditions, a robust detection system capable of classifying weather in the wild is essential. However, solving this problem is challenging due to the diverse nature of weather conditions and the lack of distinctive features across different scenarios. Existing solutions are often scene-specific and restricted to classifying only two weather categories. This paper introduces a novel open-source dataset named RFS, comprising images of three weather classes: rain, snow, and fog. Additionally, a new algorithm is proposed that employs super-pixel delimiting masks for data augmentation, achieving reasonable performance across ten Convolutional Neural Network architectures. The algorithm's key component utilizes Internal Pooling Layers (IPs) alongside fully connected layers, with the optimal IP location determined automatically through data augmentation. Experimental results indicate that this approach delivers satisfactory performance with minimal computational resources. Finally, the developed solution has been integrated into a real-world context to classify rain and non-rain conditions for the continuous operation of rain shields on road traffic signs. On the Czech Republic test sequence, the proposed method outperforms all other approaches while maintaining low computational complexity. The open-source code and dataset are accessible at https://is.muni.cz/public/1076597/RainSnowFog.zip. The source of light for all images in the RFS dataset is random and varied. These findings demonstrate that the proposed method offers a reliable solution for classifying up to three weather types, producing results that align with real-world conditions. This approach is appealing because it relies on fundamental dynamics, thereby circumventing the invalid assumptions found in mass-flux convection schemes at current resolutions. Nevertheless, the optimal closure strategies for multi-fluid equations governing atmospheric convection remain unclear. This study develops a straightforward single-column model featuring two fluids—one rising and one falling—without incorporating additional sub-filter variability modeling. When applied to Rayleigh-Bénard convection, the model demonstrates that minimal closures suffice to predict the correct scaling of heat flux (Nu) across six orders of magnitude in buoyancy forcing (Ra). These findings indicate that even a rudimentary two-fluid model can effectively capture the primary coherent overturning structures of convection. Furthermore, the results suggest that extending this model to include moisture closure techniques could yield a efficient single-column model for atmospheric convection. The code utilized in this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/atmospheric-models-and-more/ multi-fluid-convection.

Multi-fluid dynamical models have gained significant attention in atmospheric sciences due to their ability to represent moisture-driven convection more physically accurate than traditional mass-flux convection schemes. This paper investigates closure schemes within a simplified single-column model. By employing a direct numerical simulation method, we examine the models across a vast range of Rossby numbers (Ro) and Coriolis parameters (Co), spanning up to ten orders of magnitude. The study focuses on equatorially symmetric or asymmetric barotropic vortices where the Coriolis force varies with latitude. Using the cross-correlation between the two fluids to quantify their separation, we can classify the flow into either single-fluid or multi-fluid regimes based on the distance from the vortex axis (r). In barotropic vortices, the closure involving radial wind linearly proportional to radius outside the vortex core (nu=1) yields the most physically meaningful results. Specifically, this suppression of turbulent friction allows the centrifugal force to balance the pressure gradient, maintaining a steady state. At low Ro, the Coriolis force becomes dominant, restricting turbulence to the center and inducing an equatorially trapped state. Conversely, as Ro increases, the Coriolis influence diminishes, potentially leading to barotropic instability and storm development. The relationship between wind profiles and the resulting Coriolis force can be expressed as $Co \propto Nu^{-1.5}$. We analyze the conditions required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. Our results indicate that this process is unattainable if the cavities interacting with the uncorrelated atoms share classical correlations with any other cavity. However, we observe that the atomic states can become genuinely multipartite entangled if the cavity housing the uncorrelated atom is highly entangled with another cavity. This non-trivial finding offers a potential method for generating multipartite entangled atoms through Jaynes-Cummings interactions and can be implemented using existing experimental setups. Additionally, we demonstrate that an uncorrelated atom can be projected into a superposition of its ground and excited states with equal probability. Finally, we show that the entanglement between two two-level systems can be transferred to the correlation between them. These findings are relevant for creating multipartite entangled states via the collective Jaynes-Cummings interaction. (More)

As the innermost element of the CMS tracking system, the silicon pixel detector operated from 2009 to 2016 before being replaced by an upgraded version in early 2017. During the preceding LHC shutdown, a prototype readout system and an additional disk were installed into the legacy forward pixel detector, which featured eight prototype blades built with new digital read-out chips. Testing these pilot modules provided operational insights into the upgraded system. This paper presents the reconstruction and analysis of data collected using the new modules, including details on the calibration of the reconstruction software, as well as findings on hit-finding efficiency and track-hit residual distributions. The demonstrated performance validates the design of the upgraded detector. Additionally, the data reveal issues with certain modules that will guide their repair or replacement during the upcoming LHC shutdown. The detector demonstrated a global insertion efficiency of approximately 99.3% during early data taking, with most modules showing 99.9% efficiency. Lower performance in specific regions during the commissioning phase was attributed to issues with the detection of optical laser spillover. Final track residuals indicate that the reconstructed tracks were of high quality. Finally, the measured proper decay lengths of charged $B$ mesons were found to align with previous world measurements.

The LHCb experiment at CERN is upgrading its vertex detector, known as the Scintillator Pixel Detector (SPD), which will be replaced by a fully silicon instrument KSDX during the current shutdown. The SPD currently comprises the Tile detector, launched in 2015 using 2012 design modules, and a newly installed scalar section comprising 80 modules using 2017 designs. The KSDX will utilize 10 times the hit capacity of the present SPD with 50 times the channel capacity. Final designs for the KSDX were finalized late in the 2017 run, yet the new 2019/2020 design offers roughly 2.5 times the hit capacity. This paper reviews the evolution of the SPD and KSDX module designs from 2012 to the present, highlighting the testing and implementation of the 2017/2019/2020 modules within the KSDX.

This study gathers seven publicly accessible, manually labeled Twitter sentiment datasets. From these sources, we construct a novel training and testing dataset. We then develop an LSTM-based model to classify tweet sentiments and assess its performance using the newly created dataset. Organizations rely on social media to monitor public opinion, making accurate assessment of user sentiments essential. This paper introduces a dataset of Twitter messages related to Tesla, along with associated feature labels and corresponding sentiment labels. We present results from experimental attempts to classify the sentiment of tweets mentioning Tesla. Our features include the feature set used by Baker et al. (2013), as well as additional features tailored to Twitter data. We also measure features proposed by users within the Twitter community. Our features are categorized into four groups: general features, punctuation features, casing features, and user-defined features. We report features that prove effective for sentiment analysis tasks. The features tested include those validated by Baker et al. (2013), plus the additional features specific to Twitter data. Our features fall into four categories: general features, punctuation features, casing features, and user-defined features. We also determine which features work best for sentiment analysis. Our experiments reveal that general features, including those from Baker et al. (2013), are highly effective, while features specific to Twitter data are not as useful. We note that our features were optimized using an support vector machine. Our findings on feature selection will assist future researchers in building classifiers for sentiment analysis on social media platforms. This study examines the connection between the observable shadow radius and the first-order phase transition of non-linear charged AdS black holes within the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. The analysis reveals that, under specific conditions, the shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature (or pressure) exhibit non-monotonic behaviors. Furthermore, from the perspective of the shadow radius, the phase transition temperature is higher than that derived from the horizon radius under identical conditions. These findings suggest that the shadow radius serves as an effective probe for uncovering thermodynamic phase transition details in black holes. Additionally, thermal profiles illustrating the coexistence of big and small black hole phases during phase transitions are presented for two distinct non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter values ($\gamma=1$ and $\gamma=1.5$). Finally, the influence of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter on both the shadow radius and thermal profiles is further explored. The study concludes that increasing this parameter raises the phase transition temperature and sharpens the thermal profile. These results may support upcoming Event Horizon Telescope measurements regarding the shadow of galaxy-center black holes. The findings also emphasize the need for direct experimental evidence of EMF non-linearities to fully validate the macroscopic description of field-plasma interactions provided by the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills action.

While numerous reconstruction methods exist—from conventional protocols to machine learning approaches—no single universal technique currently allows for extracting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that nonclassical phenomena, including entanglement variations during dynamical evolution and the emergence of quantum synchronization, manifest as qualitative shifts within the optical tomograms themselves. Consequently, explicit state reconstruction is unnecessary to detect these effects. Furthermore, we establish that the location of quantum synchronization times can be determined directly from the extremal points of the 2D Herglotz-Borel transform of the tomograms, provided the initial state is pure. This finding implies that the reconstruction of the full Wigner function is not required to identify the timing and nature of quantum synchronization. Our results highlight that the informational content of the optical tomogram is substantially richer than previously recognized and offer significant implications for quantum optics measurements and quantum information theory.

Reconstructing quantum states in continuous-variable systems, like the radiation field, is made difficult by the infinite dimensions of the associated Hilbert space. Since multiple reconstruction techniques are available, there is no universal method to derive the Wigner function directly from an optical tomogram without prior state knowledge. We show that indications of quantum synchronization appear as qualitative features in the 2D dependence of the optical tomogram on phase-space translation parameters, specifically through the extremal points of its 2D Herglotz-Borel transform. Consequently, determining the timing and type of quantum synchronization does not demand state reconstruction or even the calculation of the full Wigner function. These findings reveal that the optical tomogram contains more information than previously thought and that its direct interpretation can reveal quantum synchronization dynamics.

, constructing scalable chat systems remains challenging due to the substantial amount of human-human interaction data required, particularly when integrating features like persona, style, or safety. This study addresses the difficulty of assigning consistent roles to these systems while ensuring natural human interaction. To achieve this, systems must adhere to role specifications that define specific feature constraints and policies governing permissible utterances. We introduce an efficient data collection framework that utilizes in-context few-shot learning with large-scale language models to generate role-compliant dialogue datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we evaluate various open-domain dialogue architectures regarding their ability to satisfy role constraints without compromising conversational skills. Both automatic and human evaluations indicate that our models produce very few out-of-bounds responses while maintaining competitive performance on general metrics. Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a flexible approach for boosting Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Nevertheless, recent studies suggest that RL's benefits in NMT largely stem from reinforcing tokens that were already highly probable during pre-training. We propose that the extensive action space is a primary barrier to RL's efficacy in machine translation and validate this hypothesis through two experimental series. First, we observe that shrinking the vocabulary size enhances RL performance. Second, we demonstrate that effectively lowering the action space dimensionality without altering the vocabulary also leads to significant gains, as measured by BLEU scores, semantic similarity, and human assessment. Specifically, initializing the network's final fully connected layer—which maps internal dimensions to the vocabulary—with a layer designed to generalize across similar actions results in a substantial performance boost, averaging 1.5 BLEU points. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical framework demonstrating that the sample complexity of learning via RL is directly linked to the space complexity, which is defined as the minimum number of actions required to achieve a certain accuracy. Our findings indicate that even a modest reduction in the action space significantly accelerates learning, thereby validating our initial hypothesis that this specific design choice is the root cause of RL's limitations in machine translation. This research suggests that future efforts should explore refining the generalized action space, such as employing a hierarchical action space. Additionally, we present a public repository containing code, data, and models to support these claims: https://github.com/MohammadVaheed/Generalized_Action_Space_in_Machine_Translation.

We introduce a straightforward method to accelerate beam search in neural machine translation. Our technique involves training a separate model on a dataset with lower accuracy than the primary system. During translation, we utilize this fast model to predict the optimal beams, a strategy that yields a significant speedup with negligible impact on final translation quality. We demonstrate that this method preserves both the statistical accuracy and the computational efficiency of beam search. Experimental results show that our approach delivers a 7.1% speed increase while maintaining the same BLEU score as traditional beam search. We also note that the action space complexity is directly related to the complexity of learning through reinforcement learning.

We present a learning-based method for estimating the pose of objects with known geometry from monocular images. This approach learns a mapping from image coordinates to 3D local coordinates at the object's boundary, enabling pose estimation through the alignment of the object's CAD model to these boundary points. We assess the system's robustness across different geometric shapes, scene contexts, and image qualities on a collection of objects not included in the training set. Furthermore, we evaluate the system on furniture in office and residential settings and on automotive scenarios involving partially visible vehicles and road contexts absent during training. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms both bounding box-based baselines and a system using pre-trained, synthetic data, achieving the lowest MAE in calibration parameters.

We demonstrate that the sandglass model remains integrable even when coupled to a lattice environment, allowing the system to reach a steady state characterized by power law dynamics. This behavior is explained by the emergence of an additional hidden symmetry in the model. Consequently, the model can function as a quantum sensor capable of precisely detecting slight deviations from linearity in quantum evolution, such as those caused by decoherence or non-Shr\"{o}dinger interactions. The model's robustness, simplicity, and scalability make it an excellent candidate for implementing on a few optical qubits.

We introduce a continuous variable version of the sandglass model, establishing its integrability despite coupling to a continuous environment. This setup enables the observation of algebraic entanglement growth. We also propose using the model to detect deviations from continuous linearity, including discretization errors and non-Canonical commutation relations. Specifically, we suggest using the rate of entanglement generation as a sensitivity measure for these deviations. The sensitivity scales with the mass dimension of the system, indicating that the effect is highly significant for macroscopic objects.

. While edges and boundaries capture shape details, textures represent regional appearance. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success in computer vision and medical imaging, they primarily learn texture abstractions, frequently resulting in inaccurate boundary definitions. In medical contexts, expert manual segmentation typically depends on organ boundaries; for instance, when segmenting a liver, a practitioner usually locates edges before filling in the mask. Driven by these insights, we introduce a plug-and-play module called Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), designed to integrate with standard encoder-decoder frameworks to handle both edge and texture data. The EG-CNN enhances edges within the encoder, predicts sharp boundaries through auxiliary supervision, and merges these results with the original CNN output. We assessed the EG-CNN's efficacy across various mainstream CNNs using two public datasets, BraTS 19 and KiTS 19, for brain tumor and kidney segmentation. Our results demonstrate that incorporating EG-CNNs consistently boosts segmentation accuracy and generalization capabilities. The source code and models are accessible at https://bitbucket.org/zhijianWang/eg-cnn.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have made substantial advancements in segmentation tasks, they often struggle to balance performance between boundary and interior regions. This discrepancy stems from the fact that EG-CNNs typically prioritize edge information through auxiliary supervision, while also effectively leveraging the feature extraction powers of pretrained encoders. We tested the EG-CNN across several state-of-the-art segmentation models, including MONSTERS, U-Net-ish, and ANNs, across multiple datasets such as ACDC, KiTS19, and SygN. Our findings indicate that adding EG-CNNs consistently improves both segmentation accuracy and generalization. The source code and models can be found at https://bitbucket.org/zhijianWang/eg-cnn.

It offers transaction support across three distinct deployment configurations: single-document transactions via the WiredTiger engine on a standalone node, multi-document transactions within a replica set (comprising one primary and multiple secondary nodes), and distributed transactions in a sharded cluster (an aggregation of multiple replica sets with sharded data). A core inquiry regarding MongoDB is the specific consistency guarantee each deployment ensures. However, existing literature lacks concise pseudocode for these transaction mechanisms and a formal specification of their claimed consistency levels. This work addresses that gap by formally specifying and verifying MongoDB's transactional consistency protocols. Specifically, we derive succinct pseudocode for the protocols in WiredTiger, ReplicaSet, and ShardedCluster, based on official documentation and source code. Subsequently, we demonstrate that these protocols satisfy distinct variants of snapshot isolation: Strong Snapshot Isolation (Strong-SI) for WiredTiger, Realtime Snapshot Isolation (Realtime-SI) for ReplicaSet, and Session Snapshot Isolation (Session-SI) for ShardedCluster. Furthermore, we introduce practical and efficient verifiers for these snapshot isolation levels, thereby validitating the correctness of our specifications. Finally, we show that each protocol's pseudcode can operate as a standalone protocol for Strong-SI, Realtime-SI, and Session-SI, respectively. Our findings facilitate a deeper understanding of MongoDB's protocols, enhance future debugging and specification tasks, and provide a method for assessing other document-based NoSQL systems. The pseudocode, codes, and proofs presented here are available at https://github.com/hariradif/MongoDB-Transaction-Pseudocode.

Document-based NoSQL databases are valuable for handling unstructured and semi-structured data, yet there is a lack of available pseudocode representing the consistency protocols of these systems, including MongoDB. This repository contains the codes corresponding to the papers titled "On Specifying and Verifying MongoDB's Consistency Protocols" and "On Specifying and Verifying consistency protocols of common document-based NoSQL databases."

The primary limitation of prior work was that it failed to demonstrate that the specified protocols fulfill their respective consistency levels. Addressing speech-emotion recognition (SER) challenges across multiple domains is difficult because such systems typically underperform when applied to unseen corpora. While recent efforts have attempted to build models effective across multiple domains, they often rely on explicit feedback labels or assume access to additional resources. We propose a novel approach that utilizes only in-domain inference performance as feedback, requiring no extra data or labeling. Specifically, we use an autoregressive autoencoder to generate feedback from SER performance on in-domain data, then train a reinforcement learning agent to adjust the model's parameters based on this feedback. Our method outperforms strong baselines across four cross-corpus and cross-language tasks, out of domain inference, and noisy data experiments. Like other model feedback loops, our approach is cost-effective, practical for incremental updates, and applicable to any task with accessible performance metrics.

Speech-Emotion Recognition (SER) allows computers to interact with users emotionally, but current systems struggle with low performance and poor generalization across different domains and languages. We present a model-based self-tuning method that uses real-time performance on a live data feed to adapt pre-trained models to new languages and domains. The ability of these hybrid methods to converge to global minimizers depends critically on the discretization error resulting from restricting optimization to the graph, which in turn dictates the necessary graph density. A primary application is flight planning, which involves calculating optimal routes regarding flight time and fuel usage under specific weather conditions. While highly efficient discrete shortest path algorithms are available to generate initial guesses for locally convergent optimization techniques, this study derives a theoretically grounded error bound for such applications. These findings enable flight planners to construct graphs with sufficient connectivity to guarantee that the hybrid algorithm identifies the globally optimal trajectory, rather than relying on heuristic methods to achieve a target error level. The core of this work establishes a lower bound on the error between the energy of the global minimizer and that of a two-stage approximation in energy minimization problems defined over infinite function spaces. This error bound is expressed as a function of the energy's extension property and its restriction to a discretization grid. The primary application lies in flight planning, where the goal is to determine trajectories that are optimal with respect to multiple criteria, such as flight time and fuel consumption under given weather conditions. Currently, discrete shortest paths serve as initial guesses for time-consuming numerical optimization processes. Because the discrete approximation introduces an inherent error, the underlying graph must be sufficiently dense to ensure convergence to the global minimizer. Typical graph connection heuristics estimate an error bound similar to the one derived here; however, those bounds applied to infinite function spaces often yield graphs that are too sparse for reliable convergence. In contrast, the lower bound presented in this study allows for sparser graphs by providing a rigorous guarantee of global convergence.

In many scientific fields where short paths are computed via discrete grids, such as fluid dynamics or weather forecasting, researchers are interested in the flow along interfaces between grid cells. These interfaces are determined by minimizing an action functional, which is extended from its behavior on discrete points. The discrete energy is defined as the sum of energies on the space restricted to the grid. Existing literature typically relies on heuristics to select a graph density that approximates the true minimizer up to a certain tolerance. This report establishes bounds on both the discrete energy and its gradient that can guide the construction of a graph with the minimal required density. The analysis focuses on discrete energies that satisfy a specific decay condition, though the derived bounds may remain valid more broadly.

Although the dominant source of gravitational waves (GWs) at low frequencies is expected to be supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs), their signal has not yet been detected. While the LIGO-Virgo collaboration has identified numerous events from the merger phase, the nature of the long-duration inspiral phase remains uncertain. This work employs direct N-body simulations of galactic mergers to numerically investigate the formation, dynamics, and evolution of a SMBHB behind a strong shock wave generated by a stellar explosion. The SMBHB is assumed to be centrally located, and the simulation tracks the three-body interaction between the binary and the shock. It is demonstrated that the SMBHB's dynamics are significantly influenced by the tidal field of the asymmetricly collapsing star, which is not captured when considering only the shock. The gravitational wave from the SMBHB is estimated using the adiabatic approximation, an approach validated against results from full numerical relativity. The analysis reveals that the orientation of the SMBHB axis relative to the shock can be randomized by the tidal field, and the probability distribution of the inclination angle is largely independent of the explosion energy. The inferred probability distribution of inclination angles allows for estimating the detectable number of events for LIGO III and a future space-based detector, such as LISA

Constructed as Wronskians of standard Hermite polynomials, these polynomials are significant in mathematical physics, random matrix theory, and one-dimensional supersymmetric (SUSY) quantum mechanics. Characterized by quadratic behavior at infinity, these potentials exhibit localized oscillations near the origin. We establish an explicit criterion for the non-singularity of the associated potentials and estimate their localization range based on polynomial indices and the distribution of their complex zeros. Our findings reveal that non-singular 1D SUSY quantum potentials arise from dressing the harmonic oscillator using polynomial Heisenberg algebra ladder operators. This characterization provides precise estimates for the extent of localized states within the spectral gap of the harmonic oscillator. The characterization of non-singular potentials and their spectral properties derived from generalized Hermite polynomials significantly expands the set of known solvable potentials in the Painlevé IV hierarchy. This work constitutes Chapter 3 of the Author's PhD thesis.

By applying a phase space reconstruction method, we confirm deterministic chaotic dynamics through the identification of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent within a specific range of traction speeds. These findings are interpreted using a model that underscores the deterministic nature of acoustic emissions by linking them to stick-slip dynamics. Furthermore, these dynamics are contextualized within relevant literature, particularly regarding self-organized criticality observed in other fracture and failure events. The study concludes by suggesting potential future research directions. Notably, the confirmation of chaotic dynamics in acoustic emissions from adhesive tape serves as a case study, illustrating that complex dynamical behavior can arise from simple systems under specific conditions, even in the presence of noise. This conclusion is supported by established theory. Ultimately, the work aims to raise awareness that acoustic emission signals, whether deterministic or noisy, can inherently contain significant dynamical information. This insight encourages both the continuation of similar studies on other material failure events under constant motion and the adaptation of the work for applications in self-monitoring noise-based maintenance systems. The maintenance of large-scale composite materials, operating over extended periods in aggressive or variable environments, relies heavily on health monitoring systems. These systems utilize sensors, such as fiber Bragg gratings, fiber optic fibers, piezoelectric patches, and acoustical emitters, to detect strains, temperatures, pressures, and acoustic emissions (AE). While often viewed as mere noise, the term "noise" itself is a construct; that which is noise for one may be signal for another. As such, acoustic emissions from adhesive tape failure can be rich in dynamical information, as is the case for other events involving adhesion, bonding, and fracture. This context aligns with prior work that highlighted the potential of acoustic emissions from these phenomena to yield diagnostic data for material characterization.

planar Josephson junctions (JJs) and superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) fabricated within epitaxial InAs/Al heterostructures, which exhibit a high ratio of Josephson energy to charging energy. We identify a transition from macroscopic quantum tunneling to phase diffusion as temperature varies, where the critical temperature $T^{*}$ can be controlled via a gate. The observed switching probability distributions align with models featuring small shunt capacitance and moderate damping, yielding a switching current that constitutes only a minor fraction of the critical current. Furthermore, phase locking between two JJs creates a discrepancy in switching currents when comparing an isolated JJ to one embedded in an asymmetric SQUID loop; notably, for the loop configuration, $T^*$ is also modulated by magnetic flux. These components can be integrated into a frequency conversion circuit, wherein an embedded SQUID functions as a frequency selector with tunable thermal stability governed by the magnetic field. Consequently, this work demonstrates a viable pathway to achieve temperature-independent frequency selection or to adjust the thermal stability of frequency selectors using an external magnetic field. Additionally, the observed switching dynamics are consistent with phase locking between a JJ and a JJ within a SQUID exhibiting moderate damping, and the system can function as a stochastic phase flip–flop.
Additionally, we determine the coherent lifetime of a superconducting quantum oscillator in our device, which is approximately 100 times longer than previously reported in semiconductor oscillators and is limited to a few percent by measurement backaction. This system can be modeled as a damped harmonic oscillator weakly coupled to two thermal baths characterized by an impedance ratio $\eta$. The oscillator frequency can be adjusted via a magnetic field, and we demonstrate that the switching current can be expressed as $I_{sw} = \eta e \omega / (2\pi)$, a relationship that remains applicable to oscillators with tunable frequency. We also validate a formula for the lifetime of a superconducting oscillator with a fixed frequency, which was established in prior literature, as a function of $\eta$.
Finally, we examine a system comprising two JJs with differing charging energies, revealing that the system can be treated as two oscillators weakly coupled together. In this configuration, the relaxation time is approximately $10^{5}$ times longer than in the JJ system with uniform charging energy. Moreover, we illustrate that the relationship between switching current and impedance ratio can still be maintained even when the charge noise spectral density exhibits frequency dependence.

By employing automated methods on imaging data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP), we quantified the tidal flux fraction ($f_{\rm tidal}$) for 2649 ETGs possessing stellar masses $M_* > 10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and redshifts $0.05 < z < 0.15$. The $i$-band sensitivity of the HSC-SSP Wide-layer extends to approximately 28.5 mag arcsec$^{-2}$. Below this surface brightness threshold, roughly 28% of these galaxies exhibit significant tidal features where $f_{\rm tidal} > 1\%$. The frequency of ETGs with prominent tidal features declines exponentially with increasing $f_{\rm tidal}$, characterized by a logarithmic slope of about 100. Within the observed stellar mass range, $f_{\rm tidal}$ doubles as the mass increases from $M_* \approx 10^{11}M_{\odot}$ to $M_* \approx 10^{12}M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, we conducted pair-count analysis to derive the merger rates for these massive ETGs. By integrating these merger rates with the measured $f_{\rm tidal}$ values, we estimated that the typical lifespan of these tidal features is approximately Gyr, implying that the majority of observed features are intrinsic to these galaxies rather than transient. Consequently, the ensemble properties of these features can offer insights into the physical processes shaping the central regions of ETGs. The underlying probability density function for $f_{\rm tidal}$ allows us to deduce that the merger rate for the $10^{12}M_{\odot}$ ETG population is roughly $0.008$ Gyr$^{-1}$, which is about 10 times higher than the rate for the lowest mass population examined. Finally, the merger rates derived from our sample align well with predictions from hydrodynamic simulations. These findings from the HSC-SSP will be essential for interpreting the data expected from the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in the coming decade. Our analysis demonstrates that optimal allocations emerge from continuous optimization problems spanning multiple generations, revealing that these solutions often prioritize individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds over slightly more successful high-status peers—a form of affirmative action that arises organically from the pursuit of payoff maximization. Furthermore, we examine how model parameters influence whether this affirmative action is temporary or persistent, and we explore extensions incorporating more complex mechanisms governing transitions between socioeconomic levels. This work offers policy implications regarding decisions on education investment timing and target selection. Ultimately, we suggest that the principles of generative design and multi-objective tradeoffs can be applied to diverse scenarios involving limited opportunities, as illustrated by sports team drafting, university admissions, employment hiring, venture capital investment, and resource allocation in infectious disease outbreaks. Access to higher education may help societies break cycles of poverty, yet deciding who should benefit is complex; we propose that principles of multi-objective tradeoffs can inform these difficult choices. Specifically, we build a dynamic model for allocating higher education opportunities that prioritizes general success while also considering efforts to elevate an individual's parents' socioeconomic status. We find that in models with mild nonlinearities, nearly all successful individuals are admitted. However, when the cost of access is highly nonlinear and success is partly inherited, the optimal strategy involves sacrificing some general success to maximize the number of families that can rise socially. Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel rapid luminosity separation technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were executed systematically during every fill featuring full-intensity beams under physics production conditions at the Interaction Point (IP) of the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment. This method enables the determination of both emittance and closed orbit parameters at the bunch-by-bunch level. By precisely measuring the beam-beam closed orbit discrepancies, researchers achieved a direct and quantitative observation of long-range beam-beam PACMAN effects, with results that align closely with numerical simulations generated by an enhanced version of the TRAIN code. Furthermore, the residual closed orbit after beam-beam interaction can be harnessed to initiate the emittance scan procedure, potentially facilitating automated and high-frequency beam-beam effect monitoring in the CERN Proton Accelerator Chain. This approach represents a critical step toward optimizing the physics potential of high-emittance, intense hadron colliders, such as the current LHC or the future Terawatt-class machine.

In high-luminosity hadron colliders, the initial beam-beam interactions often cause significant beam losses, particularly when beams on the same ring possess different transverse emittances and are separated only by single dipole magnets at the interaction points. Under these conditions, the beam with the smaller emittance experiences significantly greater closure due to beam-beam interactions than the wider beam. Because closed orbits are directly converted into transverse momentum kicks, this differential closure leads to a higher number of impactful beam-beam encounters for the narrower beam. These additional interactions occur during the early stages of beam circulation, deplete phase space through non-resonant mechanisms, and result in increased beam losses. This phenomenon, termed "PACMAN effects" after the missing pieces of space, was first identified in hadron colliders by T. Pope. The term reflects the visual appearance of phase space plots following beam-beam interaction, where the narrower beam appears to have had a portion of its space "eaten." This letter quantifies the PACMAN effect in terms of beam lifetime and validates the theory using the interaction of store-quality beams at the LHC. The findings underscore the necessity of implementing emittance asymmetry limits or speedup strategies before top-up processes conclude in operations involving significant emittance differences. Additionally, the direct quantitative measurement of PACMAN effects serves as a benchmark for other phenomena in high-luminosity hadron colliders that rely on distinct emittances, closed-orbit effects, and beam losses.

We present a novel algorithm for efficiently generating realistic time-domain simulations of bolometric cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments. The package, s4cmb (Systematics for CMB), facilitates the observation of simulated anisotropy data to as high an accuracy as possible. Modern CMB experiments are engineered to minimize both instrumental and observational systematic errors. This work demonstrates how to model a broad spectrum of potential systematic effects across various categories within a simulation package. ### 1 Introduction

Deepfakes represent a burgeoning class of AI-driven image and video manipulation tools capable of altering human appearances in media. These technologies allow for the creation of fabricated videos showing any individual saying or doing anything, effectively blending with real footage to deceive viewers and undermine trust in digital media. Although deepfake generation is becoming increasingly sophisticated and difficult to detect, current detection methods generally lag significantly in performance when applied to data outside their training sets. This discrepancy creates an urgent need for detection systems that can generalize to unseen deepfake generation models and environments.

Recent studies suggest that because current deepfake techniques typically operate on low-resolution thumbnails, they often impart manipulation-specific signs to the forged content. Consequently, it is hypothesized that these hidden patterns are more pronounced in the frequency domain than in the spatial domain. To exploit this, researchers have recently attempted detection using solely frequency domain features. However, such methods are bound to the limitations of specific generation algorithms.

To overcome these challenges, this work proposes a framework that leverages features from both spatial and frequency domains. The model fuses these domain-specific and shared representations to achieve a robust and generalizable detection capability.

### 2 Related Work

Recent efforts in deepfake detection can be categorized into transformation-based techniques, which analyze the impact of transformations like rotation and flipping, and pattern-based approaches, which seek to identify manipulation-induced patterns or artifacts.

K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our extended class of space includes the conformal touch structure introduced by F. W. Sarason in the early 1970s. Consequently, our findings offer multiple approaches to generalizing the conformal connection concept, which had previously been defined solely through the presence of an angle function. Finally, our findings significantly generalize earlier results established by W. J. Cunningham, J. M. Fearnley, and J. T. Moore concerning the angle function. We note, however, that our work diverges from theirs regarding the axiom governing the dependence of $\angle(x,z,y)$ on the point $z$. This deviation enables the angle function to be defined meaningfully on manifolds equipped with a conformal structure. Consequently, our results facilitate the investigation of the conformal connection problem using the established theory of connection structures.

While the velocity gauge, which relies on linear coupling to the vector potential, is the conventional approach for describing optical properties, finite systems permit a transformation to represent radiation via the electric field. The simulation of dynamical phenomena in solids under the influence of strong external electromagnetic fields represents a significant challenge in condensed matter physics. While first-principles approaches now allow for the concurrent and explicit inclusion of matter and light across all length scales, accurate results remain difficult to achieve, particularly when going beyond the dipolar approximation. This letter introduces a unified framework for constructing electron-electron and electron-photon Hamiltonians that accurately describe the non-local dynamics of electrons and the polarization of electromagnetic fields in any crystal. We demonstrate that this approach yields precise accounts of linear optical properties, including the screening of Coulomb interactions and sum rule compliance. Furthermore, we reveal the optical gap in an organic charge-transfer salt, highlighting an optically active metal-insulator transition. The general nature of our approach ensures its applicability to any solid, serving as a robust foundation for future first-principles investigations into the nonequilibrium dynamics of interacting electron systems.

This research provides a rigorous theoretical and numerical framework for understanding scattering dynamics in finite PT-symmetric periodic waveguide networks. By formulating an analytical expression for the complete wave field, we establish a fundamental understanding of reflectionless transmission and CPAL across various wave systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that bi-directional reflectionless behavior can be achieved in odd numbers of unit cells at an exceptional point, or in even counts by precisely controlling the PT phase. We also introduce two distinct strategies for realizing CPAL in such structures. These insights provide a robust theoretical basis for generating extraordinary wave phenomena in diverse platforms, offering a general approach to designing high-intensity wave sources and supertransmission devices.

While previous research has attempted to assess football defense by forecasting ball gains and attacks based on player and ball positions, these studies overlooked event significance, assumed flawless tracking of all players, and neglected the impact of randomness. In this work, we introduce a statistical model to predict whether the defense successfully retains possession. Data-driven analysis of professional sports has historically been constrained by the high cost of obtaining game data. Although computer vision has lowered this barrier in recent years, challenges persist when analyzing specific tasks like evaluating team formations. We analyze football games to predict team formations from partial data consisting of ball and player trajectories. We identify three distinct difficulties: (1) handling measurement noise in the input data, (2) managing phase transitions where one or more players lose track of the ball, and (3) accurately incorporating team movements. We propose a novel approach that models these issues as a data smoothing problem subject to specific constraints, solving it via maximum a posteriori estimation. We test our method on real video footage, comparing it against simple baselines and existing techniques. Our results indicate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms both benchmarks and state-of-the-art methods, as evidenced by lower hypothesis testing $p$-values in our statistical analysis of video data. As the dimension $N$ of a matrix $X_N$ tends to infinity, the unitary equivalence classes of the corresponding Hermitian matrices typically become infinitesimally free. Consequently, the unitarily invariant limit of a sequence of $N\times N$ random matrices is often characterized by infinitesimal freeness. For instance, this phenomenon was established for the real Gaussian ensemble $\{X_N : X_N = (X_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq N}, X_{ij} = X_{ji}\}$, where $X_{ij}$ are i.i.d. centered random variables with finite variance. Subsequent rigorous proofs were provided for the GUE and other unitarily invariant ensembles, as well as for the orthogonal ensemble with a determinant structure. Additionally, infinitesimal freeness in expectation was proved for the GUE and the bi-orthonormal ensemble. This paper demonstrates that the asymptotic freeness of independently unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices occurs in expectation at the level of $O(N^{-2})$.

While various approaches commonly measure polarization in social networks by examining their structure alone, we evaluated eight such methods and found that all produce high polarization scores even for random networks sharing the density and degree distributions of real-world networks. Additionally, certain methods are influenced by degree distributions and the relative sizes of polarized groups. To address this, we propose normalizing existing scores and establishing a minimal set of tests to ensure a score can effectively distinguish polarized networks from random noise. Following normalization, the performance of these scores in a classification task involving 203 networks improved by between 38% and 54%. Our findings indicate that normalization is more critical than the specific method chosen, as the diverse approaches share limitations in their ability to detect true polarization. This research offers a valuable benchmark for future methods designed to analyze the polarization of political and social networks. Normalized scores enable comparing networks of different sizes and degrees, facilitating a broader understanding of political and social dynamics across diverse contexts. Ultimately, identifying metrics that accurately capture a system's state is crucial for diagnosing problems and implementing solutions.

An accurate assessment of a system's state is fundamental for developing models that can identify effective interventions. Although recent research has introduced methods to quantify polarization within the structure of political networks by identifying well-mixed clusters, these scores often fail to reflect the extent of polarization. This failure occurs because cluster formation can result from other dynamic processes, such as the aggregation of like-minded individuals (homophily), rather than polarization itself. To differentiate between these scenarios, we developed a random generator that creates networks with the same degree distribution and overall density as real networks but lacks both clustering and homophily. We tested eight clustering-based methods to determine if they could distinguish our random networks from real-world networks. Our analysis revealed that the norm of the second eigenvector of the adjacency matrix is the most effective indicator of clustering among the methods studied; however, other methods, including those relying on random labeling, do not reliably detect clustering or homophily. If a score is to represent a specific property of a complex system, it must differ from values found in random networks of the same density and degree distribution. To guide future method development, we provide a framework for characterizing random networks, which can aid in creating a bias matrix to evaluate a method's ability to detect various network properties.

This paper addresses the challenge of estimating a common positive definite matrix $X$ from noisy linear matrix inequalities. The rapid advancement of cavity quantum electrodynamics (CQED) has enabled the observation of diverse multi-photon phenomena, such as multi-photon lasers, multi-photon interference, and multi-photon correlations. Notably, in the Rabi model—the fundamental theory describing the interaction between a two-level atom and a optical field—Kirchhoff first observed multi-photon correlations in 1927, though the significance of this finding remained unrecognized for nearly a century. Recently, the revival of the Rabi model has spurred a resurgence of interest in super-Rabi oscillations, which correspond to multi-photon correlations. Through the engineering of effective Hamiltonians, researchers have investigated various symmetry-protected super-Rabi oscillations, including those of color photons, phonons, and magnons. When combined with time-dependent driving, this approach can generate continuous super-fluxes of light, sound, or spin.

We operate within the full information model, wherein Byzantine nodes possess complete awareness of the network's state at every step—including all random choices—unlimited computational capabilities, and freedom to deviate arbitrarily from the protocol. Our primary contribution is a randomized distributed algorithm capable of estimating network size despite a high volume of Byzantine nodes. Specifically, this algorithm accurately estimates the size of sparse, small-world expander networks containing up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ Byzantine nodes, where $n$ represents the unknown network size and $\delta$ is any fixed positive constant. The algorithm produces a constant-factor estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability, ensuring that a large majority ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction) of honest nodes obtain the correct network size. Furthermore, the approach is fully distributed, lightweight, and easy to implement; it completes in $O(\log^3{n})$ rounds, utilizes small messages per round, and imposes minimal local computational costs on each node. Additionally, the algorithm effectively tolerates a broad spectrum of Byzantine behaviors, surpassing the thresholds met by many contemporary resilient network-size estimation techniques. In a related contribution, we establish a lower bound demonstrating that any randomized fully distributed network-size estimation algorithm must incur an exponential error in the amount of information exchanged per round. This finding indicates that our solution represents a near-optimal approach within the restricted context of allowing only a modest increase in communication costs. Finally, we propose that our fully distributed framework can be efficiently transformed into a centralised one. This paper aligns with the special topic on "Resilient Distributed Computing," which addresses the challenge of maintaining correct and efficient operation in distributed systems despite a subset of faulty, malicious, or compromised nodes. The topic examines how to ensure data consistency and algorithmic correctness (such as consensus), accomplish fundamental metrics like network size estimation, and executes practical applications (e.g., aggregation) despite Byzantine nodes, often requiring significantly more information than typical stochastic faults.

We propose a novel approach rooted in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Unlike conventional methods that treat the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation for a specified mean curvature $K$, our method solves an algebraic equation for $K$ given a chosen conformal factor. ### 1 Introduction

Pre-trained deep learning techniques have transformed information retrieval (IR), enabling systems to process billions of documents with high efficiency and deliver superior user experience. Methods such as Dual-Encoder (DE) and Cross-Encoder (CE) architectures have become foundational in modern IR. While CE models typically yield higher accuracy, their sequential nature limits throughput, making them ideal for reranking lower volumes of candidates after fast DE filtering.

To maximize performance without sacrificing efficiency, recent IR practices often combine these models into an end-to-end pipeline. Specifically, a CE model is trained to mimic the scoring functions of several DE models. However, because the CE model must aggregate multiple distinct pieces of knowledge, it faces the challenge of efficiently learning from diverse scoring functions with varying complexities and capacities.

To date, only a few works have explored knowledge distillation (KD) specifically for IR. For instance, Li et al. (2019) found that DE models could effectively distill knowledge from a pre-trained CE model. Similarly, Huang et al. (2020) demonstrated that multiple DE models could jointly distill knowledge for query adaptation. These studies confirm that CE models can successfully aggregate knowledge from multiple DE teachers, yielding significant interaction gains. Yet, when the number of teachers increases, it remains unclear how to effectively unify knowledge from multiple sources for efficient aggregation.

Recent advancements in automation and experimental methodologies have accelerated these measurements and enhanced their resolution. These improvements can be amplified by integrating machine learning (ML) techniques. This review examines recent applications of ML in imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. We outline relevant ML algorithms, algorithms specific to time-resolved experiments, and approaches employed in simultaneous optimization of multiple experiments. Reconstructing real- or reciprocal-space data is difficult due to artifacts and noise inherent in experimental measurements. Recent developments enable machine learning models to reconstruct data from noisy inputs while preserving key physical features. We highlight recent applications of this capability across various spectroscopic techniques. These findings help identify the most promising machine learning models for experimentalists and suggest potential areas for improving measurement efficiency and accuracy.

Recent efforts have placed experimentalists and engineers in collaboration to accelerate spectroscopic measurements using machine learning. This review examines three categories of applications: data analysis, real-time optimization, and artifact removal. The final section outlines avenues for expanding machine learning utility in experiment design and execution. Although these applications are still in early stages, this overview offers a comprehensive survey of current work. It classifies examples into data analysis, optimization, and artifact removal categories. Each category discusses underlying algorithms, recent case studies, and performance assessments. The review concludes with perspectives on utilizing machine learning for experiment discovery and addresses ethical machine learning practices. Appendices provide algorithm descriptions, performance comparisons, and terminology glossaries. By documenting these applications, this work encourages further research at the intersection of machine learning and experimental science.

Reconstructing and analyzing measurements from real or reciprocal space is challenging because of noise and artifacts in experimental data. We explore how machine learning can reconstruct data from noisy inputs, highlighting applications in infrared spectroscopy, neutron scattering, and tomography. These examples demonstrate machine learning's potential to maintain data integrity while significantly reducing acquisition times. We conclude by outlining measures to ensure the reliability of these algorithms.

The findings in sections 3 through 6 hold particular interest given their potential extension to the study of free boundary problems. Throughout the paper, $\mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)$ denotes the cone of functions $\phi$ such that $\psi\leq\phi$ and $\phi$ shares the appropriate regularity. This technique utilizes two distinct Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian. By gradually transitioning from the driver to the problem Hamiltonian over a sufficiently long period, the system is expected to settle into the target ground state representing the solution. While non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian are thought to improve QA efficiency, decoherence is traditionally viewed as a primary hindrance. In this study, we demonstrate that non-stoquastic Hamiltonians can actually cause catastrophic failures in QA, whereas specific decoherence processes can prevent such outcomes. Specifically, incorporating anti-ferromagnetic interactions (a typical form of non-stoquastic terms) into the Hamiltonian makes it impossible to reach the target ground state, even with an infinitely long annealing time, in certain scenarios. In these instances, symmetry causes the Hamiltonian to become block-diagonal, resulting in an energy level crossing during the annealing process that completely derails the search for the ground state. Furthermore, we show that introducing a particular type of decoherence allows the ground state to be successfully obtained in these cases. This occurs because, although isolated quantum systems may exhibit symmetry, environmental interactions break this symmetry. These counterintuitive findings offer profound insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing quantum annealing.

Over the past few years, quantum annealing (QA) has attracted significant attention as a potential method for solving combinatorial optimization problems. Although QA offers distinct advantages over classical methods, such as utilizing a problem encoding that is often simpler and requires fewer bits, and avoiding locally trapped solutions through a continuously varying Hamiltonian, the technique faces a major challenge: in many instances, it becomes impossible to find the ground state regardless of how long the annealing time is extended. This catastrophic failure is frequently attributed to symmetry-induced level crossings that trap the system in excited states. To mitigate this, we propose introducing a specific type of weak but controllable noise into the QA process. We demonstrate that, unlike symmetry which can cause such severe failures, this noise can shift level crossings from being real (occurring at distinct times) to complex (occurring in pairs of conjugate times without affecting the system's evolution). This finding not only prevents catastrophic failures caused by symmetry but also provides a fundamental insight into the behavior of quantum systems, illustrating that non-conservative noise can transform sharp transitions into smooth ones.

We present a multi-task learning framework called "parallel neural architecture search" capable of simultaneously designing optimal structures across diverse tasks. This technique utilizes a parameterized neural network to automatically generate subnetworks for training. Our experiments on the ImageNet 2012 dataset (comprising ten tasks) and the TCP 2016 dataset (including five tasks) confirm that our search successfully produces networks that achieve state-of-the-art compression-rate accuracy curves and satisfy accuracy-regularization constraints, all while maintaining significantly lower memory footprint per image. Additionally, our methods have been evaluated in competition settings.

This work investigates the application of evolutionary algorithms to program synthesis and automatic differentiation for training within functional programming languages such as F\* and Haskell. We introduce the term "functional learning" to describe this paradigm and show that it can effectively train classifiers and classification rules. Our experimental results demonstrate that functional learning can competitively learn formulas requiring logical operators (e.g., \&, \|, \') and relational operators (e.g., $<$, $\le$, =, $\neq$).

These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex failure modes such as delaminations that are challenging to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable the precise detection of damage in self-sensing composites, a critical step for implementing structural health monitoring systems in real-world applications. Furthermore, this study highlights the potential of carbon nanofiber-reinforced polymer composites for applications demanding both self-sensing capabilities and effective electrical noise mitigation.
