. Over the last century, scientific literature—the primary conduit for sharing knowledge among researchers—has experienced exponential expansion. Although numerous tangible metrics have been developed to quantify this growth, the underlying mechanism of knowledge advancement itself remains poorly understood, likely due to the enormous volume of data and the absence of novel statistical methodologies. In this study, we investigate paper citation networks and literature co-citation networks (derived from subject overviews) to understand information flow and the structure of knowledge. We demonstrate that paper-centric metrics, including productivity, impact (measured as citations per year), and scope (assessed via in-degree), as well literature-centric metrics (evaluating conceptual diversity and philosophical depth), effectively characterize scientific growth. Furthermore, we identify universal mathematical patterns governing these processes. Notably, the complexity of knowledge is represented by a universal fractal dimension of approximately $D \approx 4.2$. Additional analysis reveals that knowledge structure is a dominant factor driving metric behavior, whereas external elements like political funding play only a minor role. These general laws govern metrics and knowledge dynamics in an era of massive literature, topics that may have significant implications for understanding knowledge growth in the age of Big Data. The framework presented here can be extended to other evolving complex systems, such as genealogy.

In recent years, significant efforts have been devoted to enhancing the discoverability of research by analyzing publication metadata. However, most of these initiatives operate independently, with only a few attempting to incorporate content-level information. This paper introduces a novel framework for modeling publication networks that utilizes topic metadata extracted via Latent Dirichlet Regression (LDR). We highlight the relevance of this approach to various fields, including science计量metrics, information retrieval, and social network analysis. Specifically, we introduce two new visibility metrics for publications and authors that reflect both the quantity and the diversity of information they contribute. These metrics are computed using only metadata, notably content-derived topics, without requiring access to the full text of the documents. Additionally, we provide directions for future work, including the extraction of additional content-based features and the creation of multilayered network models. Our findings indicate that papers with higher visibility, as measured by these new metrics, attract more citations, suggesting that such publications are more actively used by the scientific community. The code used in this study is openly available at {\url{http://能见bility.github.com/Publication-Visibility-in-Metadata}}.

In contemporary wireless networks, security has become a critical concern. While network layer security manages threats via encryption and access control, physical layer security (PLS) leverages signal processing and the unique characteristics of the wireless channel to mitigate eavesdropping and interference. Although prior studies have explored PLS in single-hop, multi-hop, and device-to-device (D2D) communications, rigorous investigations into multi-hop, OFDMA-based wireless systems remain scarce. This work addresses such a system where an base station (BS) offloads data to destination users via intermediate relay nodes. The proposed protocol allocates orthogonal sub-carriers to both source-relay and relay-user links. Although this simultaneous transmission introduces mutual interference, the protocol relies on diverse channel characteristics to facilitate decoding at the correct destinations. The Hofstadter spectrum, consisting of discrete bands separated by gaps, arises when electrons occupy lattice sites subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field. When this lattice is mapped onto an optical honeycomb structure, the spectrum closely resembles that of graphene. Although both lattices share a similar unit cell, their symmetry properties differ significantly. We demonstrate that it is possible to engineer effective hexagonal symmetries for electrons moving within the disparate bands of the Hofstadter spectrum by employing multi-beam laser configurations that create position-dependent couplings between nearest-neighbor lattice sites. Consequently, electrons can be guided into artificial graphene bands despite being located physically on a non-hexagonal lattice. This ability to selectively activate or deactivate electronic states by opening or closing specific band gaps allows for the precise routing, filtering, and entangling of electrons into isolated band modes. We illustrate this control by showing how to trap electrons in quasi-quantized life-times, where the decay rate is directly linked to the Chern number of the band, and by designing topological "giant atoms" that behave like their photonic counterparts. Additionally, we propose a simpler protocol for creating non-local time-bin entangled states, which only requires a single modulation of the atomic potential and can be generated from the spontaneous emission of a giant atom placed in the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-degenerate Dirac cones of graphene

This study tackles the challenge of generating safe CAV trajectories in such environments, with a specific focus on preventing rear-end collisions when preceding HDVs approach yellow or red signal phases. We introduce a predictive control framework that utilizes a recursive least squares algorithm to estimate the real-time driving behavior of leading HDVs, subsequently applying this estimation to compute safety-conscious trajectories over a finite horizon. The efficacy of our proposed framework is verified through numerical simulations, alongside an analysis of its robustness. Furthermore, we establish a sufficient condition for the stability of the overall system, alongside corresponding control design strategies. The core contributions of this paper are broadly applicable to the control cycles of existing signalized intersections, offering potential immediate practical implementation value. Additionally, the problem formulation aligns with federal funding priorities regarding automated vehicle deployments at current signalized intersections and lays the groundwork for future research into cooperative controls involving CAVs and HDVs.

At their core, online learning algorithms function as predictive models for reward structures. This paper advances the theoretical understanding of multi-armed bandit problems equipped with cyclic rewards. We introduce the Generalized Cyclic Multi-armed Bandit Problem (GCBMP), a conservative abstraction of intersections where vehicles move in the same direction under a leading signal. We demonstrate that any algorithm adapting to the general cyclic reward process can achieve a regret bound matching our established lower limit, effectively operating as if it were handling the simpler task of constant rewards. However, we also identify specific instances of GCBMP that exhibit exponentially worse adaptation requirements. Consequently, we define a set of easily verifiable conditions indicating when an algorithm can successfully adapt to cyclic rewards given only a known lower bound on the cycle's length. Satisfying these conditions is sufficient to guarantee that the algorithm's regret on GCBMP will not exceed the limits imposed by the "constant reward" adaptation capability, thus effectively bounding its overall regret.

Text-based games offer structured settings for testing common-sense logic and language understanding, yet they historically constrain experimental scale due to slow simulation speeds. We report a text-wide acceleration of these games and related writing simulations—such as Interactive Fiction, Dream Simulator, and Text Adventure—improving performance by over a thousandfold on modern desktops. This breakthrough paves the way for new text game experiences, updates to classic titles, and significantly expands the scope of scientific research in common-sense reasoning and language comprehension.

a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, we introduce the FDHT-LSTM, a model based on a fully decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure that maintains high accuracy with ultra-low complexity. To leverage these algorithmic advantages, we designed a specialized hardware architecture capable of executing the FDHT-LSTM efficiently. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Compared to state-of-the-art compressed LSTMs, FDHT-LSTM offers order-of-magnitude reductions in model size alongside significant accuracy gains across various video recognition datasets. Furthermore, against the state-of-the-art tensor decomposed hardware accelerator TIE, our FDHT-LSTM architecture achieves higher throughput, better area efficiency, and improved energy efficiency on the LSTM-Youtube workload. Similarly, on the LSTM-UCF workload, our design outperforms TIE in throughput and energy efficiency while maintaining comparable area efficiency. The accompanying code and evaluation scripts are accessible at https://github.com/baryong/LDHTEval. In summary, this research delivers the first specialized hardware accelerator for FDHT-LSTM, establishing it as the most efficient solution for both model size and computational performance for both the proposed FDHT-LSTM and existing LSTM variants.

However, this reliance on vast amounts of data hinders the deployment of NLP models in low-resource scenarios or novel domains, where acquiring labeled text demands substantial time, financial investment, and expertise. Recently, researchers have investigated data augmentation techniques to enhance data efficiency by generating synthetic samples that expand existing datasets. Despite these efforts, there has been insufficient empirical comparison of various augmentation methods in NLP, likely due to the scarcity of suitable benchmark datasets across diverse topics. To address this, we introduce a comprehensive suite of data augmentation strategies tailored for NLP and establish detailed evaluation protocols incorporating multiple metrics and downstream tasks. These evaluations reveal the significant potential of data augmentation in improving model performance on limited data and highlight the notably disparate results across different domains. Consequently, we advise against relying on a single domain-specific dataset for assessing augmentation techniques and emphasize the critical need for broader benchmark datasets spanning diverse topics in the future. Finally, we provide all evaluated codes and datasets as open source to facilitate ongoing research into efficient deep learning approaches for NLP.

In recent years, numerous challenges have arisen from deploying deep neural networks in real-world scenarios, particularly when labeled data is scarce, such as in new domains where annotating documents is difficult, expensive, or time-consuming. This has spurred interest in domain adaptation (DA), a learning framework designed to minimize distributional differences between source and target domains to enhance performance on unseen target data. Although various distributional measures and optimization algorithms have been proposed for DA, there remains a gap in systematically evaluating these approaches across different distributions and distributional measures. This paper presents a reproducible empirical study of distributional measures within self-supervised domain adaptation. We conduct an extensive experimental analysis across three distinct distributions and ten distributional measures. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals the current state of distributional measures in self-supervised domain adaptation and introduces several promising new techniques for future work. We release all code and datasets as open source to support the reproducibility of our findings and the community's continued exploration of distributional measures in self-supervised domain adaptation.

Model-space QITE (MSQITE) maintains orthogonality while propagating the model space toward the exact space, allowing it to describe multiple states at once. To enhance convergence, the quantum Lanczos (QLanczos) algorithm is adapted for MSQITE. Our scheme demonstrates superior performance compared to both standard QLanczos and the recently introduced folded-spectrum QITE when simulating excited states. Furthermore, we show that spin contamination can be effectively mitigated by exploiting the symmetry of the Hamiltonian to keep the Hamiltonian real, enabling the propagation of complex-valued states without requiring high-precision arithmetic. Finally, we examine the impact of Hamiltonian noise containing pure imaginary components, showing that while it causes decay in the norm of the wave function, it does not alter the states within the model space. This means that, similar to the unfolded QITE evolution, the quenching of higher-order excited states occurs at rates governed by the difference in excitation numbers between the target state and the model space. Consequently, convergence can still be achieved for excited states if the initial state on the quantum computer contains a significant component from the corresponding excitation level. This noise analysis also clarifies the mechanisms of convergence and relative performance for MSQITE and QLanczos in excited-state calculations. Finally, we address the preservation of norm in the limit of long evolution times within our scheme. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through examples including a transmon quantum circuit, a hydrogen molecular anion, a benzene dimer, and a four-node Kagome lattice. We conclude that the MSQITE is viable for computing excited states, offering improved stability and, in certain cases, faster convergence than its counterparts. The code is accessible via GitHub: https://github.com/ahmadreza-r/Model-space-QITE.

In contemporary arithmetic statistics, researchers often assume that the distribution of isomorphism classes of algebraic varieties over $\mathbf{F}_q$ converges, as $q$ tends to infinity, to a distribution over isomorphism classes over $\mathbf{Z}$ (or a suitable analog). This paper clarifies the connection between varieties defined over $\mathbf{Z}$ and those defined over $\mathbf{F}_q$, with a primary focus on the significance of reduction modulo $p$. Although the central concepts are intuitive, a rigorous treatment requires formalism; consequently, the main results are developed within the framework of tame topology for Grothendieck rings, as established in a preceding note by the author. The main theorem of this work, formulated using Grothendieck rings of smooth, proper schemes of a fixed dimension relative to a field $k$, asserts that the generating function enumerating isomorphism classes of these schemes over $\mathbf{F}_q$ (for a wide range of $q$) is rational when viewed as a function of $q$. This result extends a finding by Larsen and Rubinstein to a more general context. A similar argument, potentially supplemented with further refinements, could probably be adapted to yield analogous outcomes for other modern arithmetic statistics, such as those concerning Galois representations. In the final section, we consider the specific case of symmetric powers of elliptic curves, where the dimension of the schemes varies. Here, the reasoning is sufficiently explicit to serve as a foundation for a future, fully rigorous treatment in that setting. Along the way, we also establish necessary results regarding the "tame" Grothendieck ring, including a Chevalley-Deformation map homomorphism that parallels the characteristic map in classical tame representation theory.

This letter demonstrates that the HLS of group VI elemental monolayers, exemplified by Tellurene, can achieve dynamic stability when functionalized with Oxygen. The model represents fractures as $(d-1)$-dimensional interfaces within a $d$-dimensional domain, where $d$ equals 2 or 3. Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed {\it conductive}, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed {\it blocking}. Conductive fractures are modeled using a standard hybrid-dimensional interface approach assuming continuous pressure across the interface, whereas blocking fractures utilize a recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach that enforces continuity of the normal Darcy velocity component. A key innovation of this scheme is its ability to handle nonconforming meshes regarding blocking fractures, a capability enabled by the Dirac-$\delta$ formulation. Additionally, the numerical method yields locally conservative velocity approximations and generates a symmetric positive definite linear system defined solely on pressure degrees of freedom located at the mesh skeleton. Benchmark tests in both two and three dimensions demonstrate the method's performance, with results showing it to be highly competitive against existing literature approaches. This study represents the first application of the Dirac-$\delta$ formulation for solving Darcy flow problems. The proposed method is further illustrated through various applications, including well tests, doublet configurations, and fracture networks. Finally, the technique is extended to incorporate contact conditions for rocks containing blocking fractures and to simulate water injection in a fractured salt formation. conducting spin-triplet valve. The device comprises a superconducting film deposited on a metal exhibiting intrinsic spiral magnetism, which arises from either competing isotropic exchanges or asymmetric Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya exchange in crystals lacking central symmetry. Depending on the anisotropy, this metal's magnetization can transition from a spiral to a uniform state, as observed in Ho and Er, or align with the spiral direction, as seen in B20-type crystals like MnSi, (Fe,Co)Si, and FeGe. This nonuniform magnetic ordering governs the emergence of long-range triplet superconducting correlations under strong exchange fields, thereby influencing the nature of the proximity effect. We demonstrate that magnetic control of the spin-valve behavior is also achievable at moderately low exchange fields—typically insufficient for long-range triplet correlations—due to an orientation-dependent averaging mechanism of magnetic inhomogeneities relative to the Cooper pair scale. Our numerical simulations indicate that the spin-valve effect is actually enhanced at these moderately low exchange fields when the exchange splitting in the spiral magnet is not the smallest anisotropy component. Furthermore, we show that the high magnetic fields required for spin-valve operation in conventional ferromagnets can be reduced by approximately two orders of magnitude using an alloy such as Mn/Ge. These findings suggest that long triplet superconducting correlations can appear in superconductor-magnet heterostructures at relatively low external magnetic fields, providing critical insights for designing spin-triplet devices. Additionally, the demonstrated magnetic control of spin-valve effects opens possibilities for creating magnetic proximity valves with low threshold fields and high sensitivity to magnetic field variations within the low-field regime. These structures could serve as foundational elements in superconducting qubits, potentially offering significant improvements in their coherence times. Additionally, the proposed superconducting spin-valve may serve as a sensitive detector for nonuniform magnetic ordering, potentially offering an alternative method to probe the order parameter in systems with spiral magnetism. Finally, the increase in superconducting current caused by long-range triplet correlations may facilitate the observation of odd-frequency superconductivity through Josephson tunneling experiments. In conclusion, the proposed superconducting spin-valve opens up a broad spectrum of research and application prospects, including the observation of nonlocal superconducting currents, femtosecond magnetometry via terahertz voltage generation, superconducting qubits, and the detection of magnetic skyrmions.

Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Hypothesis testing serves as a crucial mechanism in science for determining which of several competing hypotheses best explains a dataset. Bayes factors provide a straightforward framework for this process by directly comparing the predictive accuracy of competing models against the data. While potentially more complex methods exist, they often lack the accessibility of Bayes factors, particularly for analysts with limited statistical training. We investigate the dependencies of Bayes factors on three key elements: the underlying statistics, the behavior of computational approximations, and the impact of errors in estimation. Specifically, we examine the variability of Bayes factor estimates when derived using bridge sampling, an approach that may not yield unbiased results for complex analyses—a concern we validate through both analytical methods and simulation studies. Our research underscores the need to view Bayes factor estimates as subject to uncertainty, ideally supplemented by utility functions to guide decisions under uncertainty. The findings presented here build upon the preliminary reports by Koster & Lee (2020) and Koster (2019), both located at https://osf.io

Recall from our previous discussion that a fundamental challenge in modeling the brain with artificial neural networks is the lack of a biologically plausible learning rule, particularly for backpropagation. To address this, we examine a training algorithm introduced by [1] that avoids backpropagation. Our analysis reveals three key aspects of this approach:

First, the algorithm sidesteps the non-biological nature of backpropagation itself. By utilizing local statistics rather than global error signals, it offers a biological alternative to backpropagation for artificial neural networks.

Second, the method establishes a biologically credible pathway for training multi-layer networks. As demonstrated in [2], this approach allows such networks to achieve high classification accuracy without requiring complex learning rules, implying that the cortex may be sufficient for training them.

Third, the algorithm provides a valid mechanism for learning in a discrete-time manner. By discretizing the activation function and applying the corresponding learning rule, the method effectively captures the network's training process.

Collectively, these insights underscore that backpropagation is not a prerequisite for artificial neural networks to attain high classification accuracy.

Artificial neural networks have demonstrated remarkable success in image classification [1], [2]. A longstanding hypothesis has been that the brain employs backpropagation for training [3]. However, this theory faces a significant obstacle: backpropagation requires identical gradients forward and backward through the network, a property that necessitates shared weights across layers—an arrangement not found in the brain [4]. This paper presents a training algorithm designed for a specific two-layer network architecture that avoids this contradiction. Our method computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to the first-layer weights directly from the target function, then uses this gradient to update the second-layer weights. Consequently, the resulting algorithm is both biologically plausible and highly effective.

Consequently, explosive synchronization transitions—enabling rapid, sudden shifts between these states—have recently attracted considerable research attention. Although prior studies have pinpointed specific properties of complex systems that enable explosive synchronization, these efforts have largely been conducted in an ad-hoc manner. In this work, we establish an exact criterion for explosive synchronization within coupled phase oscillator ensembles by examining the essential link between structural and dynamical disorder. This finding represents a pivotal advancement in disentangling the interconnected characteristics of complex systems that drive abrupt phase transitions and bistability in both biological and engineered contexts. Furthermore, by establishing a framework to investigate the complex dynamics of such platforms, our results offer promising prospects for achieving explosive synchronization in experimental coupled oscillator setups.

Phase transitions in finite-sized complex systems can occur suddenly and exhibit bursting behavior, phenomena that are critical for the functional operation of living organisms and the resilience of power grids and other engineered networks. While the mechanism of bursting has been associated with the coexistence of multiple attractors, the underlying mechanism for the abrupt nature of the transition remains unclear. We demonstrate that in finite-sized systems, the suddenness of the transition arises from the disorder of interactions, which can be exact in regular lattices but is often absent in random networks. Specifically, we show that near the critical point, the motion of the order parameter becomes ordered only in regular lattices, whereas it remains disordered in random networks. This explains the bursting dynamics as a combination of ordered motion on the critical manifold with the inherent stochasticity inherent to finite-sized disordered systems. Our findings provide a unifying framework for understanding previous reporting of bursting dynamics in magnetic, optical, and electrical coupled oscillator systems. Additionally, we utilize our analytical approach to predict the shape of the transition curve for any coupled system.

Previous investigations into explosive synchronization have typically relied on the existence of a macroscopic order parameter to detect the transition type, a method that is often impractical when the number of oscillators is limited. We examine a ring of coupled oscillators with long-range interactions to identify a signature of explosiveness that does not depend on order parameters. By analyzing the variance of the order parameter distribution, we establish a universal sign of explosive synchronization applicable to the majority of coupled oscillator systems. Based on the strong convexity of the geodesic line, the convergence rates of the geodesic gradient flow and the reparameterized gradient flow along this line are derived and compared. By altering the dimensions of the swimmer's body and helical tail, we demonstrated that the effect of viscoelasticity is highly dependent on the swimmer's geometry. Our introduced "social-learning" variants successfully establish this equilibrium, whereas "individual learning" versions fail to converge strategies to the Nash outcome. The paper addresses the issue of efficiently storing and retrieving images bearing semantic labels, aiming to deliver relevant images in response to user queries expressed in natural language. To achieve this, we develop a system comprising three core modules: (1) extracting discriminative features from images, evaluated against state-of-the-art methods and extended to handle parameter tuning via a meta-learner; (2) deriving semantic features from natural language queries using a neural network-based approach that achieves competitive performance on external validation datasets; and (3) combining these queries and image features into a dense vector representation using a cross-encoder strategy inspired by document ranking in Information Retrieval. This system has been deployed at scale, handling millions of daily queries and tens of millions of image updates. Extensive experiments indicate that our proposed framework significantly enhances relevance metrics compared to baseline systems.

Structuring security knowledge as an ontology enables anomaly detection, threat intelligence, reasoning, and attack relevance attribution, which in turn requires the dynamic and automated enrichment of such ontologies. The extent of this transmission relies on how virus-laden droplets evolve spatially and temporally amidst changing environmental factors. Consequently, this study examines droplet evolution considering Brownian motion, evaporation, gravity, and varying weather conditions. We track droplets until they either settle on the ground due to gravity or evaporate into aerosols measuring 2$\mu$m or smaller. Droplets with radii of 2$\mu$m or less can persist in the air for extended periods through diffusion. Our findings indicate that relative humidity and temperature significantly impact evaporation rates. Under strong airflow, droplets can travel considerable distances. Larger droplets tend to fall to the ground because gravitational forces dominate over diffusion, even as they lose mass through evaporation. Conversely, smaller evaporating droplets often remain suspended due to the supremacy of diffusive forces. The trajectory of intermediate-sized droplets is contingent upon weather conditions and plays a critical role in infection spread. These environment-dependent dynamics suggest that relying solely on physical distancing is insufficient to prevent viral transmission, thereby underscoring the necessity of wearing face masks. Finally, the study concludes that staying home during pandemic periods remains the most effective strategy to limit infection rates. This framework of COVID-19 dynamics involving droplets, aerosols, immunity, and infections is recognized as a droplet-based model. To address uncertainty regarding the proportion of asymptomatic individuals, we employ two sampling strategies: uniform and beta distributions. Simulations demonstrate that the infection timeline is influenced by asymptomatic cases, while the ultimate infection scope is more heavily affected by infectious sampling uncertainty and mask usage. Although mask efficacy is not uniform across all individuals, wearing masks benefits the community by reducing infection spread, even if some people wear them incorrectly or inconsistently. Furthermore, the impact of mask-wearing becomes more significant as the proportion of asymptomatic individuals rises. The simultaneous adoption of face masks and physical distancing is recommended to effectively curb infection outbreaks. This research aims to raise awareness of pathogen behavior and the factors governing infection dynamics. The study's code is available at https://github.com/pradeepl7/cov_droplet_model.

In conclusion, the simulation results indicate that the time to infection is affected by the prevalence of asymptomatic cases, whereas the total number of infections is more dependent on the uncertainty of infectious sampling and mask-wearing practices. We achieve this goal through the implementation of face masks and physical distancing within a droplet-based model.

However, quantifying errors and uncertainties within NN-based inference is significantly more complex than in conventional approaches. This complexity arises not only from aleatoric uncertainty linked to noisy data but also from epistemic sources such as limited data, NN hyperparameters, overparametrization, optimization and sampling errors, and model misspecification. While recent studies have touched upon uncertainty quantification (UQ) in NNs, there remains a lack of systematic investigation into effective and efficient methods for quantifying total uncertainty, even for basic function approximation. Furthermore, research on solving partial differential equations and learning operator mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces using NNs is particularly scarce. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, both novel and established solution techniques, evaluation metrics, and post-hoc improvement strategies. To validate the framework's applicability and reliability, we conduct an extensive comparative study testing various methods on prototype problems, including those with mixed input-output data and high-dimensional stochastic scenarios. Additionally, the Appendix provides a detailed description of all employed UQ methods, which will be released as an open-source library containing the complete code for this framework. The primary goal of this work is to establish a foundational framework for designing, evaluating, and enhancing future data-driven computational methods. By offering a robust assessment of uncertainty, this study will inform the creation of intelligent systems capable of making accurate decisions in real-world scenarios characterized by noisy data and complex environments.

This research addresses two critical challenges in learning operator mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces using neural networks: selecting an appropriate marginal distribution and optimizing the corresponding energy function. The proposed distributional learning approach employs a Schauder decomposition to model the marginal distribution of random coefficients for a basis function expansion of the output function. To avoid intractable high-dimensional integrals inherent in energy evaluation, we leverage recent advancements in random feature maps for defining the empirical energy. For parameter optimization, we utilize the limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (L-BFGS) algorithm due to the non-stochastic nature of the energy function. Numerical experiments on solving ordinary and partial differential equations validate the method's effectiveness. Finally, the supplementary material offers a thorough discussion on selecting the optimal marginal distribution and the count of random features.

By utilizing the Bessel process of the first kind, we derive the exact eigenvalue two-point functions for both models. We demonstrate that at finite $N$, the eigenvalue two-point correlation functions for the U($N$) and SU($N$) models are identical. Furthermore, we compute the leading $N$-cutoff correction to the large $N$ free energy at the critical temperature by applying the exact parton holography technique. It is demonstrated that the specific heat's logarithmic divergence at the transition temperature, a known field-theoretic feature of the pure $SU(N)$ Yang-Mills theory in four dimensions, arises from instanton effects rather than the beta function. Finally, we explore the non-Abelian tomography application of this framework, showing that the model's exact eigenvalue two-point functions can be leveraged for phase-retrieval algorithms. This Tomography-SEIRD approach enhances the standard two-point method by incorporating additional information about the initial eigenvalue distribution. We prove that tomographic information reduces the number of measurements required to reconstruct a random symmetric matrix by a factor of two, and we propose that non-Abelian tomography could similarly halve the puriton number needed to reconstruct the pure $SU(N)$ gluon field amplitude from its density. Consequently, tomographic techniques may offer a significant efficiency gain in small $N$ lattice simulations. Additionally, we speculate that the same approach could be applicable to quantum simulations of gauge theories, potentially reducing their computational cost. To achieve a speedup by a factor of two in lattice simulations of the pure $SU(N)$ gluon theory, one would need to double the lattice spacing, a modification that can be incorporated without disrupting the lattice discretization. We also note that the specific heat's logarithmic divergence at the transition is not merely an artifact of the finite $N$ limit; it appears in the $N\to\infty$ free energy when expressed in parton variables. This indicates that pure $SU(N)$ Yang-Mills theory possesses an intrinsic kinematic structure that decouples its dynamics into independent modes, as encoded in the exact parton wave functional. This structure could facilitate the implementation of the mode elimination technique, effectively solving the theory's dynamics. We conclude by suggesting that the findings of this and related works may aid in resolving the AMM controversy.

We address the challenge of optimizing nonconvex, high-dimensional machine learning problems, including deep neural networks, when the objective function evaluation involves uncertain parameters. We introduce a generic framework that casts these tasks as stochastic quasi-Brownian optimization problems and proves their equivalence to standard problems with access to a black-box gradient oracle. Leveraging this equivalence, we propose an algorithm combining stochastic integration Briley den Hester (2019) with local linear model assumptions. This approach is particularly useful for analyzing and creating hybrid methods that utilize additional problem information, like gradients, more efficiently. Our numerical evaluations on high-dimensional quadratic and nonconvex objectives, deep quadratic assignment problems, and convolutional neural networks confirm the algorithm's efficacy and demonstrate up to a tenfold reduction in training time for CNNs.

When solving high-dimensional machine learning problems with uncertain parameters via finite samples, the resulting objective functions are typically nonconvex. To locate near-global minimizers, it is essential to understand the landscape of these functions. This paper offers explicit upper bounds on the global optimality gap across various settings, derived directly from the function's global Lipschitz constant or growth rate. These bounds apply to randomly restricted graphs, random quadratic forms, and training error functions for fully connected and convolutional neural networks. Consequently, they yield novel sample complexity results for the guaranteed optimality gap and clarify the nonconvex nature of high-dimensional learning tasks. Practical implications are also discussed.

a concept with significant economic implications, shaping inter-company exchanges and interactions. Briefly, netting offers an alternative to standard payment methods by establishing an agreement where parties offset mutual debts. Instead of settling all individual transactions, a direct settlement is calculated based on the net amounts owed between two or more parties. This paper introduces a suite of graph algorithms designed to determine optimal netting solutions suitable for the scale of a national economy. These algorithms deliver results efficiently and have been validated using invoice data from the Romanian Ministry of Economy. Our findings demonstrate that classical graph algorithms remain effective in addressing critical modern challenges. Specifically, A* outperforms other methods in locating shortest paths within large graphs, APL finds maximum connected subgraphs nearly ten times faster, and Hopcroft-Karp is particularly effective for computing minimum card matchings in extensive graphs. Consequently, these algorithms are ideal for reserving computational resources for other pressing issues. Finally, we elucidate the mathematical foundations of netting and present an application framework for implementing these algorithms in this context. In conclusion, this study aims to stimulate interest among computer science professionals in developing solutions for economic problems.

The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted governments worldwide to impose movement restrictions on their citizens. While these measures successfully slowed the virus's spread, they simultaneously triggered significant isolated outbreaks on digital platforms. Understanding digital virus propagation is now essential for formulating anti-epidemic strategies in the virtual world. This study utilizes data from Twitter to provide a comprehensive understanding of COVID-19 dynamics across the United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom. By employing standard graph algorithms and leveraging the geographical context of social platforms, we categorized digital outbreaks into distinct clusters. Our results indicate that COVID-19 propagation follows a branching process with a basic reproductive number (R0) ranging from 1.1 to 1.5. These outbreaks manifest as country-specific phenomena with distinct temporal and spatial characteristics. To mitigate COVID-19 on digital platforms, we recommend targeting the most influential users, as even a minimal reduction in R0 can completely halt the infection's spread.

This study seeks to extend an epidemiological non-local model, previously effective in describing the 2005 French riots, to include the topological structure of Santiago's subway network and account for the observed spatial distribution of rioting. While the model accurately replicated the aggregated temporal progression of the disorders, it failed to reproduce the actual spatial pattern of activity in Santiago. This discrepancy is primarily due to the model's absence of a population displacement mechanism, a factor deemed essential for explaining the unrest episodes in the city. The discussion of these findings may offer insights into addressing similar issues in other urban environments. Finally, the conclusions are expected to inform discussions on the design of new control strategies for managing civil unrest. These outcomes underscore the value of mathematical modeling in addressing real-world challenges and highlight the necessity of incorporating additional variables to further refine such models.

The September 11, 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center in New York triggered a significant liquidity crisis within the financial system, largely due to the disruption of key funding markets that sustain the global economy, including G-Sec, repo, commercial paper, and interbank lending. This paper employs a DSGE framework to calibrate a model against the liquidity shock and its associated costs, offering a structural account of the event and contrasting it with narrative explanations found in economic literature. The findings indicate that the shock was too brief and intense for the entire duration of the attack to be the sole cause; instead, a secondary shock occurred later, contributing to the prolonged liquidity shortage. The study also explores policy implications and the advantages of utilizing a structural model in this context.

Although the first decade of GPS operation was thought to leave no remnants in the sky due to radio frequency interference (RFI), recent observations during deep sky surveys have detected a coherent signal at 1.274 GHz, the L1 GPS frequency. This study characterizes the signal's properties and investigates its origin using large-scale simulations of RFI from global surveys. The results confirm that the detection is plausible only if a substantial population of monkeys chirps at this specific frequency. Consequently, monkey chirps are proposed as a novel cosmic signal. Consequently, the detection of monkey chirps makes it possible to study their statistical properties and potential uses in both fundamental research and technological applications. Furthermore, the analysis of these chirps from different geographical regions allows for the estimation of the participating monkey population in RFI generation.

, the low-energy effective $3\times 3$ leptonic mixing matrix (LMM) typically becomes non-unitary. We re-examine our current understanding of individual LMM elements without relying on the unitarity assumption. By establishing two minimal categories of experimental constraints—direct and inherent bounds versus indirect bounds—we analyze their respective implications for leptonic non-unitarity. Furthermore, we clarify the handling of flux and cross-section predictions, specifically addressing new physics contamination within hadronic inputs. Additionally, we highlight the significance of long-baseline oscillation data in establishing precise general unitarity constraints for the LMM. . Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes. Furthermore, the model's efficiency is confirmed by using a lightweight network architecture, with the core component requiring less than 13 MB of memory. Our code and model are accessible at https://github.com/zeyadnassif/External-Memory-Attension-VO. In summary, our key contributions are: (1) a new efficient framework for visual-inertial odometry that effectively attends to visual information within a continuous memory space for pose estimation, (2) the development of an inward attention module that integrates visual features with inertial data to update visual memory for future use, (3) the creation of a reversible cross attention mechanism for accessing stored memory, (4) addressing the limitation of previous methods by handling diverse image illuminations and difficult textures, and (5) strong empirical evidence of the model's superiority over baseline systems for both regression and classification tasks. The overall model is compact, occupying less than 46 MB.

FedSA), a novel knowledge-amalgamation problem aimed at training a student model for a specific new task using multiple decentralized teacher models. These teachers possess pre-training tasks and datasets that are distinct and mutually unknown. Our motivation arises from a current challenge in model sharing: despite significant investments in training large, capable networks, researchers and institutions often cannot share their pre-trained models due to privacy, security, or intellectual property concerns, even when they wish to contribute. FedSA addresses this dilemma by enabling the creation of a specialized student model for a task different from any of the teachers' original domains. To achieve this, we propose a dedicated strategy where the student training process employs a new saliency-based method to adaptively select participating teachers and integrate their key capabilities. We evaluate FedSA's effectiveness across both single-task and multi-task scenarios. The experimental results confirm that FedSA successfully amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models, achieving performance competitive with centralized baselines. Furthermore, in multi-task evaluation, FedSA outperforms existing methods designed for knowledge fusion, demonstrating superior generalization to tasks that the teachers were not originally trained on. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/PranavSahai/FedSA.

In contemporary machine learning, tasks are frequently defined by the access to specific datasets. As the number of applicable tasks increases, many of these datasets become private, preventing tasks from being modeled as simple, public data classifications. To address this, we introduce PrivateTask(M), a general framework that extends the definition of a task beyond its computational algorithm to include the dataset used for training. Within this framework, we examine how algorithms can be trained to learn tasks without directly accessing the underlying datasets. We assess various extensions of Federated Learning (FL) that adapt this concept for machine learning, exploring how tasks can be made private and aggregated to form a composite task. Our study highlights both the significant advantages and the critical limitations of this approach in aggregating private tasks. These findings offer insights into extending FL, potentially informing a more robust definition of task privacy and its implications for problems like federated inverse control. Ultimately, we argue that extending FL to aggregate private tasks represents a crucial, yet challenging, evolution of the methodology.

Over the past half-century, scientists have gathered substantial evidence indicating that the brain encodes time through oscillating neural activity. However, the specific mechanism underlying this temporal representation remains unclear. Recent evidence suggests that a layer-by-layer neural network, termed the time grid, can function as an efficient time encoder. The grid-like discharge pattern observed in this model mirrors that of actual grid cells, implying that the entorhinal-hippocampal system may support a grid representation of time. This paper introduces the concept of the time grid and elucidates how it encodes temporal information. Additionally, it demonstrates that the grid firing pattern emerges naturally when the model is trained to predict future inputs based on current activity. Finally, the document highlights the significant potential of the time grid for solving various time-related problems and addresses several challenges that future research must overcome. Recent asteroseismology studies suggest that older solar-type stars may eventually reach a transition point where rotational braking ceases. Specifically, a "anti-solar" differential rotation pattern (characterized by fast poles and a slow equator) may occur in slow rotators with high Rossby numbers. If this regime manifests during the main sequence, it raises questions about its impact on magnetic generation via the dynamo process, particularly regarding whether slowly rotating stars can still exhibit magnetic cycles.

Our analysis reveals that kinematic $\alpha\Omega$ dynamos can support magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals in both rotation regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is concentrated at the tachocline. If the $\alpha$-effect is instead distributed throughout the convection zone, solar-type configurations maintain cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. In contrast, traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos fail to sustain magnetic cycles in the anti-solar differential rotation regime due to issues with flux addition. We provide graphical interpretations for these scenarios and note that hybrid models combining both approaches can still produce solar-type cycles. These findings underscore the necessity of refining global solar dynamo models to incorporate the complexities of subsurface structure. Ultimately, we argue that future magnetic-cycle cases in anti-solar stars could provide critical constraints for enhancing the physical realism of theoretical frameworks.

Quantum computing relies on superconducting circuits, which currently offer the most promising and scalable platform for building practical quantum computers. To achieve this goal, it is critical to identify and repair material defects that lead to decoherence. Terahertz (THz) imaging enables the quantitative determination of the conductivity of thin semiconductor layers, which directly influences quantum coherence. Therefore, we developed a precise extraction protocol for the permittivity of thin films using near-field spectroscopy. This protocol accounts for experimental parameters, such as the specific geometry of superconducting feedlines, and correctly handles the extraction of permittivity values, including those in the metal loss regime. The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, encompassing questions that span multiple disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, beginning with volatile sources and sinks, and trace the path from the deep interior to the upper atmosphere, covering volcanic outgassing, surface-atmosphere interactions, and atmospheric escape. Additionally, we address complex historical factors, such as the impact of Late Accretion events, the connection between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the effects of geochemical and geodynamical feedback cycles on the atmosphere. Based on modeling and observations, we outline plausible evolutionary pathways for Venus from accretion to its present state. Three specific scenarios are highlighted: first, desiccation caused by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase; second, a prolonged period of surface liquid water followed by climate destabilization and a runaway greenhouse effect; and third, inefficient outgassing that retained water within the planet, trapping hydrogen in the core and oxidizing the mantle. Finally, we discuss current evidence and the future observations and missions needed to refine our understanding of Venus's history and the intricate feedback cycles operating among its interior, surface, and atmosphere across past, present, and future timescales.

Venus occupies a critical position in solar system evolution, serving as a comparative benchmark for both Earth and Mars to shed light on planetary formation, evolution, and habitability. While all three planets possess atmospheres and are composed of similar materials in comparable proportions, their divergent evolutionary trajectories have resulted in vastly different present-day climates. Uncovering the mechanisms that drive such differences between rocky planets is vital for refining current planetary models. This article reviews plausible evolutionary pathways for Venus, Hellenic feedback cycles involving its interior and atmosphere, and the observational evidence required to validate or reject these scenarios. We outline four distinct model outcomes for Venus's long-term development: (1) a dry core due to extensive water loss via escape while the surface remained molten; (2) a dry core following a prolonged era of volcanic outgassing and recurrent surface oceans, culminating in a runaway greenhouse that drove water loss; (3) a dry core caused by inefficient outgassing that sequestered hydrogen in the core; and (4) an atmosphere lacking carbon dioxide, with surface conditions governed by direct equilibrium between outgassing and chemical reactions between water and the mantle or by fractional distillation. The "quantum-inspired" architecture of TNs allows them to be translated into parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), a capability that has spurred recent proposals to boost TN performance using near-term quantum hardware and to create hybrid training frameworks that leverage the unique advantages of both TNs and PQCs. Nevertheless, the viability of these approaches hinges on the existence of efficient and precise techniques for approximating TN states with practical quantum circuits—a challenge that remains unsolved. This study evaluates various circuit synthesis strategies for converting arbitrary matrix product states (MPS) of dimension $D$ into equivalent PQCs with qubit count $n=D/\log_2{4}$. These methods range from straightforward but slow layer-by-layer synthesis to sophisticated sequence-algorithms designed for minimal circuit depth. Our findings indicate that these synthesis techniques generally preserve the fidelity of the initial MPS to high accuracy, typically exceeding $1-\mathcal{O}(\log_2{D}/n^2)$. To demonstrate the utility of these synthesis methods for machine learning, we adapt two recent high-performance TN algorithms for PQCs: the variational uniform matrix product state (VUMPS) ground state solver and the time-evolving matrix product state (TEMPS) ground state solver. When applied to quantum circuits, these algorithms function as efficient warm-start techniques that significantly accelerate training. We also introduce a novel circuit synthesis algorithm specifically tailored to maximize MPS fidelity, which outperforms existing techniques across all tested cases. Together, these results validate the feasibility and performance of TN algorithms applied to PQCs, offering valuable insights for future research into quantum-classical hybrid systems. We release our code as an open-source library, the Quantum State Toolkit (QSTK), accessible here: https://github.com/MaxenceLhuiller/QSTK. We anticipate that these synthesis methods will be universally applicable and that our insights will advance future quantum-classical hybrid machine learning initiatives.

therapy response from tissue samples relies heavily on the phenotype and spatial arrangement of histological components, making robust tissue representations essential for computer-aided oncology. While previous methods have employed cell-graphs to encode cellular morphology and organization for machine learning applications, cellular data are inherently noisy, difficult to annotate, and sparse. To address these challenges, we introduce Cell-org, a cellular organization model that encodes cell types, morphologies, and spatial relationships into a low-dimensional embedding for tissue classification and prognosis. Unlike graph-based approaches, Cell-org utilizes a generative variational autoencoder (VAE) with a novel asymmetric posterior to learn from unsupervised cell-image patches, enabling efficient and accurate encoding even with limited cellular data. To validate the model's utility in cancer prognosis, we applied it to predict chemotherapy response in breast cancer using tissue sections varying in cellular density. The resulting low-dimensional embeddings achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.8388, surpassing both histological image-based methods (AUROC of 0.7215) and graph-based approaches (AUROC of 0.6815). Consequently, Cell-org offers a cost-effective and precise method for inferring cellular organization from histological images, demonstrating significant potential for cancer diagnosis and prognosis. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhifenghu/Cell-org.

Among these, the Hawkes process is particularly popular due to its ability to define the probability of new events based on the process's history. This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. Within a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we derive concentration rates for the posterior distribution regarding the parameters, assuming only mild conditions on the prior and the model. These findings also establish convergence rates for Bayesian estimators. Additionally, a key aspect of event-data modeling is reconstructing the interaction graph, or Granger connectivity graph. We demonstrate consistency guarantees for Bayesian approaches in estimating this structure, specifically proving that the posterior distribution remains consistent for the process's graph adjacency matrix and that a Bayesian estimator using an appropriate loss function achieves consistency. Finally, we validate our theoretical results with a numerical simulation and a case study on Twitter data concerning an earthquake. In this case study, we also address the challenge of missing data and evaluate various strategies for handling it. Our results indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing techniques in estimating the interaction graph, even when the data is incomplete.

This manuscript aims to establish consistency for the Bayesian estimation of a Hawkes process. It begins by defining the model and data likelihood, then proceeds to bound the Kullback-Leibler divergence using specific inequality techniques. Subsequently, we construct a sieve and define a specific radius, subsequently demonstrating that the logarithm of the metric entropy of this sieve is also bounded appropriately. Finally, these components are integrated to complete the consistency proof.

is renowned for its ideal conservation properties, guaranteeing exact preservation of total mass, energy, and both linear and angular momentum up to machine precision when correctly implemented. This feature is crucial for computational astrophysics applications involving binary dynamics, mergers, and the accretion of compact objects like neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs. However, in scenarios requiring gravity, the computational cost of calculating pairwise particle interactions becomes prohibitive. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) addresses this by substituting these interactions with symmetric forces between distant particle clusters organized in tree nodes. While standard FMM conserves linear momentum, it generates spurious torques that compromise angular momentum conservation. This paper introduces a modified FMM that eliminates these spurious torques and ensures explicit angular momentum conservation, all with negligible computational overhead compared to the conventional approach. This adjustment also removes the necessity for the artificial gravity screening often employed to bypass the low-order multipole limitations of conventional FMM. The resulting algorithm is especially valuable for simulating high-mass-ratio binary systems, accretion onto compact objects, and merger events, where both conservation laws are critical for accurately modeling the system's evolution. In systems where mass is not individually conserved due to particle spawning and death, the method is further extended to conserve total system linear and angular momentum, with particle deaths contributing to these quantities based on their velocity and position relative to the system's center of mass. Test systems demonstrate that this new algorithm preserves angular momentum to within machine epsilon. Finally, the paper discusses extending the technique to scenarios where angular momentum is only approximately conserved, such as when self-gravitating particle clouds are driven by non-self-similar forces like SPH. In these cases, the scheme retains the desirable conservation of linear momentum while minimizing errors in angular momentum to the level of the original FMM. The paper provides references to existing FMM applications in other fields, including electrodynamics and fluid dynamics. The supplementary material offers additional details on the derivation of the new scheme in simpler terms, along with examples of its extension to systems with approximate conservation laws. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AmirSi/ANG-FMM.

While Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) offers a path to reduce annotation needs, its effectiveness remains constrained when datasets are small or contain few labeled images. Utilizing pre-annotated datasets featuring similar anatomical structures holds promise for enhancing model performance; however, this approach faces significant hurdles due to cross-domain distribution shifts between source and target datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Semi-Supervised Learning (CSSL), a framework designed for robust tissue segmentation via transfer learning from external, pre-annotated sources. Specifically, we adapt Contrastive Learning (CL) to create robust feature extractors through self-supervised strategies, then refine them using a small pool of labeled images via fine-tuning. Our method preserves the core principle of CL—maximizing the contrast between positive and negative samples—while adapting it to the medical imaging context. A key innovation is the incorporation of rEMD loss, which optimizes the reorganized empirical measure distance to effectively leverage the external dataset's structural similarity to the target anatomy. Extensive experiments confirm that CSSSL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised and supervised methods on both synthetic and real-world medical image segmentation tasks. To encourage further research into efficient and accurate medical image segmentation, we have made the trained models and a reproducible codebase available at https://github.com/TianlongGong/CSSL.

We introduce a plasma waveplate utilizing magneto-optical birefringence under a transverse magnetic field, designed to operate under ultra-high intensity. This device offers advantages over solid-state waveplates, including scalability, flexibility, and enhanced damage resistance. By employing numerical simulations, we demonstrate that a compact waveplate under feasible plasma conditions can achieve half-wave retarding capabilities with less than 0.1% polarization error, even at peak powers exceeding 10^23 W. Furthermore, we examine its application as a switchable half-wave plate when paired with a second, variable-thickness plasma waveplate. Additionally, our analysis of solid-state waveplate performance under ultra-high intensity reveals that solid-state materials can function as half-wave plates up to powers of approximately 10^22 W, but develop significant phase errors when used as variable thicknesses for modulation, highlighting the superior adaptability of the proposed plasma design. Ultimately, this compact, highly efficient plasma waveplate holds promise for enhancing the capabilities of petawatt-class optical systems.

Plasma-based optical elements are becoming essential for petawatt-class laser facilities, which push the limits of solid-state optics. We propose using an ionized gas under a transverse magnetic field as a half-wave plate (HWP) to convert linearly polarized light into circularly polarized light. Unlike solid-state alternatives, this plasma HWP can withstand peak powers up to $10^{23}$ W (intensities of $10^{29}$ W/cm$^2$), handling a 50% phase error margin. The device is compact, weighing only a few grams with dimensions around 1 x 1 x 10 cm^3, and is fully customizable for specific applications. Its robustness at ultra-high power levels could enable new circularly polarized light experiments, potentially enabling the creation of repelling optical lattices and creating conditions where the electric field fluctuates on a timescale comparable to the light's optical cycle.

To achieve this effectively, researchers must look beyond the traditional quadratic estimator (QE), which is becoming suboptimal, and the maximum a posteriori estimator, which is still in development. (2020) demonstrated that a neural network (NN) using the ResUNet architecture outperforms the QE but remains slightly suboptimal compared to an iterative estimator for lensing reconstruction. This study advances those findings by evaluating how these estimators perform in delensing maps containing primordial tensor perturbations using both full sky and patchy sky simulations. The full sky simulation mimics the next-generation SPT-CCMCon combination ($\sim$10,000 deg$^2$ at 100 GHz), while the patchy sky sky approximates the future CMB S4 experiment ($\sim$100 deg$^2$ at 40 GHz). Our results indicate that the NN estimator achieves nearly optimal delensing performance in both scenarios, surpassing the QE in all cases. Notably, the NN estimator's performance in the patchy sky simulation is approximately 5% more effective than in the full sky simulation, suggesting that future small-scale experiments could deliver the most significant delensing gains. Finally, we assess the impact of computational constraints, showing that even with a 10-hour limitation on delensing calculations for the patchy sky, the NN estimator remains superior to the QE. These discoveries underscore the universal nature of the NN estimator's dominance and highlight the need to study its performance across various experimental configurations. Understanding the estimator's behavior under different conditions and computational limits is essential for determining the optimal strategy for maximizing delensing efficiency in upcoming CMB observations.

### I. Introduction

Rotating compact objects, such as neutron stars and black holes, are significant targets for both observational and theoretical research. Their rapid rotation is critical for interpreting high-energy astronomical data, understanding the evolution of binary systems, understanding the nucleosynthesis of rapid neutron-capture (r-process) elements, and interpreting gravitational wave signals from mergers. Theoretical investigations into the structure, stability, and dynamics of these objects demand accurate numerical handling of their complex physics and equations. Our group utilizes the general-relativistic extension of the COOLING code to simulate the dynamical evolution of self-gravitating fluid systems. Urban areas globally have implemented stringent lockdown measures to flatten infection curves and reduce strain on healthcare systems during the COVID-19 crisis. These interventions dramatically altered where, when, and how people interact. Yet, the impact of such restricted and diverse interactions on the spread of other infectious diseases, including malaria and tuberculosis, remains unexplored. This paper investigates distinct scenarios of interaction diversity using the mixing model framework. Findings suggest that even minor reductions in interaction diversity can substantially lower infection risks for other diseases. Therefore, lockdown strategies derived from COVID-19 may inadvertently offer benefits for controlling other epidemics, a hypothesis that warrants further investigation.

Understanding the diversity of urban interactions is essential for assessing their consequences on disease transmission, though measuring this metric remains challenging. This work introduces entropy-based indicators of interaction diversity measurable via mobile data, along with their connections to socioeconomic factors and urban design. Insights gained from studying these diverse interactions may yield novel insights into urban dynamics and offer actionable strategies for enhancing both interaction diversity and disease prevention.

-mass young stellar objects (HMYSOs) often fragment into multiple self-gravitating bodies, a process that may account for recently observed episodic accretion bursts. By applying a 1D code to resolve dynamics down to the stellar surface, we post-processed prior 3D simulation results. Our findings reveal that the burst-like deposition of material into the inner disc observed in 3D models does not invariably produce powerful accretion bursts; instead, only high-density clumps that have undergone collapse and crossed the inner computational boundary generate observable bursts. The complex physics of the inner disc significantly influences these bursts in four key ways: (1) While objects in standard turbulent viscosity discs may stall at migration traps a few astronomical units from the star, those in magnetised wind-driven discs can cross these traps to create bursts matching current observations. (2) Migrating objects can interact with and alter the thermal (hydrogen ionisation) instability of the inner disc, potentially causing longer-lasting, lower-luminosity bursts in HMYSOs. (3) If the central star is bloated by prior high-accretion episodes or if the migrating object is sufficiently dense, the outcome is a merger rather than a disc-mediated burst. (4) Disruption bursts from these objects may exceed the Eddington limit, driving episodic feedback on the HMYSO environment through powerful outflows. These observations offer insights into the episodic formation of high-mass stars and stellar companions. Additionally, we present results for a specific scenario where an object stalls approximately 10 AU from the star, accreting at a rate of ~10-8 Msun yr-1 for a million years before collapsing in a burst exceeding the Eddington limit. This event disrupts the surrounding disc, channeling further accretion and extending the low-luminosity phase for approximately 4.5 Myr. These effects are plausibly applicable to other HMYSOs, potentially offering a path to explaining the dual-timescale merger and disruption events seen in exoplanet simulations and the creation of high-luminosity transients from intermediate-mass star formation. Finally, we note that the dominant electromagnetic signature of these bursts is likely in the UV/X-ray spectrum rather than optical or infrared, distinguishing them from migration bursts from exoplanet-scale objects. These results align with the trend that higher-accretion rates from discs lead to more powerful but shorter-duration bursts.

This work investigates the detectability of fake news using the Mediterranean Sea as a case study. It demonstrates that one-hot encoding, bag-of-words, and pre-trained embeddings like GloVe yield suboptimal results, achieving an average accuracy of only 51%. The reduced-order modeling of fluid dynamics has seen substantial recent development, yet its application to coupled problems like FSI is still emerging. Although the reduced basis method is a well-established technique for solving large-scale computational fluid dynamics equations, its use in solving complete FSI systems requires careful selection of the reduction sequence. This work compares two such methods applied to a challenging test case. The first method reduces the discretized systems of both the fluid and solid before coupling, showing superior stability but at a higher computational cost. The second method solves the full discretized fluid and solid systems independently, coupling them to form a single system to be reduced; this approach is less stable but more efficient. These findings offer insights into selecting an appropriate reduction strategy depending on the specific characteristics of the problem being addressed.

Autonomous navigation in unknown environments relies on the robot's ability to build maps and generate obstacle avoidance routes. Since the ROS Nox system's introduction over a decade ago, dual laser line scanners have been the preferred sensor for this task, typically producing global metric maps. However, the storage required for these maps grows linearly with the robot's travel distance, making them impractical for large-scale unknown area exploration. Although probabilistic mapping algorithms like GMapping and HEbAM can operate effectively in dynamic settings, their dependence on global metric maps remains a significant limitation. Recent advancements based on semantic feature detection and keypoint matching—such as those employing D-KNN graphs or SE(3) Hammersmith networks—offer higher dimensionality and richer information. Nevertheless, the computational demands and data requirements of these approaches remain prohibitive for single-board computer implementation on small, power-constrained platforms. This work presents a solution for dual laser line scanner-based mapping and navigation that balances performance, data efficiency, and real-time capabilities. The proposed HiTMap represents a topological map structure, storing submaps as global metric maps to enable efficient local obstacle avoidance while minimizing data overhead. Additionally, frontiers are recorded as map attributes to support the exploration of new areas, and a path planning module was created to assess the HiTMap's performance. The evaluation includes results from both simulation and a real dual laser scanner setup, with the results confirming the success and advantages of the HiTMap system.

challenge in metrology. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. This approach offers an alternative to the Balian-Weshak theorem, which asserts that the local magnetic field outside a superconductor is not strictly zero but rather fluctuates with molecular significance. Furthermore, the success of this experiment may offer another sensitive probe for minute effects related to superconductivity, such as those associated with hypothetical extra dimensions. The main components of this setup have already been demonstrated in prior Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry experiments. Atomic interferometry thus provides a practical and sensitive method for detecting weak fields arising from the local field effect and can serve as a experimental test for the validity of the Balian-Weshak theorem in a macroscopic context. Additionally, the framework of this work may be applicable to other scenarios involving the detection of weak forces or fields, including the direct observation of gravitational dipole interactions or the axion-induced Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen spin dipole-dipole interaction between fermions.

Ultimately, the direction of the MCE is governed by the interplay between exchange and Rashba interactions, offering a pathway to realize anomalous, spin-polarized magnetocaloric behavior in 2D materials.
