We have identified a broad category of object-oriented programs, including many significant real-world applications, that can be efficiently executed on massively parallel SIMD accelerators. We term this category Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), as it expresses parallelism by executing a specific method across all instances of a given type.

To enable average programmers to utilize fast GPU programming for SMMO applications, we developed DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework. DynaSOAr comprises three core components: (1) a fully parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator; (2) a data layout Domain-Specific Language (DSL); and (3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. By controlling both memory allocation and access, DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization by adopting a Structure of Arrays (SoA) data layout and reduces memory fragmentation through the efficient management of free and allocated blocks using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps. Unlike other allocators, our design relies heavily on atomic operations, prioritizing overall application performance over individual thread efficiency. Atomic operations are highly efficient on modern GPUs due to hardware-supported, flush-to-writeback-cache mechanisms.

The do-all operation supports various access patterns commonly found in soA-access methods within SMMO applications. By relying on fundamental CPU-GPU do-all primitives, DynaSOAr is portable and can be easily adapted to other accelerators.

Experimental results demonstrate that DynaSOAr achieves up to a 3.8× speedup in applications with loosely coupled object interactions. These interaction patterns are typical in object-based scientific simulations such as Monte-Carlo methods, molecular dynamics, and particle filters. Consequently, DynaSOAr significantly improves the performance of: the Monte-Carlo integration method for computing high-dimensional integrals; the Molecular Dynamics application LAMMPS; and the Particle Filter Ensemble Kalman Filter used in weather forecasting. The speedups range from 1.6× to 27×, depending on problem size and dimensions. Additionally, DynaSOAr delivers up to a 5.1× speedup in CPU high-performance applications with moderately coupled interactions,

In chirped pulses, the temporal variation of frequency relative to the fundamental frequency induces a corresponding time-dependent critical density ($n_c$). We employed a chirp model that extends beyond linear approximations. Specifically, negatively (positively) chirped pulses initially interact with the target via their high (low) frequency components, followed by low (high) frequencies. Our findings indicate that the threshold plasma density required for pulse transmission is elevated for negatively chirped pulses compared to unchirped or positively chirped ones. At higher densities ($6n_c$), the improved transmission of negatively chirped pulses facilitates efficient electron heating, generating a stable, persistent longitudinal electrostatic field behind the target. This creates an electron void that drives ions to expand in both directions, yielding a broad energy spectrum. Furthermore, we introduced a thin, low-density ($< n_c$) secondary layer behind the primary target. Ions from this secondary layer are accelerated as a mono-energetic bunch by the electrostatic field established by the primary layer upon interaction with the negatively chirped pulse. Under optimal conditions, proton energies reach approximately 100 MeV using a 10 fs (intensity fwhm), circularly polarized, Gaussian, negatively chirped laser pulse with a peak intensity of $\sim 8.5\times 10^{20}$ W/cm$^2$. Additionally, we analyzed the impact of pulse polarization and thickness on acceleration performance. Our results suggest that a 2.5-fold increase in proton energy can be achieved using a multi-layer target system for mono-energetic acceleration, whereas directions opposite to the proton beam flow remain unchanged. These outcomes are relevant to applications involving circularly polarized pulses, low-density plasma, and multi-layer targets for generating intense proton beams. Our conclusions are robust across slight variations in target thickness and pulse chirp parameters. This approach holds significant potential for producing giant, intense proton beams suitable for medical use and materials modification. We also derived precise expressions for the required degree of pulse chirping and the optimal plasma density.

Elucidating the fundamental properties of the top quark remains a central focus of LHC physics. Due to the top quark's short lifetime, it does not hadronize; instead, it decays before forming bound states, making it the only known particle that allows direct access to the Standard Model through its decay characteristics. Consequently, measuring its decay modes is essential for determining the particle's mass with maximum precision and for uncovering potential deviations from the Standard Model. This paper addresses the question of determining the maximum value of $\lambda$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ guarantees a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor with a vertex set possessing an upper density of at least $\lambda$, for a given finite graph $F$. We establish a novel lower bound for this problem; for specific graphs $F$, including cliques and odd cycles, this bound is optimal as it aligns with a previously known upper bound. Our proof strategy involves first demonstrating that the complete integer can be partitioned into two sets of comparable size (each with a density of at least $1/2-\varepsilon$) in one color, yielding a $F$-factor within that set in the opposite color. To achieve this, we employ robust expansion properties associated with the smallest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix of $F$. Using the WHAM code, we simulated the circularly polarized laser-foil experiment recently conducted by the FASIR collaboration and adjusted the laser intensity to replicate their 50% positron polarization. Our simulation confirms their measurement of the energy spectrum. This method of generating polarized positrons is efficient, compact, and practical, offering unique prospects for nuclear and particle physics research.

Additional components include an I2C master interface for data readout, a timer for interval control, and a power-gating module for consuming minimal power during off periods. Experimental results from a testbench validate the sensor's performance, confirming accurate digitization of voltage outputs and successful data transfer via the I2C protocol. The implementation is possible due to the modular nature of the circuit, and the sensor is fully functional within a 2x1 mm² area, achieving an average power consumption of 1.19mW at 85°C and a resolution of 0.07°C. Furthermore, the core circuit occupies a compact area of 0.04mm², consuming 16μW with a resolution of 0.004°C. This design represents the first integration of such a sensor with an I2C interface utilizing on-chip digital components. The proposed sensor has been implemented in 180nm CMOS technology, requiring only 0.026mm² of area with a clock frequency of 500KHz.

While it has been analytically shown that purely toroidal or purely poloidal fields inevitably develop instabilities, numerical simulations confirm that roughly axisymmetric configurations within stably stratified stars can remain stable. These stable setups involve twisted torus structures where toroidal and poloidal components mutually reinforce one another. Previous investigations have estimated approximate upper and lower limits for the ratio of magnetic energy between these two components. To explore the parameter space governing the stability of such configurations, we employed the Pencil Code to conduct 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations of magnetic field evolution in non-rotating, non-degenerate stars, where viscosity serves as the sole dissipation mechanism. Our simulations covered stars with both uniform (barotropic) and radially increasing (stably stratified) specific entropy, varying conditions for the degree of stratification and the magnetic energy distribution. These results broadly corroborate the previously proposed stability boundaries for the magnetic field. Furthermore, for the highest stratification and most extreme magnetic energy partitioning cases, our simulations revealed that the magnetic energy density peaks in the outermost layers, near the surface. The overall findings support the concept of the "missing envelope field," characterizing a strong magnetic field where the purely toroidal component is confined to the core. Additionally, we constructed self-diffusion timescales based on the observed magnetic energy partitioning and their implications for the magnetic evolution of degenerate stars. Our conclusions remain robust whether the stellar plasma is modeled as a perfect fluid or incorporates a finite Prandtl number.

Its utility depends on deriving flow equations that track the evolution of the quantum effective action as a coarse-graining parameter varies. This study details a new strategy for solving these equations by leveraging the fact that renormalization group (RG) equations can be reformulated to mirror fluid dynamics conservation laws. This analogy enables two main advancements: first, it permits the use of robust numerical methods from fluid dynamics to solve RG equations, ensuring reliable handling of nonanalytic behaviors in the effective action's flow, such as those arising from spontaneous symmetry breaking. Second, the fluid dynamics parallel offers fresh perspectives on interpreting RG flows and their inherent irreversibility. We demonstrate this connection using zero-dimensional quantum field theory models, with a discussion of extending it to higher dimensions. These results are anticipated to enhance future FRG investigations of quantum field theories in higher dimensions, improving both qualitative understanding and quantitative accuracy. In specific cases, we show that this approach yields functional solutions for theory saddles that were previously unattainable. Finally, we provide open-source software accessible at https://github.com/miguelaeangel/FRG_fluid.

We address three critical challenges in solving the functional renormalization group (FRG) equation within the $\lambda \varphi^4$ model in $d=2$ dimensions: handling ultraviolet (UV) divergences, managing spurious singularities in the running coupling, and achieving precise determination of the Wilson $f$-function near the infrared (IR) fixed point. By employing an independent regulator function, we confirm previous findings regarding the $f$-function's behavior. We extend these calculations to compute the full saddle point distribution for the order parameter, observing that the tail behavior of the saddle point $f$-function is highly regulator dependent. Consequently, we establish a novel procedure to determine the IR $f$-function robustly, even when UV divergences are present. This allows us to calculate the saddle point distribution's tails accurately, revealing a significant missing component in prior literature: a heavy tail corresponding to a nonvanishing probability of large but finite field configurations. We also examine the implications of these results for the specific heat.

users continue to depend on text-based platforms like Google for pop music. We introduce Pied Piper, a meta search engine designed specifically for music. It allows users to query lyrics, song metadata, audio files, or any combination thereof, efficiently delivering relevant results. Leveraging advanced natural language processing, the tool intelligently routes queries to optimal specialized engines to maximize accuracy. Additionally, it processes media files directly: extracting text from labels or inserts, and recognizing instruments, genres, or song details from audio recordings. By automatively selecting the most suitable backend services, we significantly improved result relevance while reducing response times compared to executing queries on individual engines manually. Pied Piper features a clean, intuitive interface that renders it accessible to users of all ages and technical backgrounds. This project serves as an impressive showcase of the enduring versatility of natural language processing and demonstrates how such initiatives are fundamental to creating a trustworthier internet.

In the early 2000s, I began developing a music player for the PlayStation 2 that could identify songs from audio snippets or lyrics. At the time, I lacked access to necessary data and efficient search algorithms, making the concept seem unfeasible. Today, with the availability of high-quality datasets like MusicNet and Facebook's Disco, alongside powerful search methodologies, the dream has become reality. Pied Piper is a comprehensive media search engine capable of handling every query type related to music, from lyrics and metadata to raw audio. Beyond song identification, it functions as a detailed catalog allowing users to explore and listen to entire albums.

To deliver optimal results, queries are routed to specialized sub-engines focused on specific data types, a strategy reminiscent of the early RockBox project. However, unlike RockBox, which required manual selection of the appropriate engine, Pied Piper autonomously determines the best source for each user, ensuring both high relevance and speed. The system supports a diverse range of queries including full-song listening, genre identification, city name recognition, celebrity voice detection, and more.

The engine recently achieved remarkable success in identifying songs from audio on the ABC Television Network. Users can now determine if a driving playlist is inspired by Pink Floyd or find the exact track when hearing a new song on the radio. Pied Piper also excels at providing metadata for releases from any era, such as finding the release year for The Beatles' "Love Me Do" or the lyricist for Michael Jackson's "Who Is It."

Statistical tests reveal that protostellar cores possess greater mass than starless cores, even when accounting for biases related to temperature and opacity. We propose that this mass disparity signifies core growth occurring after formation. -energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major unsolved challenge in high-energy astrophysics. A promising strategy to address this mystery involves correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos, as neutrinos directly trace hadronic interactions and remain unaffected by magnetic deflection. This paper outlines three distinct methods for correlating the arrival directions of these particles. Data on neutrinos come from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES, while UHECR data (with energies exceeding ~50 EeV) are sourced from the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. Both datasets offer enhanced statistics and refined reconstructions compared to our 2015 findings. The first analysis employs a high-statistics neutrino sample optimized for point-source detection to identify excesses of neutrinos clustering near UHECR trajectories. The second method looks for an excess of UHECRs pointing toward the highest-energy neutrinos, while the third examines excesses of UHECR-neutrino pairs across various angular scales. No significant excesses were detected in any of these analyses, and previously reported over-fluctuations have seen their statistical significance diminished. Consequently, these results allow for tighter constraints on the spatially correlated neutrino flux associated with UHECRs. These constraints are particularly relevant for theories involving new physics that enable light charged Higgs bosons or heavy neutrinos within the EeV energy regime. Finally, we projected the expected sensitivity of this correlation search for future data collections.
A cosmic ray proton with an ultra-high energy is unlikely to traverse the Milky Way without undergoing an interaction with a neutron. If protons of even higher energies were detected originating from within our galaxy, they would imply a threshold-violating interaction cross-section or a mechanism for evading hadronization. This study investigates whether neutrinos can resolve this paradox. Specifically, we calculate the probability that a high-energy proton survives travel to Earth without interacting, noting that even a minuscule interaction rate or detection efficiency among produced neutrinos can significantly lower the effective threshold. We also determine the observed atmospheric neutrino flux resulting from such interactions. These findings enable us to update constraints on the cross-section of new physics, the associated matter opacity, and the flux of interacting high-energy protons.

By integrating stress measurements with visual observations of various rough surfaces moving through dry liquid foams, we demonstrate the existence of three distinct friction regimes: slippage, stick-slip motion, and anchored soap films. Our stress data aligns with established models for the slippage and anchored regimes, while we introduce a leverage rule to characterize stresses during stick-slip events. Furthermore, we determine that the transition between stick-slip and anchored regimes is governed by a roughness factor, defined as the ratio of surface asperity size to the radius of curvature of the Plateau borders. Finally, within the slippage regime, we demonstrate that the magnitude of slippage is substantially determined by the surface's roughness. These findings offer a unifying framework for describing the interfacial behavior of dry foams across both smooth and rough surfaces. Documenting these complex interfacial dynamics under varying roughness conditions is essential for accurately addressing related phenomena in other two-phase systems.

We analyze both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, detailing the influence of membrane tension in each scenario. When the inner fluid is denser than the outer fluid, both systems display a centrifugally induced Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability that competes with restoring forces from curvature and tension, ultimately determining the finger scale. Numerical continuation methods are employed to calculate strongly nonlinear primary finger states up to self-contact, as well as secondary branches involving mixed modes and circumferentially localized folds, varying with rotation rate and external pressure. The analysis includes both reflection-symmetric and symmetry-broken chiral configurations, with results illustrated through bifurcation diagrams. Furthermore, the ratio of the system scale to the natural length scale is identified as the key factor governing the sequence of primary bifurcations from the unperturbed circular state, as well as the resulting solution profiles and the initiation of secondary bifurcations. The investigation concludes with the localization of resonant, randomly oriented primary finger states and the examination of the flow dynamics and membrane deformation in the resulting two-phase, rotating, radially unbounded, annular configuration. This work contributes to the nonrotating elasticity and interfacial instability literature by incorporating the effects of external pressure, density mismatches, and inextensibility. These findings may be relevant to the growing of patterned, radially symmetric, and rotationally asymmetric soft matter structures from cast, flat, two-fluid layers.
This paper investigates the Rayleigh-Taylor (RT) instability at the interface between two fluids under the influence of rotation and magnetic fields, utilizing Ginzburg-Landau equations. We derive the primary growth rate as a function of rotation and magnetic field strength for a single mode and explore the impact of varying rotation and magnetic field directions (parallel, anti-parallel, and perpendicular) on the growth rate and critical radius. The results indicate that rotation and magnetic fields can either amplify or suppress the RT instability depending on their relative orientations. In the presence of rotation and/or magnetic fields, the flow exhibits a pinched shape rather than the typical finger-like projection. Additionally, we analyze the influence of multiple modes on the instability. To validate our linear analysis, we perform numerical simulations for the governing equations using spectral methods. The simulation results align well with our linear predictions regarding the growth rate and interface shapes for both single and multi-mode scenarios. In these scenarios, the counts of initial and final microstates differ, preventing connection via unique Hamiltonian trajectories. This issue frequently arises when phase space volume changes and has not previously been examined using Hamiltonian trajectories capable of being inverted to create an identity mapping between microstates as Hamiltonian parameters vary. To address this challenge, we propose a specific technique, focusing on free expansion within an isolated system where the notion of dissipated work remains ambiguous. Our approach demonstrates thermodynamic consistency and offers significant utility for simulations. We provide justification that the dissipated quantity corresponds to the thermodynamic average of internal microwork performed by a microstate; this internal microwork differs from exchange microwork with the vacuum, which is zero. Furthermore, we establish that microwork remains nonnegative during free expansion—a notable finding, given that its sign is not fixed in general processes. We also establish a lower bound for microwork, showing it to be substantially higher than the first law energy term that is constant during free expansion. Additionally, we introduce an offset to the stochastic entropy production definition that ensures it adheres to a nonnegative constraint during free expansion. However, we observe that generating a target word relies not only on the source input but also heavily on previously generated target words, particularly distant ones that recurrent neural networks struggle to model effectively. To address this, we introduce a novel look-ahead attention mechanism designed to directly capture dependencies between target words. Additionally, we devise three integration patterns to incorporate this mechanism into conventional attention models. Experiments conducted on Chinese-to-English (NIST) and English-to-German (WMT) translation tasks demonstrate that our proposed look-ahead attention mechanism yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, the results indicate that incorporating look-ahead attention into simple feedforward neural networks can produce satisfactory translation quality, suggesting that the technique itself is highly effective and does not strictly depend on costly components. Finally, we present evidence that the method is efficient regarding both training time and inference speed on large-scale corpora. In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) we provide a theoretical analysis of language modeling to justify modeling dependencies between target words; (2) we design a flexible framework for integrating look-ahead attention with conventional models; and (3) we explore the effectiveness and efficiency of these models on large-scale translation datasets.
Attention mechanisms in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) have achieved success in improving translation quality, yet they focus exclusively on source sentences, ignoring the potential of introducing look-ahead attention among target words. On the theoretical front, we provide analysis to construct a framework for integrating look-ahead attention. To validate the model's effectiveness, we test it on two large-scale translation tasks: Chinese-to-English (NIST) and English-to-German (WMT). Our approach is also efficient in terms of training time and inference speed on these large corpora. These findings offer new insights into the application of attention mechanisms within NMT.
In this paper, we present an attentive neural translation model that generates each target word by attending to both the source sentence and the previously translated words. Applied to two machine translation tasks, our model achieves competitive performance with substantial improvements in handling long-distance dependencies compared to previous approaches.
Recent advancements in translation evaluation have enabled more accurate assessment of machine-generated output, facilitating better modeling of target-side dependencies in NMT. Leverlying these improvements, we introduce a novel neural mechanism that explicitly captures dependencies between target words. Our approach proves effective and efficient when applied to both training and inference in practical machine translation

Abramson and Parashar contend that a comparable divide exists between sophisticated computational technologies and increasingly demanding applications, necessitating a parallel field known as translational computer science. In this discipline, the intentional transition of research findings into large-scale practice becomes a primary research objective rather than a secondary consideration. Examining the evolution and deployment of grid computing from the mid-1990s through this lens reveals that a translational framework effectively elucidates both the technology's development and its impact on the broader technology enterprise, offering a framework that can be applied to other systems and applications. Furthermore, the authors highlight the significant potential of translational computer science to enhance the efficacy and efficiency of the COVID-19 response.

Building on the work of Abramson and Parashar, this paper extends the translational computer science framework to the acquisition and utilization of open-source AI models for pandemic-related challenges. We illustrate this with a case study of the TransfORMCovid project, which adapted and deployed the COVIDNet image segmentation model to identify face masks in images for remote mask-wearing monitoring. Our findings demonstrate that translational computer science can significantly contribute to solving real-world problems with immediate relevance to society during crises.

El trabajo de Abramson y Parashar sobre el computer science translacional se expande en este manuscrito para abordar problemas de pandemia, específicamente la detección remota del uso de mascarillas con el fin de proteger la salud pública. Se documentan los desafíos técnicos enfrentados al utilizar una red neuronal convolucional pre-entrenada (ResNet-50) para crear una solución de código abierto capaz de segmentar imágenes de caras con uso de mascarilla. El título internacional de este trabajo es: The Translational Computer Science of Repurposing Open-Source AI Models for Remote Mask-Wearing Detection.

We introduce a novel framework employing the $f(R, T)$ formalism, where the stress energy tensor is raised to the power of two. We define the general form of the stress energy tensor such that the resulting $f(R, T^2)$ theory can mimic the essential characteristics of the $\Lambda$CDM model. We derive the field equations and employ the Lie symmetry method to obtain exact solutions for a plane symmetric metric. We demonstrate that the general solution encompasses the $\Lambda$CDM model as a particular case and that the model can be reformulated in terms of the $\Lambda$CDM form. We investigate the cosmological implications of the general solution by examining the evolution of the universe through the deceleration parameter, the effective equation of state of dark energy, the volume of the universe, and the thermodynamic behavior of the matter

Although many educational systems inadvertently diminish curiosity by prioritizing test preparation, educators are increasingly focused on methods to stimulate it, recognizing the necessity of lifelong learning and reskilling in the future. Despite this, the influence of peers in triggering curiosity remains underexplored. This study introduces a novel theoretical framework offering an integrated socio-cognitive perspective that links observable peer behaviors to internal curiosity states. We distinguish between individual and interpersonal functions that drive curiosity, along with the multimodal behaviors that fulfill them. Using a longitudinal latent variable modeling approach, we validated the framework, confirming that both individual and interpersonal functions positively predict curiosity, with interpersonal factors exerting a notably stronger impact. Furthermore, we identified key behavioral manifestations of these functions through data-driven analysis. We have developed specific strategies and tactics based on this framework, which can be integrated into learning technologies to signal, inspire, and support curiosity. This research advances the design of systems capable of detecting and evoking real-time curiosity within social learning environments, contributing to more comprehensive multimodal learning analytics. The principles established here are broadly applicable for enhancing computer support for various other metacognitive and socio-emotional competencies.

While numerous Gaussian process models exist for Euclidean input spaces, options for undirected graph inputs are significantly more restricted. This study utilizes the stochastic partial differential equation formulation of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes—a popular model in Euclidean contexts—to develop their corresponding analogs for undirected graphs. We demonstrate that these graph-based processes retain key advantageous properties found in their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts and introduce methods for training graphs via kernel conditional Gaussian sampling. Consequently, our graph conditional processes can be trained independently and applied to new, unseen graphs, offering a robust framework for learning functions across combined Euclidean and graph domains or exclusively over graph structures. This technique holds particular promise for enhancing functions that map to high-variance outputs, such as regression, ranking, and resource allocation, as well as for estimating uncertain quantities like disease spread or climate patterns. The code supporting our findings is available at https://github.com/brian-ng/Graph-Conditional-Gaussian-Processes.
Gaussian processes are potent nonparametric models used for learning unknown functions when data is limited. Although various Gaussian process models and kernels exist for Euclidean and Riemannian spaces, there is a notable absence of equivalent models for undirected graphs. We define such processes using a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) formulation that establishes correlations between data points based on their proximity within a common network. This graph-based formulation is computationally efficient, closely approximating the standard Mat\'ern Gaussian process used in Euclidean and Riemannian settings while enabling training on large datasets. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that these graph processes can be trained in isolation and then extended to learn functions on graphs with new, previously unseen nodes. This capability facilitates learning functions across datasets that combine both Euclidean and graph data. Our implementation is provided at https://github.com/brian-ng/Graph-Conditional-Gaussian-Processes.
While powerful models exist for predicting functions on Euclidean and Riemannian spaces, there remains a lack of equivalent frameworks for finite, undirected graphs. This paper introduces graph conditional Gaussian processes, which enable the learning of functions defined on graphs, including those with missing nodes or entirely new datasets. These graph processes can be trained separately and subsequently applied to functions on existing graphs with newly added nodes or to hybrid functions that integrate both graph and Euclidean data. Our GitHub repository is located at https://github.com/brian-ng/Graph-Conditional-Gaussian-Processes.

Existing sensing methods, which rely on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data from commuters (such as Google Maps), suffer from significant drawbacks, including high costs, restricted coverage, and low reliability due to insufficient user participation. This study explores an innovative drive-by sensing approach that utilizes large-scale ridesourcing vehicles (RVs) to monitor and infer the status of urban road networks. By analyzing the performance of the RV fleet, we evaluate metrics such as the unique number of road segments visited, sensing reliability derived from repeated visits, and the implicit information inferable from explicit data combined with network topology. We introduce an optimal rerouting model designed to simultaneously maximize both sensing coverage and reliability within a defined time horizon. Additionally, we developed an application on a 4,300-square-mile network in Northern California to demonstrate the potential of this cost-effective, scalable, and privacy-preserving sensing technique for implicitly deriving road statuses, such as travel times, from user-generated data. Our findings indicate that a small proportion of the RV fleet can visit up to 75% of the road network, with at least 50% of these segments being traversed repeatedly. Furthermore, this approach can implicitly infer up to 92.5% of the road network's status, with at least 97.5% of the coverage occurring on high-degree roads. This study confirms that the ridesourcing vehicle framework effectively enhances urban road sensing coverage while remaining privacy-conscious. The open-source code for this study is available at GitHub.com. The corresponding author can be reached at zhao@eecs.berkeley.edu.

Recently, there has been a growing interest in designing incentive mechanisms to motivate commuters to voluntarily participate in traffic sensing activities. We formulate the maximum constrained sensing coverage problem for a fleet of taxis over a multi-day horizon. The problem aims to uniquely sense all road segments (where no two routes share the same set of segments) within a specific time window while minimizing the total cost, which includes both the extra distances traveled and the monetary incentives offered to the drivers. We prove that the general version of this problem is NP-hard and present a heuristic algorithm to address it on real-world road networks. Our experiments, conducted on networks in California (USA) and Shanghai (China), shows that our algorithm can achieve near-optimal coverage (exceeding 99%) with at least 90% of the routes sensed uniquely. Utilizing low-energy effective field theories (EFTs) to model general neutrino interactions and Dirac fermion DM coupled to charm quarks, we conduct likelihood fits for individual neutrino and DM operators featuring distinct Lorentz structures and photon spectra for the process $J/\psi\to \gamma+{\rm invisible}$. We derive limits on decay branching fractions across various neutrino and DM scenarios, converting these into lower bounds on new energy scales. The strongest constraints on the energy scale for neutrino and DM EFTs are found to be 12.8 GeV and 11.6 GeV, respectively. Additionally, the purely invisible decay $J/\psi\to {\rm invisible}$ offers complementary constraints on effective operators, with energy scale bounds exceeding 100 GeV for dipole operators. We also determine limits on the DM-nucleon scattering cross section based on $J/\psi$ data. These invisible decay measurements are sensitive to light DM masses that remain unprobed by current direct detection experiments. Furthermore, the future Super Tau Charm Factory is projected to improve these limits by two orders of magnitude after a one-year run. We have established fit results for diverse EFTs and prepared the necessary data for experimental physicists to conduct similar analyses on other EFTs using the measured $J/\psi$ photon spectra.

The search for dark matter (DM) has become increasingly precise, yet the parameter space of DM interacting via forces with mediators lighter than approximately 50 MeV remains largely unexplored. This region remains viable despite recent constraints from DM direct detection experiments and the Planck satellite's analysis of cosmic microwave background data. As the lightest particle, DM contributes to the energy content of the universe; however, because its annihilation cross section is suppressed by $1/v^4$, only DM with a mass below roughly 5 MeV can account for the observed dark matter density through thermal production. For heavier DM, alternative mechanisms such as the misalignment effect, cosmological production, or decay from heavier states are proposed. While many of these alternatives lack the extensive experimental support of thermal production, they remain unruled out. Consequently, it is crucial to explore additional constraints on light DM using all available data. We derive the order conditions for these methods, specifically targeting order $p$ with stage order $q=p$, and provide explicit examples achieving up to fourth-order accuracy. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed methods in addressing nonstiff problems and validate their theoretical convergence orders. The study concludes by confirming the applicability of the fourth-order variable stepsize SGLM for solving nonlinear Volterra integral equations of the second kind. The appendix contains the proof for the convergence of the fourth-order variable stepsize method when applied to nonlinear Volterra integral equations of the second kind.
This paper introduces implicit general linear methods (GLMs) designed for resolving second kind Volterra integral equations (VIEs). Initially, the fundamental characteristics of these new schemes are examined to establish their order of convergence when applied to the equivalent Volterra integral system (VIS) originating from a given Volterra integral equation. Although the primary focus of this study is on GLMs adhering to the Adams structure, the presented findings remain valid for a broader category of GLMs not necessarily conforming to the Adams structure. Furthermore, this research extends prior implicit GLM developments for VIEs, which were constrained to order $p \le 2$, by demonstrating the feasibility of constructing admissible orders up to $p=5$. To facilitate this advancement, an algorithm is proposed to compute the stability function associated with the $p$-stage, order $p$ GLM-Runge Kutta (LRM) subset of a specific implicit GLM family. Additionally, it is demonstrated that for any admissible order $p$ and any specific method within a selected GLM family, there exists an associated LRM of order $p$ that can be applied to the fundamental integral equations of the VIS. A numerical experiment confirms the theoretical order of convergence for a second kind VIE with a smooth kernel using the new implicit GLMs and their associated LRMs. Finally, the paper notes that while the primary objective was not to develop efficient methods for solving VIEs, the observed behavior in the experimental section suggests that greater efficiency could be attained if the GLMs were designed

MFSSA), a functional extension of Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (MSSA) designed for various dimensional domains. We present the comprehensive theoretical foundations underpinning the functional extension of MSSA filters, alongside their corresponding functional counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of this novel method through a simulation study and a real-world empirical application. The findings indicate that Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Analysis serves as a robust tool for both exploratory research and solving practical problems within functional data analysis. In this paper's supplementary materials, we provide an R-package that facilitates the calculation of MFSSA.
This research aims to assess the order and parity estimation accuracy of a functional waveform using the auto-function clique test. The proposed method relies on estimating the Hurvich parameter $d$ via the lof method, with estimations for parabolic, sinusoidal, and mixed function shapes occurring in subsequent steps. Additionally, the study incorporates a break test to identify functional changepoints and locates them temporally. An extensive simulation was conducted to validate the method's effectiveness. The findings indicate that the Auto-Function Clique Test is a robust technique for analyzing functions and their derivatives. The accompanying RP package enables users to perform auto-function clique testing, estimate behavior order and parity, and detect changepoints for functions.
Functional data often exhibit periodicity, and this work utilizes a periodic functional autoregressive model of order $p$, denoted as PERFAR($p$), for changepoint estimation. We employ a Bayesian approach, specifically the Gibbs sampler, to simultaneously and recursively estimate the number of changepoints, their locations, and the PERFAR($p$) model parameters. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, both simulation studies and an empirical example are presented. Simulations show that the proposed technique outperforms existing methods, while the empirical application concerns the sudden shifts in daily minimum air temperatures across 260 Iranian stations over the past few decades. The functional analysis package is also available for users to apply this methodology.
Functional change point analysis remains a critical area of ongoing research, with functional data frequently displaying periodic patterns. This paper introduces a new functional time series model capable of capturing such periodicity and estimating change points, offering higher precision than current methodologies. The proposed method proceeds in two stages: first, fitting a periodic functional time series model to the data, and second, utilizing the resulting one-step-ahead prediction errors to estimate change points using a specific functional test. The simulation study and real data application both confirm the superior performance of the proposed approach. Additionally

systems are widely deployed by governments and testing agencies to assess millions of candidates on high-stakes matters, including university admissions and visa eligibility. Despite this prevalence, there is a scarcity of research dedicated to interpreting the opaque nature of these deep-learning algorithms. Existing studies suggest that such scoring models are easily manipulable. This paper investigates the causes of their surprising adversarial brittleness. Leveraging recent interpretability advancements, we examine the relative importance of features like coherence, content, vocabulary, and relevance in automated scoring. We analyze the phenomena of oversensitivity (where minor input changes cause significant score fluctuations) and overstability (where major input changes yield minimal score shifts). Our findings reveal that, despite being trained as "end-to-end" models with rich contextual embeddings like BERT, AES models function similarly to bag-of-words models. A few isolated words often dictate the final score without necessitating context, rendering the models largely overstable. This contrasts sharply with recent probing studies on pre-trained language models, which demonstrate their ability to encode complex linguistic features such as morphology and parts of speech. Furthermore, we observe that these models have internalized dataset biases, leading to oversensitivity. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose detection-based protection models capable of identifying samples exhibiting oversensitivity and overstability while maintaining high accuracy. Our results show that these models can successfully detect anomalous attribution patterns and flag adversarial inputs. Additionally, we note that current AES models fail to score multilingual inputs for which they were not trained. We outline strategies to incorporate multilingual data during training to enhance the model's adaptability to multiple languages. We release the code, datasets, and models used in this study as open-source resources.

The objective of automatic essay scoring models trained via attention mechanisms is to assess student-written responses to prompts using a predefined rubric. Although prior research has attempted to uncover the black-box nature of scoring models, the attention weights they learn are often misleading. This paper introduces an adversarial attack method that exploits these deceptive attention patterns. The attack is particularly effective against models employing attention mechanisms, such as Google's T5, Microsoft's BART, and an end-to-end linear model, achieving a success rate that is ten times higher than when utilizing other adversarial techniques.

—defined as the likelihood that the fraction of time up to $t$ during which a random walk $S$ with i.i.d. zero-mean increments (taking finitely many values) remains non-negative exceeds $x$ for all $s \in [1,t]$—decays according to the power law $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$. In this expression, $\phi(x,b) = \mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$, where the parameter $\kappa(x,b)$ is given by $\frac{\sqrt{1-x} b - \sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x} b + \sqrt{1+x}}$. The coefficient $b=b_S \geq 0$ quantifies the asymptotic asymmetry between positive and negative excursions of the walk, taking the value $b_s=1$ when the increments are symmetric. Specifically, we examine random walks whose moment $k$-th moments of $|S_1|$ exist for $k < 2$ but not for $k+0.01$, analyzing four distinct scenarios based on whether the distribution is symmetric or asymmetric. Our findings demonstrate that the exponent $\phi(x,b)$ applies universally to the tail behavior of $p(t,x)$, with the asymptotic dynamics differing among the four cases. Furthermore, for the asymmetric walk, the limiting distribution of $S_t/t$ is non-degenerate only within the interval $(-1,1)$. The results also clarify the behavior of the conditioned walk at the critical threshold $\pm t$. Notably, when $x=1$, the exponent $\phi(1,b)$ simplifies to $1/2$ regardless of the asymmetry parameter $b$. These discoveries have significant implications for the asymptotic fluctuations of the area under the scaling limit of the fraction of time a random walk remains positive.

(IShTAR) serves as a specialized facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany, designed to study the interaction between ICRF waves and plasma. A plasma source, measuring 1.5 meters in length and 2.8 meters in diameter, generates and condition the plasma before it enters the main chamber, where it reaches a quasi-magnetic field created by four magnetic coils. This source, which was recently upgraded, includes ten ion extraction probes (IEPs) strategically distributed along the antenna path. These probes are customized for in-situ measurement of ion cyclotron resonance (ICR) frequency and ion saturation current. The upgrades enabled precise, location-varied ICR frequency scans under differing plasma conditions. By analyzing data from these IEPs, researchers can investigate resonant heating effects, such as ion temperature rise due to cyclonic energy deposition. Furthermore, the facility's design allows for complex plasma configurations, making it well-suited to model specific scenarios from fusion reactors like ITER or DEMO, where ion heating via ICRF is a critical operation. The upgraded source enhances the realism of these simulations and facilitates detailed examination of associated phenomena, including impurity ion behavior. The proposed configuration of ICRF antenna and plasma source is distinct from that of the operational system, specifically tailored for these measurement objectives. Additionally, potential applications extend to other fusion facilities, such as ADS-2 at IPP, where the antenna and source are separated, and TCSO at IAEA-CNPT in Pakistan, featuring a separate plasma source.
Introduction: Cyclotron resonance heating is employed to elevate ion temperatures within a plasma plasmaHeating at the ion cyclotron frequency ($\omega_{ci}$) and its harmonic (usually the first) is utilized to raise ion temperatures in magnetic confinement fusion reactors, including the ITER demo reactor. In these systems, electrons and ions are confined within strong magnetic fields, and their temperature difference drives an unfavorable energy transfer from ions to electrons, reducing plasma efficiency for nuclear fusion. ICRF heating helps mitigate this by equalizing electron and ion temperatures. Additionally, in inertial confinement fusion, raising ion temperature helps create a monotonically decreasing ion velocity distribution, thereby suppressing the pinching effect on impurities. The IShTAR facility is designed to study ion heating and related phenomena. To investigate how impurities behave inside fusion reactors, it is essential to simulate real-world plasma conditions; consequently, the facility features a separate plasma source and antenna. To simulate their inhibitory effects, this study introduces a model describing how entomopathogenic nematodes not only kill target insects but also suppress their birth rates. By continuously releasing these nematodes, the model demonstrates the ability to restrict or eradicate pest populations. Through an analysis of the equilibrium stability and the stability of Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions, the optimal strategy for pest control is identified. These findings are supported by illustrative examples and numerical simulations. Furthermore, the paper concludes by addressing potential extensions of the model. In formulating the pest control strategy, the dynamics of pest inhibition were explored using various biological control agents. While plant viruses and entomopathogenic nematodes were previously examined, this work focuses on infected predator insects. Specifically, we investigate a system where infected predators exert pressure on prey populations. A core assumption is that these infected predators, while effective hunters, are also vulnerable to pests and may be entomopathogenic to them. To model this dual dynamic, we employ an SIR framework for infected predators and incorporate a term representing the death of these predators due to entomopathogenic effects. The outcomes of this approach align with those achieved using entomopathogenic nematodes. Finally, the findings regarding periodic solutions, bifurcations, and pest control strategies derived in this paper can be applied to designs involving infected predator insects.

Nucleus segmentation technology is commonly employed to automate these tasks; however, training robust segmentation models remains challenging due to issues like nucleus adhesion, stacking, and excessive background fusion. Although recent approaches based on point annotation have significantly enhanced model performance, they still require experienced pathologists to provide the necessary annotations. To leverage the benefits of point-annotation-based methods while reducing manual workload and improving the efficiency and accuracy of cancer diagnosis, an automatic nucleus detection algorithm is needed to efficiently locate nuclei and extract valuable information from pathological images. This paper introduces a W-shaped network for automatic nucleus detection. Unlike traditional U-Net-based methods that directly map pathology images to target masks, our approach decomposes the detection task into two sub-tasks: first mapping the original image to a binary mask, and then mapping that binary mask to a density mask. This task splitting significantly reduces complexity and enhances the network's overall performance. Furthermore, we introduced several auxiliary structures to further optimize the W-shaped network's effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance across various metrics compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. By enabling the extraction of quantitative information from pathological images, our proposed technique can improve the efficiency and accuracy of cancer diagnosis.

Pathology images are essential for diagnosing and treating cancer. Deep learning-based segmentation models can automate tasks such as cell detection and counting, thereby reducing pathologists' workload. However, the high quality of these images and the complexity of the segmentation task have led to saturation in the conventional SU-based modeling approaches. Recently, density mapping has emerged as a successful technique for cancer cell detection; however, it requires precise point annotations from professional pathologists, a process that is both time-consuming and labor-intensive. To effectively utilize the advantages of density mapping without the burden of manual annotation, this study proposes an automatic nucleus detection algorithm. Our method maps pathological images to density maps directly. To achieve this, we developed two innovative mapping subtasks in sequence: su-based mapping followed by density mapping. To support this dual-task framework, we designed a novel W-shaped network architecture. To further optimize the mapping from binary mask to density mask, we incorporated three auxiliary structures to convert the single-channel binary mask into a multi-channel image before processing it through the secondary network. Extensive experiments indicate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art algorithms. The proposed method not only reduces the effort required to obtain point annotations but also delivers higher segmentation quality, offering significant potential for cancer diagnosis and

ean local field where the characteristic is not $2$, and let $G$ denote either an odd special orthogonal group ${\rm SO}_{2r+1}(F)$ or a symplectic group ${\rm Sp}_{2r}(F)$. This paper proves the local converse theorem for $G$: specifically, if two irreducible admissible generic representations of $G$ share the same central character and yield identical local gamma factors (twisted by all irreducible supercuspidal representations of ${\rm GL}_n(F)$ for $1 \leq n \leq r$ with a fixed additive character), then the two representations are isomorphic. By applying the theory of partial Bessel functions developed by Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai alongside the classification of irreducible generic representations, we surpass the rank limitation of $n \leq 2r-1$ previously established by Jiang and Soudry. Furthermore, we generalize Q. Zhang's findings, which were restricted to characteristic $0$, to include all supercuspidal representations. The results also extend to the case where the characteristic of $F$ is $2$. As in the work of Jiang and Souddry, the isomorphism between the test functions and associated gamma factors remains valid. Consequently, the local converse theorem remains established for generic representations across all primes. Additionally, the discussion in the final section of this paper demonstrates that the converse theorem holds for all irreducible admissible representations of ${\rm Sp}_{2r}(F)$ and ${\rm SO}_{2r+1}(F)$, provided the irreducible gamma factors are taken against all irreducible L-parameter representations (of any group) whose L-parameters do not lie on the wall. To fully resolve the problem for ${\rm Sp}_{2r}(F)$ and ${\rm SO}_{2r+1}(F)$ without character or characteristic assumptions, it suffices to prove the irreducibility of certain L-parameters for the generic case. The current paper addresses this final step. Isomorphic test functions between Jaccard-Lapid representations can be constructed, and the corresponding arguments remain applicable. Thus, the proof for the generic case carries over to the irreducible case. The only distinction is that the L-parameters for generic representations can be defined over the ring of integers of a finite extension within the completion of the maximal unramified extension of $F$. This observation allows us to directly import the necessary arguments to finalize the proof.

death, plays a significant role in the cytokine storm observed in severe COVID-19 cases. This process is driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome, which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2. Certain anti-inflammatory medications have the potential to suppress inflammasome assembly and, consequently, pyroptosis. This study introduces a single-cell mathematical model, structured as a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs), to simulate NLRP3 inflammasome formation, pyroptotic death, and the impact of interventions that block inflammasome development. Our findings indicate that anti-inflammatory drugs can postpone inflammasome formation, potentially shifting cell death from the inflammatory pyroptosis pathway to non-inflammatory modes like apoptosis. In partnership with a multidisciplinary group studying within-host COVID-19 dynamics, this model is being integrated into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator. This paper offers an overview of that simulator and emphasizes the cellular-level effects of pyroptosis. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how the simulator can model pyroptosis, apoptosis, and the efficacy of anti-inflammasome therapies. Both our theoretical model results and the capabilities of the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator are accessible on a public website. Finally, we highlight how the simulator can support the design of future anti-inflammasome treatments.

In many forms of cell death, including apoptosis and pyroptosis, the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane becomes enriched with phosphatidylserine. This redistribution can be visualized using flow cytometry, fluorescence microscopy, or single-cell mathematical models. This work builds upon the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, a virtual within-host platform for testing anti-inflammasome therapies. The simulator comprises three linked models: a genetic model for inflammasome components, a morphological model for inflammasome structure, and the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator for combining these aspects while incorporating other cell death forms, cell types, and cytokines. We illustrate how changes in the simulator's parameters alter the amount of phosphatidylserine exposed on the cell surface and the resulting cell behavior. Additionally, we show how the simulator can process flow cytometry data to estimate the potency of pyroptosis-suppressing medications. Consequently, this platform enables the creation of patient-specific virtual models to assess the effectiveness of anti-inflammasome drugs.

We provide a formalization of these exogenous components and define the conditions allowing an MDP with exogenous states to be split into an exogenous Markov Reward Process (handling only exogenous states and rewards) and an endogenous Markov Decision Process (defined solely by endogenous rewards). Furthermore, we establish a variance-covariance criterion that accelerates Monte Carlo policy evaluation on the endogenous MDP relative to using the complete MDP, with similar performance gains expected across other RL algorithms. We introduce a unifying framework that formulates option discovery as multi-task reinforcement learning, enabling the discovery of options from transient goals rather than rewarding tasks. This framework provides a theoretical justification for why options are beneficial when goals are temporary and offers a new method for their discovery. We evaluate the approach on both simulated environments and a real-world robot navigation task. The proposed method not only facilitates option discovery through transient goals but also enhances performance compared to techniques relying on reward matching, particularly in terms of sample efficiency and generalization. Furthermore, the system can discover hierarchical abstractions without requiring hand-crafted features, rewards, or matching multiple components of the state and reward vectors simultaneously. These findings offer a solution for robust option discovery in dynamic settings where tasks are incomplete, such as when an agent can only observe partial components of the goal. The methodology is applicable to biological contexts, helping explain how brains may discover behavioral options using transient goals, and inspires new techniques for robotic task decomposition.

We address the task of super-resolution (SR) in a fully unsupervised manner, eliminating the need for low-resolution training data. The core of our method is a multi-scale alternating cycle-consistency framework consisting of two generators and an identity generator. The alternating cycle-consistency constraint enables cross-scale and cross-domain image reconstruction, facilitating SR from lower-resolution inputs. Specifically, we enforce consistency between the upsampled low-resolution input and the downsized output of the SR image, and vice versa, across multiple scales to capture both fine and coarse image details. The dual generators handle forward and inverse translation tasks, while the identity generator manages cases where input and target domains are identical. Because this framework relies on cycle-consistency rather than paired data, it is entirely unsupervised. The alternating multi-scale design produces significantly sharper images compared to conventional single-scale cycleGANs. On the Celeba dataset, our method achieved an PSNR of 32.67 dB, using 2.5 times fewer parameters than the existing state-of-the-art cycleGAN-based cycle-UNet.

Model-based reinforcement learning achieves sample efficiency by utilizing a dynamics model of the environment. While recent model-free multi-task agents benefit from a shared policy network that captures task similarities, we investigate if a shared dynamics model offers comparable advantages. Our results indicate that a single dynamics model trained across multiple tasks causes the agent to become confused by similar but distinct transition distributions, resulting in subpar performance. We address this issue by designing a structured, task-specific component within the dynamics network. This approach yields significant performance improvements with no additional parameter overhead compared to a monolithic shared model. We test both our challenge and solution on both a simple gridworld and a more complex VizDoom multi-task learning setting.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents can learn multiple similar tasks simultaneously or sequentially, often achieving better generalization when these tasks are comparable. We examine if a single dynamics model can effectively capture the environment's dynamics across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that such a shared model can lead to degraded performance. To resolve this, we suggest training a task-specific component alongside the shared one, a strategy that enhances performance without adding parameter complexity. We validate these results in both a basic gridworld and a more demanding VizDoom multi-task learning scenario.

Although high atmospheric absorption typically limits THz links to short ranges, multi-hop directional transmissions can extend coverage. However, traditional beam training methods, including exhaustive searches or fixed-level hierarchical approaches, incur significant time overhead when applied to multi-hop THz scenarios. To overcome this, the paper introduces a novel hierarchical beam training scheme featuring dynamic training levels to enhance multi-hop THz link performance. Specifically, an optimization problem is defined to maximize the overall spectral efficiency by dynamically and jointly determining the number of beam training levels for each single-hop segment. Addressing uncertainties such as unknown channel state information, noise, and path loss, the authors develop a reinforcement learning solution utilizing multi-armed bandits (MAB). Simulations demonstrate the scheme's rapid convergence under random channel conditions and noise. Multi-hop directional communication can resolve this by establishing separate directional links for each hop, allowing advanced beam training protocols suitable for single-hop THz communications to be applied. This paper presents an analysis of 34 years of Arecibo data regarding PSR B1133+16, yielding high-quality dynamic spectra and their corresponding scintillation arcs generated by screens along the line of sight. We identified six distinct screens responsible for these long-lasting arcs. Assuming the screens remained relatively stable over this period, we modeled variations in arc curvature across Earth's orbit to determine the position, orientation, and velocity of five of the six screens. Our most precise distance measurement places one screen at $5.46^{+0.54}_{-0.59}$ pc from Earth, which we associate with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble. Additionally, we determined that another screen moved at a perpendicular velocity of $10.6^{+0.6}_{-0.7}$ pc Myr$^{-1}$, likely associated with the shock of a supersonic stellar wind. For the remaining screen, we measured an arc curvature variation of $0.20^{+0.07}_{-0.08}$ ly$^{-1}$ Myr$^{-1}$, but our screen's distance exceeds the maximum velocity permissible if the arc variation is attributed to the recoil from a supernova remnant. We also developed concise models for two screens based on the assumption that their arc variation stems from Earth's orbital motion around the Sun. Finally, we derived general formulae for the distance and orientation of screens using arc curvature variations, which can be applied to assess the supernova recoil hypothesis for screens observed in other systems. In conclusion, these findings support the hypothesis that at least some interstellar scattering screens arise from supersonic stellar winds.

This study concentrates on temperate worlds possessing massive hydrogen-dominated atmospheres, investigating the chemical reactions and transport mechanisms triggered by the photodissociation of H2O, CH4, NH3, and H2S. Using K2-18 b, PH2 b, and Kepler-167 e as case studies for temperate or cold planets orbiting M and G/K stars, we observe that ammonia (NH3) is likely depleted by photodissociation down to the cloud layer on planets around G/K stars, whereas it remains intact in the mid-atmosphere of those around M stars. A recurring feature among temperate planets is that ammonia photodissociation in the presence of methane produces hydrogen cyanide (HCN) as the primary photochemical byproduct. Additionally, the combined photodissociation of methane and water yields carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO2), while hydrocarbon synthesis is inhibited. Temperate planets exhibiting super-solar atmospheric metallicity and significant internal heat may harbor extra CO and CO2 from their interiors, resulting in reduced NH3 and consequently lower HCN levels. Our models for K2-18 b successfully replicate the transmission spectrum observed by Hubble and suggest that future observations within the 0.5–5.0 µm range could offer the sensitivity to detect multiple chemical species indicative of advanced photochemistry. Our simulations for PH2 b align with the 2.15 µm feature detected by Hubble, predicting that the atmospheric composition of such planets can be ascertained through near-infrared transmission spectroscopy. However, the predictions for Kepler-167 e contradict the direct imaging spectrum derived from Maris for a high-gravity case, though they match the transmission spectrum reported by exoplanet-imaging-methods. Shifting from thermal to photochemical regimes alters the anticipated atmospheric composition of temperate exoplanets, meaning that the atmospheric profile inferred from transmission spectroscopy may differ substantially from that determined via direct spectroscopy. While applicable across all frequencies $\omega$, the method demonstrates particular efficiency in high-frequency scenarios. A critical component is a front-tracking mesh adaptation algorithm employed in stage \emph{ii)}. By leveraging the localized nature of the wave front, this strategy significantly reduces the dependency of the required degrees of freedom on the frequency $\omega$ to achieve a specified accuracy. To illustrate these gains, we present an academic benchmark evaluating the performance of the three computational phases across a range of frequencies. While end-to-end architectures aim to eliminate this by utilizing a single system, they are hindered by a lack of training data. This study investigates zero-shot translation, a method that allows translation between unseen language pairs without requiring specific end-to-end ST data. Although effective in multilingual machine translation, zero-shot capabilities remain unexplored in the speech domain. Our approach constructs models trained exclusively on ASR and MT tasks that perform ST during inference. A primary obstacle is the significant disparity between audio and text representations, causing the models to learn these tasks differently and leading to incorrect language outputs in zero-shot scenarios. To address this, we incorporate additional training data and an auxiliary loss function designed to minimize the gap between text and audio representations. Experimental results indicate that these methods are promising for zero-shot ST. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed approaches are feasible and beneficial for low-resource many-language settings, achieving improvements of up to +3.7 BLEU points. Finally, we prove that incorporating auxiliary loss functions is particularly advantageous when end-to-end ST data is scarce, yielding gains of up to +5.2 BLEU points.

We determine that spherical multipoles are most effective for modeling the scattering of electromagnetic radiation, a finding demonstrated using an amorphous silicon sphere. Subsequently, these multipoles are applied to compute the optical forces exerted on semiconductor, dielectric, and metallic particles across a broad spectrum of wavelengths, spanning from the dipolar to the Mie regimes. Results indicate that irreducible multipoles are preferable when the particle diameter is much larger or much smaller than the wavelength, whereas spherical multipoles are superior for particle sizes comparable to the wavelength. These multipoles will serve as the foundation for developing an efficient analytical approach to compute optical forces on arbitrary particles within the framework of the Mie series expansion. This research contributes to optical manipulation, atomic physics, and related disciplines, offering an exact solution for optical forcing suitable for use with particles of any size, shape, or material composition. The findings are expected to support optical applications such as sorting, trapping, and moving micro- and nano-objects, as well as progress in optical tweezers, photovoltaics, and photonic crystals. The presented multipoles are constructed to satisfy optical reciprocity conditions.
This study introduces a straightforward analytical model to predict the output voltage of an receiving antenna placed within the near field of a magnetron, accounting for variations in antenna position, distance from the source, and polarization. Validated experimentally using a 2.45 GHz magnetron, the model correlates well with observed data across frequencies, distances, and orientations. The article further examines how antenna placement relative to the magnetron influences both output voltage and internal heating effects, ultimately proposing safe operating distances for microwave packaging that protect the antenna from excessive heating.

The tool incorporates various statistical techniques, including standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA), elastic maps (a non-linear PCA variant), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), multilinear regression, K-Means clustering, and a decision tree algorithm variant. Featuring intuitive interfaces for customizing data point attributes (size, shape, color) and a rapid 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables users to build interactive 3D scenes representing data within multidimensional space. This allows for efficient and insightful statistical analysis, ranging from fundamental to sophisticated methods. The utility was developed using the open-source web framework jQuery and can be deployed on any web server, requiring only a modern browser for use. A web-based interface at https://expert.bu.edu allows users to explore its functionality, with a server-side version available for integration into specialized scientific computing environments. The platform supports automated high-throughput analysis, benefiting fields such as image analysis in biological and biomedical research.

Although numerous standalone tools and cloud-based services exist for statistical analysis and visualization, many lack user-friendly interfaces, rely on complex installations, fail to generate interactive views, or are restricted to specific datasets and analyses.

ViDaExpert addresses these shortcomings by offering:
- A straightforward interface for importing data;
- A robust suite of multivariate analysis methods;
- An efficient interactive 3D renderer;
- Utility for programmatically integrate into high-throughput workflows.

The resulting applications include a standalone version (available at https://github.com/alexeivida/ViDaExpert) suitable for analyzing up to a few thousand objects, an optimized variant designed for datasets containing up to several hundred thousand objects, and a high-throughput version tailored for automated analysis and visualization.

The name ViDaExpert is a pun on Microsoft's AI chatbot "Xbox Expert," derived from "life" (vida in Spanish/Portuguese) and "masterpiece" (maestro in Spanish).

The platform is accessible via a public interface at https://expert.bu.edu, an optimized configuration at https://expert.bu.edu/opt, and a high-throughput setup at https://expert.bu.edu/ht. Additionally, source code can be downloaded from https://github.com/alexeivida/ViDaExpert.

Complex geometries usually necessitate unstructured mesh discretization, making direct potential evaluation via quadrature computationally expensive. This paper introduces a straightforward, high-order algorithm for calculating Newtonian potentials by leveraging Green's third identity to convert volume integrals into boundary integrals, which are then processed using the Helsing-Ojala method. Consequently, the time required for traditionally costly near-field and self-interaction calculations on unstructured meshes becomes comparable to that of far-field interactions computed via the Fast Multipole Method (FMM). A central component of this algorithm is the high-order 2-D monomial approximation of functions across the elements of unstructured meshes; the performance of the overall algorithm is directly influenced by the efficiency of this local function approximation. Numerical test cases demonstrate that this monomial approximation is both accurate and can be computed very efficiently using precomputed multivariate Chebyshev polynomials. These findings provide a robust foundation for developing a universal algorithm for Newtonian potential evaluation that utilizes high-order FMMs, high-order local approximations, and efficient near-field/calculation kernel evaluation for solving 2-D boundary and volume integral equations accelerated by high-order fast multipole methods. Notably, this algorithm is fully universal, requiring no special handling for self-interactions or near-field interactions.

The solution to an interior Dirichlet boundary value problem for the Laplace equation can be expressed as a single-layer integral. This study employs the boundary element method (BEM) combined with the fast multipole method (FMM) to solve such problems on unstructured meshes, specifically utilizing the high-order FMM variant developed by Jensen et al. It further calculates Newtonian potentials required for the integral evaluation using the universal algorithm presented by Hansbo & Peterseim. The results confirm the accuracy and efficiency of the combined high-order BEM and high-order FMM for these computations.

For time-harmonic acoustic scattering in an unbounded 2D space with a simply connected obstacle, the sound pressure satisfies the Helmholtz equation. The integral equation formulation replaces the standard Newtonian potential with the fundamental solution to this equation. This research accurately computes the fundamental solution to the Helmholtz equation via an integral over a circle centered at the field point, employing the same high-order universal algorithm described in this paper.
